div.head: Moan!.
div.p: Moan!.

A VISIT FROM THE SEA. Far from the loud sea beaches, Where he goes fishing and crying, Here in the inland garden Why is the sea-gull flying? Here are no fish to dive for; Here is the corn and lea; Here are the green trees rustling; Hie away home to the sea!

1 ' Fresh is the river water, And quiet among the rushes; r '. This is no home for the sea-gull, But for the rooks and thrushes. Pity the bird that has wandered! - Pity the sailor ashore! Hurry him home to the ocean, - Let him come here no more! High on the sea-cliff's ledges, Phi Nyhite gulls are trooping and crying; Here among rooks and roses VVhy is the sea-gull flyipg ? .—R. L. Stevenson, in "The Magazine of Art."

div.head: VOICE OF THE SLUGGARD.
div.p: THE VOICE OF THE SLUGGARD.

_ Have you brought my boots, Jemima ? -Leave them at my chati,ber-door. Does the water boil, Jemima ? Place it also on, the floor. Eight o'clock already, is it? How's the weather, pretty fine? Eight is tolerably early; I can get away by nine. Still ,I feel a little sleepy, though I came to bed at one. Put the bacon on, Jemuna ; see the eggs are nicely done! I'll be down in twenty minutes—or, if possible, in less; I shall not be long, Jemima, when I once begin to dress. She is gone, the brisk Jemima ; she is gone, and little thinks How the sluggard yearns to capture yet another forty winks. Since the bard is human only—not an early village cock— Why should he salute the morning at the hour of eight o'clock? Stilled be the voice of Duty; Prudence, prythee cease to chide - While I turn me softly, gently, round upon my other

_ side. Sleep, resume thy downy empire; reassert thy. sable ' reign ! Morpheus, why desert a fellow? Bring those poppies here again! What's the matter note, Jemima? Nine o'clock? It , cannot be! Bast prepared the eggs, the bacon, and the matutinal tea? Take away the jug, Jemima. Go, replenish it anon; Since the charm of its caloric must be very nearly gone. She has left me. Let me linger till she reappears again. Let my lazy thoughts meander in a free and easy vein. After Sleep's profounder solace, nought refreshes like . the dose. Should I tumble off, no matter; she will wake me, I
suppose. Bless me, it is you, Jemima? Mercy on us, what a . .•.
knock! - Can it be—l can't believe it—actually ten o'clock? I will out of bed and shave me. Fetch me warmer water
up? - Let the tea be strong, Jemima. I shall only want a cup! Stop minute! I remember some appointment by the
' way, 'Twould have brought me mints of money; 'twas for teia
o'clock to-day. Let me drown my disappointment, Slumber, in thy seventh heaven! You may go away, Jemima. Come and call me at eleven !

An egotist's story extends as far as I can reach. ROW to make a tall man short: Rob him of his purse. How to make a barrel of flour go a great way: Ship it to Australia. Hazing been sent a book entitled "Summer Poems," after a careful scrutiny we have decided that "Summer poems and Summer not." Since Mr. Bucolic has learned that there are but four pecks to a bushel-, he has come to the conclusion that he cermet afford to feed his hens on corm. "There's something in this cigar that makes me sick.," said a pale little boy to his sister. "I know what it is," responded the little girl; "it's tobacker !" He that has energy enough to root out a•vice should go a little further and try to plant a virtue in its plade, otherwise he will have his labour to renew. The young woman who had many suitor's, and from the time she was sixteen until she was twenty-one re- jected them all, referred in her later life to that period as her "declining years." An ambitious young writer having asked, "What magazine will give me the highest position quickest?" was told, "A powder magazine, if you contribute a fiery article." "How do you pronounce s-t-i-n-g-y ?" Prof. Stearns asked the young gentleman nearest the foot of the class. And the smart boy stood up and said it depended a great deal whether the word applied to a man or a bee. There is no death; what seems so is transition; This life of mortal breath It ia but a suburb of the life elysian, Whose portal we call Death.—Longfellow.

"Will you cave it rare or well done;? the carver to an Irishman, as he was cutting a slice of roast beef. "I take it well done ever simile I came to this country," replied Pat, "for it was rare enough I ate it in ould Ireland." . A friend was informing a satirist that a German band had invaded the legal precincts of Lincoln's Inn Fields, and suggested that it must cause considerable annoyance to the solicitors. "Not a bit," said he, "so long as they play in 6-8 time." - A wag the other day denied that John Bunyan was the author of the "Pilgrim's Progress." Being vehe- mently contradicted, "Nay, said he, "1 question even if he contributed to the work; for it is impossible that bunion should contribute to any pilgrim's progress." "Dear me," exclaimed a lady, as she looked at the boa- constrictor in a show, "why, the skin of the creature is of a regular tartan pattern I" "it is, my dear," remarked , her husband, "and that is what Shakspere alluded to -• When he talked about a snake being Scotched." When a young lady trips daintily into the parlour, and explains her delayed appearance by remarking that she has been "helping mamma to wipe the dishes, it is pretty hard to refrain from proposing on the Spot; but go slow, my boy, go slow. She may be fooling thee. - _There are many ways in which it would be well for us all to carry our childhood with us, even on into old age, if it were possible, in its truthfulness and open-hearted- ness, and willingnbss not only to love, but to show that we love, as well. Why, that last alone would cure many a heartache of to-day.—May F. Me. Kean. To do the best can seldom be the lot of man; it is sufficient if, when opportunities are presented, he is ready to do good. How little virtue could be practiced i f beneficence were to wait always for the most proper objects, and the noblest occasions—occasions that may never happen, and objects that may never be found. A gang of Italian labourers near Saratoga were re- cently cut down ten cents a day. Instead of striking, they cut an inch off their shovel-blades at night. The " boss" asked what it meant. One of the men replied —"Not so much pay, not so much dirt lift; all right— job last the more long. Italian no fool, like Irishman; "he' no strike!" A French speculator, who had just been ruined, met one of his friends recently. "And what are you going to do now?" inquired this person. "Well," responded the ruined speculator, "there is nothing left for me but :the other world." "What, kill yourself?" exclaimed the kiorrified friend. "Oh dear, no!" replied the ruined speculator. "I sail for New York tq-morrow." A Cockney of recent importation dropped into a -restaurant in New York one day, and made a hearty meal, topping off with a piece of pie.' The latter upon tasting, he found to be cold, and calling to the Ethiopian . waiter, who stood near, he said to him, "Take this pie to the fire and 'eat it." His consternation was great when Sambo walked to the stove and quietly devoured the pie. A little girl ate her dinner with so good an appetite, that by the time dessert was placed on the table she could eat no more. She sat silent and sorrowful, and looked mournfully at the dainties which lay piled on her plate. "Why don't you eat, my darling?" asked her fond and anxious mother." "Oh, mamma!" cried the disconsolate infant, "because only my eyes are hungry." - There is hardly a roadside pond or pool that has not as much landscape in it as above it.. Nay, the ugly gutter that stagnates over the drain-bars in the heart of -the foul city is not altogether base; down in that, if you will look deep enough, you may see the dark, serious passing of pure clouds. It is blue of far-off sky and the at your own will that you see in that despised stream. either the refuse of the streets or the image of the sky. And so it is with almost all other things that we un- kindly despise.—Ruskin. Lucius Hart tells a capital story of the ingenuity ----e-xercised by a little boy in calling attention to his first pair of new boots. The little fellow would draw up his pantaloons, and display the whole of his boots; then , walk up and down the room, with eyes now on the shining leather and now upon a friend of his father, who 'was present; but it was a bootless effort. At length, hover, he succeeded. Sitting in front of both, he ex- cl tithed—" Father, ain't three times two six ?" " Yes, nay son." "Well then," said he, pointing to each of th ir feet, "if three times two is six, there's just six -400 ts in this room." A minister, who was inclined to be absent-minded, while walking one day, encountered a young lady whose hulk somehow seemed to be familiar to him. Takingher to be one of his parishioners' daughters, and not wishing to pass her without notice, he stepped forward, and cor- dially shilking her hand, entered into conversation, ex- pecting that her name would immediately come to his recokleption. After comparing notes about the weather, however, and other topics, he had at length to confess, 'Well, I know your face quite well, but I cannot rteall where I have seen you before." "Oh, please, sir, I'm ybur new tablemaid, was the reply.

Night brings out stars as sorrow shows us truths.—P. J. Bailey. A holy act strengthens the inward holiness., It is a seed of life growing into more life.—Robertsoa. Trifles are often neglected because their connection is not apparent, yet they often turn the beam in matters of the greatest importance. "Auntie," said a pensive urchin to his instructress, "what comes o' a the auld moons?" "Deed, jaddie, I'm no very sure," was the tardy reply. "They'll maybe clip them doon, and mak' stars o' them." "No, I don't object to the smell of a cigar," said a widow 'to her lover. "It reminds me of dear John, who declared that although he didn't like the taste of tobacco, he had to smoke to keep the moths out of his mouth." ORATOR lIIINT was a bold rider, and, like Thomas Assheton Smith, well able to use his fists. Mr. Warde's hounds were once drawing South Grove, when some remark of Mr. Hunt's provoked a sneer from Tom Smith. Fierce words ensued on both sides, and they were in the very act of dismounting to settle it when fortunately a fox was halloed away, an attraction which neither could resist. "I always regretted this interruption," said an eye-witness of the scene, "for depend upon it this fight would have been well worth seeing, although Hunt had the Advantage in weight and height; but for all that," he added, "I would have backed the squire."—London Society. Cookutio LESSONS.—The results of the cooking lessons given in schools have, in almost every case, been satis- factory ; and.the lower the class from which the chil- dren are drawn the more clearly apparent are those good results. Dull and backward girls seem to wake and brighten up; what they are learning has a distinct bear- ing on their home life such as perhaps no other lesson has ever had, and they are interested accordingly, and become more regular in attendance; they improve in personal appearance owing to the tidiness and cleanli- ness taught by the way in the cooking class; they practice at home, and find their new knowledge valued there, and there is often seen a distinct growth in womanliness and such ways. The parents are almoAt always gratified and grateful, and in some cases the re- form of a disorderly home has dated from a girl's attend- ance at the cooking class. A PECTILIAR NUMBNESS.—A dignitary of the Church was dining out. Of the two ladies between whom he was seated the one on his right hand was an intimate acquaintance, and noting that her distinguished neigh- bour was silent and pre-occupied, said to him, sotto race, "I am afraid you are not very well this evening; you do not seem in your usual spirits." "Well," said the dignitary, "jam in rather a nervous state of mind about my health, and have a sort of presentiment that a seri- eus illness is hanging over me. lam conscious of a peculiar numbness all down my right side, which seems to forebode an attack of paralysis." His fair companion expressed her hope that such fears were ill-founded. " Ah, no," he replied, "I'm afraid there's no doubt of it, for I've been pinching my right leg all dinner time, and can elicit no responsive feeling whatever; the limb seems quite dead to all feeling." "Oh," exclaimed the ' lady. briskly and with an expression of intense relief on her face, "if that is all which troubles you Mink I can at once relieve your mind from anxiety, for the leg which you have been pinching all the evening is mine." Sstv-Couvuot.—One day, when I was a very little girl, I was watching my mother making strawberry preserves. I can see the great kettle of boiling liquid now, clear as rubies. Beside the stove stood a large milk pan containing some squash for " company " pies, with plenty of milk and eggs in it. "Now, Bridget," said my mother at last, in a satisfied tone, "it is done; take the kettle off." This was accomplished, and then, with almost incredible stupidity, the " help " actually emptied the strawberries into the squash! My mother turned her head just too late. She was quick and in-s- -pulsive, but there escaped from her mouth only a despairing "Oh, Bridget ! Then as she saw the girl's instantly regretful face, she uttered no angry reproaches, no useless lamentations. No doubt when my tired mother, who was not strong (I lost her at 15), went uji- stairs to rest, she felt disheartened, and thought that her preserves and squash, her time and labour, had all beeh wasted; but probably she never did for me a more valu- able morning's work than when she gave that uncon- scious lesson in sweet self-contra—Mothers in Council.

Warm AS A REatuDy.—There is no remedy of such general application, and none so easily .attainable, as water, and yet nine persons in ten will piss it by in an emergency to seek for something of far less efficacy. There are but few cases of illness where water should not occupy a high place as a remedial agent. A strip Of flannel or a napkin folded lengthwise, and Wilted in hot water and wrung out, and then applied round the neck of a child that has the croup, will usually bring relief in ten minutes. A towel folded several times and clipped in hot water, and then quickly wrung and applied over the seat of the pain in toothache or neuralgia will gener- ally afford prompt relief. This treatment in colic works like magic. I have seen cases that have resisted other treatment for hours yield to this in ten minutes. There is nothing that will so promptly cut short a congestion of the lungs, sore throat, or rheumatism as hot water, when applied promptly and thoroughly. Pieces of cot- ton batting dipped in hot water and kept applied to old sores and new cuts, bruises and sprains, is thetreatment now generally adopted in hospitals. I have seen a sprained ankle cured in an hour by showering it with hot water, poured from a height of three feet. - Tepid water acts promptly as an emetic, and hot water taken freely half an hour before bed time is the best of cathar- tics in the case of constipation, while it has a most soothing effect on the stomach and bowels. This treat- ment continued for a few months, with proper attention to diet, will Cure it is said, any curable case of dyspepsia. —Saturday Journal. 01YR BABY'S FIRST SraEcn.—Our small hero, - yclept Clifford, may be said to have taken the first step to- wards human speech when just twenty-seven weeks old, at which date he was first observed to pronounce articulate sounds, namely, "da ! da !" and "ha! ba !" For a long time after this he made no discoverable progress. In fact, during the first year of his existence he may be said to have acted on the German rule that while speech is silver silence is golden. During this praelinguistic period he, had a good range of sounds, but these were largely, if not altogether, expressional, indi- cating the many delicate nuances of baby feeling, and not verbal signs, properly so called—that is, names of objects. Even the "da!da !" which naturally awoke feelings of pride in the father's heart turned out in the end, much to his chagrin, to be quite empty of significa- tion. Yet this "la-la" period is an important prepara- tion for the proper exercise of the speech power. Accord- ing to one theory, human language took its rise in the impulse to express feeling by sound. And the observa- tion of this " la-la " stage of babyhood seems to lend some support to this theory. Some of these emotional sounds were very curious. Vowel sounds at first pre- dominated, and were ingeniously varied to spit the range of feeling to be expressed. Thus a long "a " sound indicated surprise with a slight dash of dis- pleasure, as when the child suddenly found himself in a difficulty. Again, a kind of "o " formed sound fo b i y sucking n the breath signified that the little monarch was pleased by some new object of contemplation, as a freshly discovered picture. The combinations of the simple vowel sounds, as " ou-a," " a-ou," were very varied. Among the more difficult combinations first hit upon were " oong " and " ang." It has been calculated by an ingenious German professor that in this spon- taneous " la-la " talk the child produces all the elemen- tary sounds which he will require when he comes to adopt the language of his forefathers. But this remark applies, of course, only to the Teutonic infant. Whether a young Britisher manages to anticipate all the sounds of his mother tongue must, of course, be decided by in- dependent observations.—English Illustrated Magazine THE CORK TREE—I/Men this tree is about five years of age, the cork, which composes the greater part of its bark, begins to increase in a very remarkable manner. Nearly all its vegetative activity seems to be concen- trated on this part, which grows unusually large, thick, and spongy. If left on the tree it becomes cracked and so deeply fissured that it is unfit for use. It is therefore removed before this happens. Its removal does not in- jure, but is beneficial to the tree, for if the cork is al- lowed to remain on its stem, the cork-oak seldom lives longer than fifty or sixty years; if, on the contrary, it is removed, the tree flourishes sometimes for upwards of 150 years. After the tree is thirty years old its cork may be removed at intervals of from six to ten years. The first crop of cork is generally inferior in quality, and is principally used for making floats for fishing nets. The crops are usually gathered in the months of July and August. Two opposite logitudinal incisions into the bark are made the whole length of the stem, and .

then several transverse ones about three feet apart. The bark is now beaten to separate it from the sub- jacent libel., and detached in cylindrical pieces by in- serting under it the handle of the instrument, which is curved and made thin at its extremity for this purpose. "In 'effecting this removal, great care is taken not to injure the newly-formed suber or cork—viz., the living layer of cork beneath. After barking, the pieces of cork are slightly charred to close the pores, then loaded with weights to flatten them, and finally stacked in square masses in some dry place, where they remain for two or three months. In drying, they lose about one-fifth of their weight. Only when the trees are forty or fifty years old is the bark suffidiently matured for making good corks. The substance is valuable for bottle corks, because it is light, porous, compressible, and sufficiently elastic to adapt itself to the neck of a bottle. It can be cut into any shape, and, notwithstand- ing its porosity, is impervious to 'any common liquid. These qualities make it superior to all other substances as a stoppering for bottles' for which it is principally used. Corks are made as follows :—The cork is first cut into slips, which by means of a 'gauge are made narrow or wide, according to the size of the corks or bungs ordered; these slips are then cut into squares of the re- quired length, which are cut circularly with a knife by the hand, and thrown ,into a basket. Cork-cutting in Catalonia and the south of France is a branch of manual labour which furnishes a livelihood for a considerable portion of the population. Several attempts have been made to cut corks by machinery, but they have hitherto failed to supersede hand labour. Many of the wealthier inhabitants of Spain have their houses lined with cork, which ensures the freedom of the rooms from damp. Spanish black and a black colour for painters are made from the calcined paringT of cork. The quantity of cork annually imported into the United Kingdom is about 3,000 tons.—The 7 echnical Educator.

SECOND CROPS OF FRUIT IN CHESIIIRE.—,Second crops I of plums and the re-bursting of the apple and pear trees into blossom have already been recorded in Cheshire and North Wales, but a more curious illustration of the re- markably open season we are enjoying is to be seen at Audlein, Cheshire, where a fine secoqd crop of peas are podding after flower, and promise to produce an abun- dant crop. GERMAN SUGAR-BEET GROWERS.—A circular has been I issued from Halle to the German sugar-beet growers to the effect that the trade in sugar-beet having been bad this year. and the foreign competition being very strong, it is very necessary for the farmers of Germany to im- prove to their utmost the condition of that industry in Germany. It is proposed that all the sugar-beet growers should agree not to sell the beet at the price of the cost of production, as they have been doing since the trade has been so bad.

SUCCESS OF SHIRE 140RSES IN AMERICA.—A contem- porary learns that Mr. J. P. Whitney, of Placer County, I California, was a successful visitor at the Sacramento Horse Show this autumn. He won first prize for three- year-old with the stallion British Oak, 3,003, bred by, Mr. H. Coy, Little Downhatn, Cambridgeshire, the winner last year of first prize at Huntingdon Shire Show, also first. and champion as best stallion against 66 competitors at the Cambridge Show at Ely. Mr. Whitney's next suc- 'cess at the Sacramento Horse Show was with his Shire. filly Catch, which obtained first prize. She is own sister to the well-known filly Cosy, bred by Mr. Walter Gilbey, unbeaten as a yearling last year, and first prize winner as a two-year-old this year at the London and other im- portant shows. THE EARL OF DUDLEY v. SAMUEL SPENCER BANNISTER. —Mr. William Mathews, of Birmingham, as umpire ap- pointed by the Land Commissioners, has made his award in this case under the Agricultural Holdings Act. The Setlgley Park Farm, in South Staffordshire, consisted of about 180 acres, of which about 80 acres are in grass. The tenancy was a parole one from year to year, and was determined on the 25th March, 1884. When the tenant entered in 1874 everything had been sold off by his predecessor. The tenant sold everything off 4 when he quitted in 1884. On the 24th January, 1884, the tenant gave notice to the landlord of his mtentian to make a claim, and presented a schedule of particulars, in respect of which he claimed the sum of £328 for lime, manures, cake, &c. The Earl sent in a counter- claim for £446175. for waste, besides what was due for rent. The umpire awarded £lO7 10s. to the tenant; and £122 10s., besides rent, to the landlord; each party to pay his own costs. How TO Comma. CATrLE DISHASE.—Mr. Dunne, in a report laid before the Cumberland and Westmorland Sessions last week, said that with regard to:the cattle disease 12 officers were daily engaged during the year in Cumberland in enforcing the deansing arid disinfec- tion Order of Council (of April, 1882) ; 13,517' inspec- tions were made at railway stations, auction marks, ports of debarkation, and other places; 3,076 hors@ boxes, 32,909 truclts, 150 vans, 2,8133 gangways, 73,694 pens, 885 landing places, 600 yards, 1,917 sidings, 78 movable carriages, 127 vessels conveying animals by sea', 7,069 stalls and sheds, and 237 other vehicles were ex- amined; total, 113,602. In Westmorland seven officers were engaged on similar duty. They made 3,121 in- spections, 2,645 horse boxes, 18,151 trucks, 1,222 vans, 14,261 pens, 135 landing places, 152 ferry boats, 440 yards, 1,062 sidings, and 5 other places were examined; total, 38,103. The weekly reports giving the details of this work have been deposited with the Clerk of the Peace for information of the Local Authority and Privy Council. THE FALL IN LAND VALVES.—The depreciation in the value of landed estates has seldom been so accentuated as it was by the sale of the Yaxley Hall Estate, a Suffolk property, of 378 acres, last week. The property consists of two farms and a mansion-house in a small park, and is of the rental value of £6OO a year. A few years ago, the Land Agents' Record informs us, £21,000 was refused for the property. The bidding the other day was started at £6,000, end the estate was actually sold for £7,600, "to the mat astonishment of all present." A few years ago 'land in the immediate neighbourhood of this estate was selling for £6O an acre. This Suffolk property only realised £2O an acre, or no more than is sometimes paid for cultivated land in California. The Record suggests that when owners mean to sell at a low figure, they should advertise it at an upset price, as people would then take trouble to inspect the property, and attend the auction. About the same time a farm of 252 acres

in Cambridgeshire was being disposed of. In 1874 4 was purchased for £17,000, but now the bidding com- menced at £7,000, and the auctioneer consideredhimsen fortunate to reach £ll,lOO. Unsuccessful attempts were made during the week to sell the I3osworth Park Estate in Leicestershire, worth £6,000 a year, the Prinknash Park Estate in Gloucestershire, and the Moor Park Estate of 1,228 acres in Hertfordshire. It is next door to an impossibility now to get a purchaser for a large estate.

RHEUMATISM IN HORSES.—The following question is asked of a contemporary :—" My cob is frequently lame in one or the other of his limbs and sometimes he is in such a state that when I first attempt to move him after standing in the stable that it is with considerable diffi- culty that he manages to walk. The stiffness, to a greltt extent, passes off after a little exercise—sometimes more than others. The lameness is usually in the knee or fet- lock when it is the fore-legs that are suffering, but when the hind ones are affected I can scarcely determine the actual seat of lameness. It seems to me like rheu- matism. Is it likely that I am right? If so, what is the best thing to relieve him without rest?" The answer is as follows :—" I have little doubt but that your cob is,bs you suspect, the:victim of rheumatism. If possible, let him lie in a roomy loose box, and when he returns from a journey see that his lees are always rubbed thoroughly dry, and then nicely bandaged with some good flannel bandages for the night. A little stimulating embroca- tion' or even whisky, may be well rubbed on the parts that are chiefly affected once or twice each day. In con- junction with this, never allow him to drink very hard water, nor to stand about without being clothed, and in wet weather use a waterproof cloth, beside which give him daily in his food half ounce of bicarbonate of potash and half ounce of resin (yellow), finely pulverised. After using these for a time, say about a fortnight, dis- continue them for a week or ten days; then use them again for a time; by so doing the effect will be greater." SAVAGE Brits.—A correspondent of the Field, writing on this subject, which is a matter every now and again of special interest to farmers, recommended the applica- tion of :" a good pair of highlows" on the bull's nose. This is rather a drastic remedy and has its risks, and we are afraid in such a case with a violent bull there would be ten chances to one in favour of the bull. Mr. T. Quickley writes :—Some years since I was attacked sud- denly in a farmyard, and, closing instantly with the enemy, it was satisfactory a few seconds later to leave him stretched on the ground, senseless, but not perman- ently injured. You can kill him with sparrow shot at four or five .yards, striking a particular spot, or you can stun him with a walking stick. The spot I refer to is in the centre of the forehead, about two or three inches above a line drawn from eye to eye. Anyone, in fact, can put his fin,„eer on the thinnest part of a bull's skull, which lies midway between the bony part below and that strong arch above which carries the horns. The small brain of the creature comes nearest to the surface just at this spot, and here you must strike him; and you need not strike him very hard to bring him to the ground. The brute was coming rapidly within the range of a stout stick, which by chance I carried, when I luckily remembered that one vulnerable spot in the forehead, and determined upon giving it a hard rap. Walking slowly towards the animal as he approached, he seemed puzzled, paused, dug a horn into the ground, and at that instant received as hard a blow as I could strike easily with precision, and at once sunk on his knees and then rolled over and lay, flat. I may add that I left the yard without delay, and watched his recovery from the other side of the fence. PROTECTIONISTS AND FAIR TRADERS.—Proteetionists are taking advantage of the low price of wheat to spread their impracticable ideas among farmers. The Fair Trade League held a meeting at Bury St. Edmunds the other day, when Mr. Manfield, Mr. Bidden, M.P. and others spoke; but no one ventured to propose a day on foreign wheat. The only important resolution carried may mean anything or nothing. It was as follows : "That this meeting is of opinion that the present de- pression of trade and agriculture in this district and in many parts of the United Kingdom demands the im- mediate adoption of measures to secure substantial ye- lief." The most thoroughgoing Free Trader might have theld:up his hand in favour of that resolution. One gentleman proposed a duty on foreign nails, which rriwt have been highly consoling to the farmers present, who are buyers of nails; and that was absolutely the only definite proposal made, so far as a report in a London agricultural paper that has just come out as a Protec- tionist organ tells us. At a recent meeting of the Devon- shire Chamber of Agriculture, again, Mr. W. J. Harris, M.P., a strong Protectionist, declared that he was not one so far as wheat is concerned, but that he was a Pro- tectionist in relation to all manufactured articles im- ported. What fools men who talk like this must suppose farmers to be! And really the supposition is excusable in relation to farmers who listen to such mischievous twaddle without protest. Surely there cannot be many farmers insane enough to encourage a demand for Pro- tection to manufactured goods, which they buy, and none for farm produce, which they sell If the Protec- tionists, or Fair Traders, if they prefer the name, would have the courage of their opinions, and ask plainly for duties on grain and meat, they might reasonably expect respectful treatment; but their present motto, Oh no!, We never mention it," is simply contemptible. The worst of it is that many of these crafty persons are playing a game of their own, or their party's. They know perfectly well that Protection is "as dead as Queen Anne" in this country; but even a dried herring serves to spoil the scent of the true quarry. They de- sire to turn farmers' attenticn from the true remedies for agricultural depression—lowered rents, security, and freedom. They also desire to stir up bad feeling against the Liberal party, and to excite hopes of Protection in the event of the return ot the other party to power, which they know are as false as false hopes can be. It is the duty of every farmer who can see further than his nose to denounce these unscrupulous tricksters. These remarks are not pointed at any of the gentlemen

named above, for I believe they are honest in their opinions on this "Fair Trade" question, as many others are also; but it is a pity that they are not as brave as they are honest—Mark Lane Express. , NORTH LANCASHIRE.—MOFing BOR/itteardB.—Potatoes, mingolds, and carrots have been got out of the land. The former is a good and sound crop, although not so heavy as last year; there being many small tubers, doubt- less owing to the dry hot month of,June. They are now selling retail in the markets at from 4d. to sd. per stone of 141bs. Mangolds are a varied crop, just as they suf- fered in proportion from the attack of maggot. Judging from the weight of one cart weighed and the number of carts taken off a given acreage, our own crops will run about 30 tons to the acre. Carrots have also turned off well. We never thin our carrots, but allow all to grow. For some reason I am unable to explain, they never do well when thinned. We have tried thinning pieces year after year, but the result is always the same and those thinned never do any good. Owing to the attack of mildew, swedes have ceased to grow, and we are getting the crop off the land. This year, owing to the inferior crop, we shall not fold any on the land with sheep, but economise by pulping, and mix with other cut foods. Another exodus of our farmers is again taking place southwards, and, as a good many of our farms are now advertised to lot, it is hoped that an abatement of rents will ensue. .Speaking to a friend who has taken a ,400 acre farm in the south at some 255. an acre: he said the land, hedges, &c., were in a sad state, and would require some large expenditure of labour to bring into. paying cultivation. From the way in which the farm had been last worked, he said it must have been utterly impossible to make it.pay. For one thing, he said, there was no shelter for the live stock, but the owner had promised to erect such buildings as he deemed necessary. I ex- pressed surprise that the owner had not preferred to do this for the old tenant, as probably by that means he might have retained him. The reply was that, from what he had seen of the manner in which live stock management was conducted in the neighbourhood of his new farm, he did not think that such buildings would have had that effect.. If this be true of the generality of arable land farmers, then the recommendation, so plen- tifully showered upon them of late, to embark more in live stock farming will be of little avail, and they may, without that knowledge of economic live stock manage- ment, saddle themselves each with white elephants. During the past ten years a goodly number of our far- mers from this district have settled on farms in the South and Midlands, and in Wales; and, so far as I know, most of them are on the original farms to which they went on leaving here, whilst some have established their sons on neighbouring farms. They occasionally visit us; but, retaining their northernly. • reticence, it is difficult to' ascertain how they are faring, except the general asser- tion that they themselves do not find that they have to work so laboriously as when here.—R. THE FIRST APPEAL UNDER THE AGRICULTURAL MILD- INGS lACT.-.VERDICT FOR THE TENANT.—At the Kendal County Court, last week, Judge Hastings Ingham gave judgment in the first appeal that has been 'taken under the Agricultural Holdings Act of 1883. The appellant was Mr. Stephen Brunskill, of Hillfrop, Kendal, and the respondent Mr. W. Atkinson, wha until May last was tenant of the Burneside Hall Farm, the property of Mr. Brunskill. Upon the determination of the tenancy Mr. Atkinson sent in a claim to his landlord for £206 as com- pensation for unexhausted improvements (money spent in feeding stuffs, artificial manures, lime, &c.). The claim was so far novel that it was under an agreement dated Sept:, 1882, and also under the /Mt of 1883. There was not any substantial dispute to the claim under the agreement, but the landlord - resisted the attempt to recover under the Act as , well. The reference pro. vided by the Act duly took place, the umpire being Mr. W. Little,. agent of the Earl of Lonsdale' and the. .referees, Mr. F. Pimchard, agent of the Earl of Bective, M.P. (for the landlord), and Mr. J. Holme, Owlet Ash, Milnthorpe (for the tenant). The referees, however, failed to make an award; and the matters in ilispute stood referred to the umpire, who found that the tenant could claim both under the agreement and. under the Act of 1883, and awarded him £133 15s. is compensation. Against this award the landlord appealed on several grounds,' The award, it was alleged,was inralid, as it related to a holding not within the Act, and on technical and other grounds. The arguments by counsel on the points raised' Were heard at considerable length, by the learned judge at the last sitting of the Court. For the landlord it was contended that the Act was net retrospective in its operation, that• as the tenant was. given compensation under the agreement of September, 1882, he could not recover under the Act of 1883; and, further, that he should havi enforced his rightaunder the Act of 1875, under which he, had, it was argued, a remedy. On the other side it was strongly contended by counsel that if there was one thing clear about the Act -of 1883 it was that it was retrospective. The tenant, it was also submitted,, was clearly a tenant under the Act. The Judge held that the aWard was valid, and he gave a verdict for the tenant, with costs, except in respect of two items of ss. each, on which. an important point arises. These twa BUM were for hay and straw used flsr bedding cattle, and by this means converted into manure, but Judge Ingham held that hay and straw used for this purpose is not "purchased manure" within the meaning of the Act: A special case . will be stated • for an appeal to a superior court.

-PR. VOELCKER ON ENSILAGE. From a valuable article by Dr. Augustus Voekker, F.R.S., in the new number of th,e R.A.S. Journal, we take the following extracts :--" Mr. George Fry has re- peatedly directed attention to the importance of allow- ing green food, when first placed in a silo, to attain & temperature not lower than 125 deg., and if possible as high as 150 deg. F., before applying considerable pres- sure by means of weights or a layer of sand. By this rise of temperatnre it passes through a process which he terms "sweet" or "hay" fermentation. Mr. George Fry is, to my knowledge, the first man who has made accu- rate observations pointing out the influence of tempera- ture on the production of .the aromatic or fruity smell which grass, clover, and similar green produce acquire when put into .a silo without any pressure beyond that exercised by the muss of ensilaged green food upon the lower layers. In my judgment, his are the only systematic and accurate experiments which have. been undertaken anywhere with the special object of study- ing the process of the heating of green food in the silo, . and great credit is due to him for his persistent advo- cacy of the plan which he pursues, and which he con- siders essential for converting grass, even of an insipid and inferior quality, and other green fodder crops, into a vCry palatable and nutritious food, which is much relished by stock of every description. As far as my present experience goes, there is a great deal in what Mr. Fry says with respect to the regulation and main- tenance of a proper, temperature in the silo. From his observations, it would appear that the too rapid exclu- sion of air by weighting the silage as soon as it is put into the silo prevents the green food from attaining a temperature of 125 deg. F., below which, in his view, sweet or hay-fermentation does not take place, but in- stead either lactic or acetic fermentation. It certainly is a fact that silage showing not more than a trace of acidity, and as gsweet and almost as aromatic as well- made hay, has been made by Mr. George Fry, and could be made by anybody who would strictly adopt the directions which he gives for making sweet silage. Such silage, I find, keeps only a short time on exposure to the air, and soon turns mouldy, whilst well-made sour silage may be kept sound for six or nine months, and even longer, when freely exposed to air, without turning mouldy. Some of the best samples of sour silage which I analysed last January, and which I kept in the Society's Laboratory, without taking any particular care to ex- clude 'air, remain at the time of writing (August) still quite sound and perfectly free from mould; in fact, even after the great heat of this summer, they are as good as they were when they first reached me. At the same time, I must mention that sour silage does not always ,keep well, as I shall presently show. lam now engaged in investigating the circumstances under which sour silage keeps well for a reasonably long time, and those under which it rapidly turns mouldy and gets spoilt on exposure to the air. As far as lam able to judge, and, I must confess, from an insufficient number of not altogether conclusive facts, I think it likely that the- whole difference in the keeping qualities of sour silage depends upon whether the silage has passed through the lactic acid fermentation (which takes place on the more or less complete exclusion of air),or through the alcoholic and subsequent acetic acid fermentations (which proceeds with facility only if air has free access). In most cases I find that acetic acid fermentation pre- cedes mouldiness:

Dr. Voelcker gives the following particulars on en- silage experiments at Woburn. The Duke of Bedford constructed in a barn, at Crawley Heath Farm, Woburn Park, five silos above ground, at the expense of about £l5O. These were filled under my superintendence last July and August as follows :-1. One silo with meadow grass, weighted with box containing stones and gravel. 2. Another silo with meadow grass, covered with about six inches of sand. 3. Oats, cut green, when the seed was still milky. 4. Clover, chaffed. 5. Clover, long. The quantities were carefully weighed into the several silos, and observations taken at first daily, and then at short intervals, of the rise and fall of the temperature at different depths of each silo, and fair average samples of the green stuffs were taken at the time of filling the silos, and submitted by- me to analyses. In the course of next month, or beginning of December, I purpose to: open the silos, weigh the contents and analyse the silage produced, and probably try it with some practical ex- periments on its milk and butter producing merits. Be- sides some larger experiments, I am making now some more on a smaller scale in 100 .gallon hogsheads, with which Mr. Gilbey kindly supplied me, each cask contain- ing about 4 cwt. of green stuff.. I am also trying Mr. Fry's system of making sweet ensilage. I have now in hand two tubs filled with sewaged rye grass obtained from the Bedford sewage farm, one tub filled with oats cut green and chaffed, and one tub filled with-clover , aftermath, and in comparison with the oats and clover 1 aftermath I have made equal weights of the quantities ensilaged into oat-hay and clover-hay. The respective weights and the analyses of the silage produced from the several products in comparison with the_ weights and composition of the original green stuffs, I hope will throw some more light on the economy of the process of ensilage than we possess at present.
Mr. Israel Hart, who was on Monday unanimouely elected Mayor of Leicester. is said to be the first Jew in England who has been appointed to that office.

div.head: REDISTRIBUTION.
div.p: REDISTRIBUTION.

iin Bill lies a larger question, which the political unwisdom of hereditary legislators has pre- vented fronireceivingthat calm Autumn discussion by the country which ought to precede the introduction of any great measure affecting every unit of our body politic. Had the Franchise Bill received the Royal Assent in August, we should ere this have had every detail of redistribution canvassed and recanvassed, and the minds of our legislators of both parties would have been turned towards the profitable discussion of a great question, instead of to unprofitable strife in a struggle which can have but one end. The question of the Fran-1 chise is simple, that of Redistribution is complex. The , former deals with individuals, on a principle which has , already found acceptance in the case of one-half the nation;, the latter deals with the haphazard aggregations of individuals which are now gathered into constitu- encies, in a manner which involves almost every species of electoral injustice. The boroughs vary in size, from Portarlington with 138 electors to Glasgow with 63,716; • the counties, from Sutherland with 340 electors to Middlesex with 38,373. The constituencies form com- munions without common interests, unions without unity. Looking at those which lie nearest at hand, we may ask, What dealings are there betwixt Chorley and Hawkshead, Garstang and Barrow; what fitness in joining Chipping and Darwen, Walton and Colne; what organised feeling can there ever arise from the bring- ing together of elements so diverse ? But it is not neces- sary, to catalogue the anomalies of the present system- less system; they are only too patent. How then shall we proceed to deal with Redistribu- tion 2 Shall we make a tabula rasa? Must we begin afresh, choose some standard—voters, population, or rates,—and make all things new? Such an upsetting 'of every tradition, such a diversion of the channels in which political life has flowed would, we are sure, meet iwith very little support. The days of uniform one- member constituencies are not yet; ndr does the nation desire the creation of uniform large constituencies re- turning equal numbers of members with:a minority vote. These two plans—one member or (say) ten member, 50,000 or 500,000 constituencies—are the only methods by which absolute mathematical equality can be obtained. We must, however, unhesitatingly reject them at present. We turn; then, to a re-arrangement on the present lines. Here we are met with the first difficulty. Taking population as a basis, each member should represent 54,000 inhabitants, or, roundly, 50;000. But, as few constituencies are exactly 50,000 or any multiple of it, we are continually met by cases in which no exact rule will apply. We must be content, there- fore, with securing substantial justice. It seems best, too,to give weight to the historical associations: of old constituencies—to draw the line of disfranchisement low, and enfranchisement high. • Dealing first, then, with disfranchisement, we will consider the small boroughs returrimg one member. Many of them must be disfranchised. No more con- venient basis for estimating the importance of a con-. ' stituency has been suggested ,than population ;and a little study of the , present constituencies suggests 10,000 as a convenient line at which to begin disfran- chisement. Twenty thousand is, too high, for then such places as Windsor (19,000), Whitehaven (19,295), Winchester (17,780), &c., would4have. to sink their individuality. A numberof seats7must also be taken from some of the boroughs which have two members, Here strict justice would draw the lino at about 60,000; but, as we have decided that leniency must be shown in the case of the one-member consti- tuencies,,we must also give the benefit of the doubt to such places as Cambridge (40,878), Exeter (47,154)„ Ox- ford (40,837), and Worcester (40,354), not diminishing their political influence; but fixing it as a principle that no constituency with less than 40,000 shall return two members. Total members lost There are several "hard cases" which we have not dealt with in this compressed sketch. For instance, it is questionable whether Rutlandshire might not be • added to some adjoining county, and both its members 'be taken. Some of the constituvicies, ;really counties, but nominally boroughs, such as Cricklade wit li 50,000 inhabitants and two members, in the midst of thelargely over-represented county of Wiltshire, might be thrown into the county. This plan would give us certainly 92 members to dispose of. So far as we have gone Lancashire has not figured iii our remarks, for our own county is one of those which should receive most benefit from a redistribution of seats. The only two over-represented towns are Wigan, (48,194) with two members, and Clitheroe (14,472) with one, and both of these exceed the limits of whole onpar- fiat disfranchisement above worked out. As we have not been mathematical in our proposals for taking away seats, we cannot be so in disposing of them. Having left members to towns below the average, we can only give them to towns or counties above the average. The limit below which no town should be enfranchised can- not well be less than 40,000; unless disfranchisement is taken much further than in the plan we have sketched. All boroughs above that limit and up to 100,000 should. have a member; 100,000 to 200,000 or thereabouts two members; 200,000 to 300,000 three members; 300,000 to 400,000 four members; 400,000 to 500,000 five; and over 500,000 six. It may be objected that anomalies will exist under this arrangement almost as bad as at pre- I sent, as small constituencies of 20,000 will possess more I popwer proportionately than the big cities. We can only repeat that the country is not ready for a scheme which shall procure mechanical precision, and that the big towns exert a moral weight not less valuable than simple, voting power, the voice of Liverpool, for instance, with six members speaking in one direction being raore valu- able than a dozen representatives for small boroughs. For the counties'we may take the population standard, as the large constituencies have not to make allowances for a number of over-represented small ones, in the same manner that the large towns have to give up re- presentatives to smaller ones. We have not attempted to deal with the question of boundaries, which requires to be considered in view of differing conditions in almost every county. Where there is a large town population surrounding an existing borough the addition of which would entitlethe borough to another member, it wonld be wise to enlarge the borough. Take the case of Sheffield, which only misses by 18,000 being entitled to four members. The division in which Sheffield is situated is entitled to 14 more mem- bers. If surrounding populations could be incorporated with Sheffield to such an extent as to raise it above the limit of 400,000, it would be well to do SO! The county members we have not attempted to allot, except in the case a North and North-East Lancashire The object of the Boundary Commission, which will/lave to do ' much of this arrangement, in inquiring into the boun- daries should be to frame such constituencies as will be compact and homogeneous. Any principle of grouping mai/ towns separated from one another must result in rendering unwieldy in size the county division from which they are taken, besides removing from it the only points at which the intelligence of voters is quickened by in- tercommunication. Nor are the constituencies so created such as commend themselves to us ; and it would be most satisfactory if the application of that principle were curtailed instead of extendecL The great argument for its application is removed by the Fran- chise Bill. When the borough franchise was distinct from the county, the claim of inhabitants of snialLtowns to have the borough franchise involved their being, in- cluded in a borough. Thus several small places came to be grouped as one borough. This was not done for the purpose of favouring the counties IoY removing bo- rough population from them, but to favour the boroughs by granting them a freer franchise than the counties. Nc.w that this invidious distinction is to be removed, any necessity, in the case of towns of small population, for separation from their surroundings is removed.. We have dealt at greater length with the case of North and North-East Lancashire in our Leading Columns; but in connection with this argument yve may ask what' would be the position of North-East Lancashire if, as is done th some cases in Scotland, all the villages of 2,000 inhabit- ants were removed? There are 43 places in Lancashire with "populations varying from 10,000 to 50,000, of which North-East Lancashire has at least its proportion. If only these urban populations were abstracted, not going lower than 10,000, the present County Division would scarcely be entitled to its present two members; it could not be divided, and would still stretch from Walton to Colne, from Chipping to Bacup. It may be objected that the agricultural interest will be swamped; to which it must be answered that as the constituencies are small, each member will be brought into close coniact with the voters of his division and agricultural voters will have their due weight. Where they are not most numerous they cannot expect to pre- dominate, but must take their place with other members of the community, none of whom have any special ar- rangement of constituencies to favour them. They will rule in certain parts of the country such as the Fylde Division which we suggest: In concluding this sketch, we have to say that the question will have to be approached in a spirit of con- ciliation. It bristles-with difficulties, and the principle which appears to be acceptable in one place may inflict disappointment in another. Al! Liberals will find before the question is settled that their support of the Govern- ment is needed, and they must be upheld in their earnest efforts to settle on a just and abiding basis the Repre- sentation of the People.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

BERTEOOT.—Owing to its being usually associated with such hardy subjects as the parsnip and carrot during its season of growth, its tender nature is apt to be forgotten, and it is left in the ground till injured by frost. This oversight is more likely to take place in a large garden than a small one where everything is daily under the owner's eye. The beet crop is exceedingly good this year, all the roots being of fair size, and none appear coarse and unsuitable for table. AS•hinted above the root suffers from too much frost, but, at the same time, the longer Oh-mains in the ground the better the roots will keep, and a few degrees of frost such as we have already experienced will not injure them; but when it continues for two or three nights, the crop must come up. Care must be taken not to cause any abrasion of the roots by the fork as they are taken up, for in that case they would bleed, as gardeners'term the act ()Me juice running out; and when the roots are boiled, this will be marked by their pale colour. The fibrous roots 'must be left as they are taken up, also any soil that may adhere to them, but the tops must be shortened to within about three inches* from the root, and for the present they'may be placed in a ridge and covered over with six inches of soil, which should protect them from all the frost we may have during the next six weeks. For immediate use, a few may be stored in a shed or cellar so as to avoid opening the ridge. ONIONS.—Keep for a greater length of time -when plaited or roped and suspended from the roof of a dry, airy building than when laid on the door. A warm, dry room is preferable to a cold, damp one, as in the latter the moisture will be sure to incite the onions to grow. It is waste of thin: to rope all as they come to hand, for some will not be sound in a month's time and will have to be removed, which spoils the appearance of the rope. Our practice is to select all the best and those of uniform size for this purpose. All split or otherwise defective ones are stored by themselves for present use. There is very little odour from an onion when thoroughly ma- tured and dried, so that those who may not have an outer shed or dry cellar need not be apprehensive of un- pleasant smell if they place them in a box or basket in a dry cupboard in their dwellings. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Haw TO PLANT Burn:la.—The depth at which any variety of bulbs are planted should be uniform. The dibber is the implement generally used for the purpose, and it is rather a dangerous one in the hand of the inexperienced, as the holes are likely to be of diverse depth in proportion to the force the operator has applied to it. If three holes are made transverse' at a distance of four, five, or six inches from the point of the dibber that enters the soil, a piece of woo/ or iron six inches long may be passed half-way through, which will prevent the dibber entering the soil beyond that depth, and it may be moved from one hole to the other as desired, and held fast by a wedge. The smaller bulbs, such as Snowdrops and Crocuses, should have the lesser depth, and Tulips the medium, whilst the Hyacinth and the larger Narcissus should have at least six inches, which even then will leave the top of the bulb four inches from the surface, as some of them are quite two inches in depth. Hyacinths would be benefited by a little sand being dropped over the bulb before-filling with soil as it preserves them from decaying;. and as it is sure to work down the sides, it will induce the forma- den. of roots more readily. PLANTING ROSES.—We always select November for this purpose, as we have observed that' they invariably make more roots before the end of the year. Rose trees that are not doing well may be improved' by taking them up and re-planting, placing at the same time a spadeful or two of turfy loam on the roots of each plant. Some growers make a practice of taking them up and re-planting them every two or three years, which is no doubt an excellent plan if fresh soil is at hand to place under and round the roots. . Standards should be carefully staked as soon as they are planted, to prevent the wind disturbing them. THE Wirmow.—Fiyacinths is glasses : This method of cultivating the hyacinth supplies an interesting pas- time for ladies, as well as an additional safe coarse for the working classes to pursue, It affords the latter special advantages, inasmuch as the hyacinths can be grottn without soil, which is a scarce article to many of the dwellers in crowded towns on account of the difficulty of procuring it. Those who adopt E glasses require nothing more than a few pieces of charcoal and water, and that from the rain-tub is considered the best. In the absence of charcoal, one cultivatol, recommends two grains of salt.

div.p: - - THE MANNOEMENT OF POULTRY.

THE IMPORTATION OF EGOS. Considerably, increased interest will this year betaken in the agricultural returns, for poultry' have been in- cluded therein, so far as England, Scotland, and Wales are concerned, for the-first time. Since-1876 Ireland has reported the number of poultry, but it has taken the intervening years to secure for Great Britain the same information. But better late than never, and we are pleased to be able to welcome this valuable addition to the statistics annually issued by the Agrieultural Depart- ment of the Privy. Council. The first years returns are confessedly incomplete; and in many. cases are an ap- proximation rather than a certainty; but the incom- pleteness is more because the information given refers only to farmers, and does not apply to urbarpor suburban poultry keepers, or to cottagers with less than a quarter of an acre of land. These will doubtless be added in a year or two, but meanwhile it is not a disadvantage to know exactly how far the farmers of the country—those who have abundance of opportunities for poultry keep- ing—try to supply the demand for eggs awl poultry. In order to show what this demand iswe- give the following figures, showing the imports during the years from 1864 to 1883—a period of 20 years : Impomas OF EGGS. • No. No. 1864...335,298,240 835,028 1874_680,552,280...... 2,433,134 • 1865...364,013,040 ' 928,247 1875...741,223,566' 2,559,860 1866...438,878,880 1,105,653 1876...753,026,040' 2,620296 1867-397,934,520 989,837 1877...751,185,600i 2,477,377 1868...383,969,040 1,009,285 1878_783,714,720" 2,511,096 1869_442,172,640 1,126,853 1879...766,707,840 2,295,720 1870...430,842,240 1,102,080 1880,747,408.600 2,235,451 1871...400,473,000 1,263,612 1881_756,719,160-- 2,322,390 1872...531,591,720 1,762,600 1882.. 811,922,400 2,385,263 1873...660,474,000......2,359,022 1883.940.436,160 2,732,055 Showing an increase in numbers of 1883 over_2B64 of 605,137,920, and in value of £1,897,027. Poultry and game cannot be given ix numbers, and we, have only their values, which are as follow :-- IMPORTS OF POULTRY AND GAMAL £ 4 1864 131,179, 1874 270,264 1865 148,742 1875 328,044 1866 174,971 1876 297,018 1877 163,629 1877 319,994 1868 155,826 1878 ....... 403,024 1869 178,481 1879 432,289 • 1870 /158,482 1880 421.645 ' 1871 1872 217,526 _ 1882 ....... 501,008 1873 257,389 1883 591,895 This shows an increase of 1883 over 1864 of £460,716, or about 325 per cent. If we add the two, sections to- gether we find that in 1864 the total imports of eggs, poultry, and gams were in value £966,207, and in 1883 £3,323,950, showing a total increase of £2,357,743, re- presenting nearly 300 per cent. These figures are a very striking instakce of the supineness of agriculturists in this country. The number given of poultry as being kept in onlat Britain are : BngLand 121334;885 Wales A 1,369,062
Scotland , ' 2,307,092 .

Total We have purposely omitted Ireland, as the records given for that country include denominations of poultry keepers not in the above returns. Now we find from the same table that in Great Britain there are 32,465,861 acres of land under cultivation, of which 15,290,820 acres are in permanent pasture or not broken up in rota- tion. This means that for every two acres cultivated there is only one fowl, and that for every acre laid down in permanent pasture or grass not broken up in rotation there is one fowl. When we findthat there are 26,068,354 sheep in Great Britain, the disproportion is at once ap- parent. Of course, sheep are largely kept where poul- try could not; but, allowing for these, there would appear to be more sheep kept on farms than there are fowls. Considering how much more easily fowls can be kept than sheep, that they need neither the provision for nor cost so much in feeding, and that their produce is constant and speedily' remunerative, we cannot but ex- press our astonishment at these figures. Fowls and sheep can be kept together in most assos,,and one would not in any way interfere with the other. Lancashire shows fairly well indeed, comparing it with other counties, in these returns., The figures given are these : Turkeys Geese Ducks 59,844 Fowls
Tetal The other returns are:— Total average cultivated

Average in permanent pasturage, &c. 576,598 acres. Number of, sheep • 280.764. Lancashire is not a great sheep county, and MIS. accounts for the smaller proportion than the whole country. It will be seen that, in round numbers, there are five fowls for every eight acres under cultivation, Or one fowl for every acre in permanent pasture, &c. But as this includes waterfowl, &c., there are only about four fowls for every acre in permanent pasure, &e. Surely' this number could be largely augmented, and the farmers of the county could easily double their present stocks, even next year. Unkss they do so the enormouS importations from abroad will continue and increase, and the money which goes in this way still remain out of the pockets of the farmers, whe might haTe a. large share of it if they- were so inclined. It would have been very interesting to havo,been able to divide-Lancashire, so as to show the Fyldc,distritt by itself, but we are -compelled ta deal with the county as a whole.

SEASONABLE HINTS. In 'srme yards there will be now a nureber et young cockerels, which it is thought may come in for Christ- mas. If this is the case, they should be fed well pre- paratory to their being put up in cages to ,fatten. About three weeks or a month is generally found long enough for this fattening process, but much can be done before- hand. The best way is to select the birds to be so dealt with, and to put them is an open run by themselves. They should there be fed well, using such feeds as boiled rice, Indian corn, and oatmeal. These wilt lay a good foundation, and then, when the proper time for the fat- tening arrives, the birds will be to some extent already prepared. Fatteningpens can be made very easily, and are best placed in a rather warm shed or room; if dark it is all the better, but it should be well ventilated,
