IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNnay. The House met at 4-15. GOVERNMENT MIGRATION IN INDIA.—Lord NAPIER and ETTRICE presented a petition from Europeans, Hindoos and Mussulmea in the Madras Presidency complaining Of the annual transfer of the Government to the hills during a long period of the year.—Lord STANLEY of alderley supported the petition.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY pointed out that Lord Lawrence, one of the hardest working Governors General of India, had always advocated the removal of the Supreme Government of India to Simla during the hot season. With regard to Madras, the noble Earl was of opinion that a similar change was equally necessary. Mr. Grant Duff, though personally not anxious for the removal had nevertheless approved it.—After a few remarks from the Duke of Argyle, who insisted on the necessity for a change of climate, the Marquis of SALISBURY supported the view taken by the Government—The subject then dropped, the petition being withdrawn on account of informality in the signatures. THE INDIAN CRIMINAL CODE.--In answer to the same noble Lord, the Earl of KIMBERLEY stated that the Indian law gave the judges a discretion as to the punishment to be Inflicted on habitual offenders, and he was not prepared le advise an amendment. ANGRA•PFQIIENA.—In answer to the Earl of Sidmonth, the Earl of KIMBERLEY said there would be no objection to lay on the table all the papers, both foreign and colonial, relative to the negotiations with regard to Angra-Pequena and the neighbouring coasts and islands. The House adjourned soon after 6-0 HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE CONGO CONFERENCE.—Lord E. FITEMAURICE, in reply to Mr. Bourke, said it had hem intimated to the Go- vernment that persons practically acquainted with the British West African trade would be present in Berlin during the meetings of the Conference on behalf of the leading traders in the North of England. The representatives of • the Government at the Conference would ha in tisa with thr:L. THE EVICTIONS TN IRELAND.—In reply to Mr. Sexton, Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN expressed his regret that there was a larger number of evictions in Ireland during the last quarter than in the corresponding quarter of last year. THE PEACEFUL SETTLEMENT OF ZULULAND." —ln reply to Mr. R. Reid, Mr. GLADSTONE said he did not think the time had arrived when the Government could usefully Interfere to promote the peaceful settlement of Zulu- land. THE UNITED STATES AND THE WEST INDIES.—In reply to Mr. Caine, Mr. ASHLEY said the negotiation for a commer- cial arrangement between the United States and oar West Indian Islands was on foot at Washington. THE FRANCHISE BILL. On the motion for goinginto Committee on the Represen- tation of the People Bill. Mr. Tostrarqsox withdrew his proposed instruction that the Committee should have power to provide for the extension and rectification of the boun- daries of boroughs. Mr. LOWTHER, in order that there might not be another application of the nemine contradicente principle, wished it to be distinctly understood that the Conservative party, by abstaining from placing amendmente on the table had no in- tention of receding from the position they had all along taken up on the question. Mr. E. C. LEWIS and Mr. MCCARTNEY repeated their pro- test against the extension of the Bill to Ireland. Mr. GLADSTONE thanked the gentlemen opposite for the reasonable course they had taken. Sir S. NORTHCOTE was anxious to say that while the Opposition assented to the passing of the Franchise Bill, they did so on the understanding that it should be accompanied by a distinct and clear measure of redistri- bution. The House having gone into Committee, Colonel STANLEY proposed to insert in the second clause the words preventing the Franchise Bill from coming into,operation till a Redis- tribution Bill had been passed. Mr. GLADSTONE observed that the proposal was nothing less than the extreme demand that had ever been urged by the Opposition, namely, that redistribution should be dealt with simultaneously with the extension of the franchise, and it came with weakened force after the recent indications of the sentiment of the nation. The declaration of the Con- servatives in favour of the Franchise Bill were made because they could not help making them, and under those circum- stances the Government were not willing to hand over to the tutelage of the Opposition the future fortunes ef that measure. Sir S. Nortriacorn asserted that the Opposition were desirous of discussing honestly and fairly the details and principles of a Redistribution Bill, and he hoped the Prime Minister would look at the matter in a more practical spirit. Sir W. HARCOURT interpreted the amendment as meaning that no Franchise Bill should come into operation till a Re- distribution Bill had been passed which would be agreeable to the House of Lords. Mr. A. BALFOUR retorted that the Government were more anxious to get political capital by fasfening a quarrel on the House of Lords than they were to pass a Franchise Bill. After a short discussion the Committee divided, and the amendment was rejected by 194 votes to 109. Colonel NOLAN proposed no to amend the 9th clause that the application for medical assistance under the Poor Law shonld not disfranchise in Ireland. The amendment was resisted by the ATTORNEY-GENERAL, and was not pressed: The four remaining clauses and schedule were agreed to, and at ten minutes past eight o'clock, amidst Ministerial cheers, the Bill was ordered to be reported without amend- ments to the House. The third reading was fixed for next day. POOR-LAW GAURDIANS (IRELAND) BILL.—TIIO adjourned debate on the second reading of the Poor-Law Guardians (Ireland) Bill was then resumed.—Mr. Ginsox objected to the abolition of proxy voting; and Mr. CAMPBELL BANNER- MAN, on the part of the Government, expressed approval of the principal provisions of the rneasure.—The Bill was read a second time. THE FRANCHISE FOR WOMEN.—Mr. WOODALL brought in a Bill for conferring the Parliamentary Franchise on duly qualified women. The House adjourned at 25 minutes to 9 o'clock.

In Monday night's division on Colonel Stanley's amend- ! ment to the Franchise Bill the Parnellites and moderate , Home Rulers voted in the Government majority of 194. , The minority,,of 109, was composed solely of Conservatives. There was loud cheering from the Minieterialists when the Bill passed through the Committee. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY, The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 o'clock. Baron Northbourne (Sir Walter James), Lord Monk Bretton (Mr. Dodson), the Earl of Arran, and Viscount de Vesci, were introduced, took the oath, and subscribed the roll. JUSTICES JURISDICTION BILL.—Lord BRAMWELL moved the second reading of this bill, and said its object was to enable Justices of Quarter Sessions to try any cases, discre- tion being given to magistrates to commit either to the As- sizes or Quarter Sessions. He mentioned that the bill was identical with a measure which was introduced by him, and which passed their Lordship's House last session--The bill was read a second time. THE LAN OF EVIDENCE AMENDMENT BILL WAS intro- duced by Lord .BRAMWELL for second reading, and was explained by the noble and learned lord to be a re-intro- duction of a bill which passed the House of Lords last session. CUSTODY OF INFANTS BILL.—Lord FITZGERALD expres- sed his regret that the Custody of Infants Bill, which pas- sed the House of Commons last session, did not become LCRD CHANCELLOR stated that he shared that feeling of disappointment.--The bill passed the second reading. Their lordships rose at 4-45. HOUSE OF COMMONS.— TUESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair a few minutes before 4-0, Sir J. HAY gave notice that on that day week he would move a series of resolutions embodying the provisions of the bill for the redistribution of seats, which he has intro- duced into the House. A writ was ordered to be issued for the election of a mem- ber for Hackney, in lieu of Mr. Fawcett, deceased. Tau CROFTERS' REVOLT,—In reply to Mr. Sexton, Sir W. HARCOLTRT condemned the reported action of the Skye crofters as entirely unjustifiable. If they bad grievances, there were other meansaif obtaining redress than a resort to force. It was the first duty of the Government to support the police, if necessary by arbitrary force. That duty they were now fulfilling. Lord KENSINGTON (Comptroller of the Household) brought up and read Her Majesty's reply to the Address from the House. THIRD REAPING OF THE FRANCHISE BILL. THE TORY CHANGE OF FRONT. On the motion for the third reading of the Representation of the People Bill, Mr. Goscuast ventured to suggest that the country would greatly regret the change of tone perceptible in last night's debate on this subject, and the apparent impossibility of arriving at such a solution of the question during the pre- sent Parliament as the country would desire. To what, he asked, was that change attributable ? WAR it the result of an isolated by-election ? He trusted the Conservative party would not think they were serving the cause they had at heart, or strengthening the position of the Home of Lords, or tending to hasten that solution which they professed to desire, namely, the speedy introduction of a Redistribution Bill that might be found acceptable to all parties, and to the country at large. (Cheers.) Lord J. MANNERS denied that the change of tone noticed by Mr. Goschen was attributable to anything which had been said or done by members of the Opposition, and as- serted that it had only becoree apparent after what he might term the hectoring speech of the Home Secretary. (Oppo- sition cheers.) The Opposition had been invited to ex- plain what their scheme of redistribution was This he re- garded as an extraordinary proposition, and he thov.ght it right, in commenting upon it, to ask whether the Govern- ment had asked the hon. members below the gangway for similar explanations of their views on the subiect ? (Hear, hear.) As matters now stood, he stated that the Govern- ment had brought about a position in which it had become impossible for the leaders on the Opposition side to commu- nicate with them, either publicly or privately, on the sub- ject. The two parties must, therefore, adopt their respec- tive courses and do the best they could to maintain the principles they had been sent to Parliament to represent. (Cheers.) Mr. GLADSTONE, who was received with loud cheers from

the Liberal benches, began by deprecating the combative tone of the speech just delivered, one made with the evident tendency to widen the breach between the two parties and extieguisla any remaining hope of a satisfactory agreement. (Hear. hear.) There were, he said, even greater issues than the vote put from the Chair that evening, the thought which weighed on his mind being, who would be responsible for events that might happen in the future of this question, a responsibility which he and his colleagues did not desire to accept. What, he asked, was the meaning of the an- nouncement that there could now be no communication on this strbject, publicly or privately, between the leaders of the two parties? Was the noble lord speaking for himself or for his party? He (Mr. Gladstone) feared that he did not speak for himself, but on behalf of those with whom be generally acted. The position of the Government on the question before the House was this—Let the Franchise Bill be pissed, and they would then be prepared to bring for- ward their Redistribution Bill. All they had desired was, if possible, to secure from the other side some indications of the views entertained by honourable members on this im. portant subject. He justified as honourable, Parliamentary, and according to precedent this invitation to the other side, and, in conclusion, said if there was not to be peace Her Majesty's Government would leave behind them some indi- cation thet they had eought te obtain peace rather than to inflerne the position by iipp sal s intended io excite contro- versy. (Cheers.) Sir R. DROSS justified the coarse he bad taken on a pre- vious occasion when he had expressed a hope that some means might be found of effecting a satisfactory arrange- tnent, and, referring to the debate of the preceding evening, asserted that the tone of the Prime Minister was defiant and uncemprotnising. He held out no promise whatever that the Goveroment was disposed to meet the Opposition on this question. Sir WILLIAM HanCOUrrr re"oceted the statement he had made to the effect that the position assumed by the Oppo- sition was one which asked for reciprocity only from one side, and in which what WAS really intended was to assent to no measure of redistribution that would not e'titfy the Hnn of Lords. Mr. RITCHIE exrdreseed his regret at the change of tone manifested since. the commencement of yesterday's pro- ceedings, and viewed with apprehension the course taken by Mr. Lowther. After some remarks from Mr. Newdegate, Mr.lllingworth, Mr. S. Wortley, and Mr. Mactarlane, Mr. Patterau, moved that the bill be recommitted, with the view of inserting an instruction to provide for the re- duction of the amount of security required for the returning officer. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL hoped to be able to deal with the question in a future measure. After a few words from Mr. SEXTON, the amendment was withdrawn' and the motion for the third reading of the bill was agreed to, there being several challenges to a division, whieb, however, were not persisted in. POOR-LAW GUARDIANS (IRELAND) Committee on this Bill, Lord CRICHTON moved an amendment to Clause 9, to prevent the abolition of proxy voting at elec- tions tor guardians.—The amendment was on a division re- jected by 83 against 28.—An amendment, moved by Mr. GIBSON, te enable the Local Government Beard to fix the elections at such dates as would enable owners of property in more than one union to vets at the election for each, was re- jected by 91 votes against 24.—An amendment to Clause 25, proposed by Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN, requiring that the number of ex-officio guardians should not exceed half the number of elected guardians, was agreed to.—On the ques- tion that the clause as amended stand part of the bill, a division was challenged. and the clause was agreed to by 84 against 23. The clause then passed through committee, and the House resumed. On the motion of Lord It. GROSVENOR, the House ad- journed at 10-0 till Thursday. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four O'clock. THE FRANCHISE BILL—The Representation of the People Bill was brought from the Commons and read a first time, and on the motion of the Earl of Nowntrutoost the second reading was fixed for Tuesday next. DEFENCE OF THE COLONIES.— Lord CARNARVON then raised a debate on the means of defence of the colonies and the condition of naval stations abroad, and urged that the garrisons abroad were insufficient, the forts not strong enough, and the guns not sufficiently powerful. In his opin- ion,tho estimates should double what they were. Lord NORTH- BROOK quite agreed with Lord Carnarvon as to the importance of the subject, and pointed out that wotics were in progress at Aden, Hong Kong. and elsewhere; that hea-y guns bad been ordered for foreign stations; and that the whole policy of the Government was based on the use of more powerful guns than could have been used when the Royal Commission made its report. The Duke of Cam- bridge supported Lord Northbrook, and, after a few words from Lord Napier of Magdala and Lord Lonford, the subject dropped. The House adjourned at half-past six. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIVRSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS.—Mr. GLADSTONE informed Mr. W. H. Smith that the Government would be ready to make a statement by the 25th or 26th inst. as to the naval defences of the country.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE stated in reply to Sir H. D. Wolff that constant but unsuccessful efforts had been made to induce the Porte to introduce the promised reforms into Armenia, and the subject would be borne in mind in framing the instructions to Lord Dufferin's successer. THE SOUDAN EXPEDITION.--in Committee of Supply, the Marquis of HARTINGTON proposed the supplementary vote for the Soudan expedition. In doing so, he stated the reasons for adopting the Nile Valley route in preference to the Suakim-Berber route, and said that Lord VVolaeley had now determined as speedily as possible to concentrate a force of 2000, mounted men at Debbeh, which was higher up the river than Dongola, and hoped it would be in his power to advance that force or the greater portion of it across the desert to Khartoum, should it be necessary, in advance of any movement up the Nile. He thought this operation might have the effect of rendering tan- necessary the advance of any further considerable I force from Dongola. While the relief of General Gordon was the primary object of the expedition, Lord Wolseley was not precluded from taking any steps in his power with the view of establishing and leaving behind him at Khartoum and in the district a settled form of government. While he (the noble Marquis) could not say that the sum now asked for (11,000,000) would cover the , cost to be incurred in the present financial year, yet it repre- sented the probable expenditure within reasonable limits.— Colonel STANLEY, after remarking that the Opposition had I no desire to oppose the vote, asked if the Government had made up their mind whether they would not in any cir- cumstances succour the garrisons beyond Khartoum, and if they had cancelled the mission which was given to General Gordon by the Khedive at the instance of Her Majesty's Government. Sir W. LAWSON opposed the vote ron political grounds, and said he should go to a division. Some discussion followed. In his reply Lard HARTING- TON said that to send expeditions all over the Soudan was not in the opinion of the Government any part of their duty, nor was it within the scope of Lord Wolselev's instructions. On a division there were—for the vote, 73 ,• against, 17. Lord HARTINGTON next moved a vote of £675,000 for oper- ations in Bechuanaland. Sir M. HICIES-BEACH hoped an opportunity would be afforded of discussing the South Af- rican question. The vote was passed by 78 to 31, and a vote of £324,000 for the expenses of the navy in Egypt was carried by 66 to 26. • MISCELLANEOUS.—The Poor Law Guardians (Ireland) Bill, as amended, was considered. On the motion for its third reading, Colonel Tottenham objected, and a division was called, when there voted for the motion 72;- against, 4. The result was received with cheers and laughter.—Several ,I bills were read a first time, and the House adjourned at 25 I minutes to one.

The writ for Hackney was received on Nednesday morn- ing. The nomination is fixed for to-day (Saturday) and the polling for Wednesday next. It was decided by the Limerick Corporation, on Wednes- day, to refuse to obey the mandamus for the payment of £466 on account of extra police tax. The Duke of Argyle and Lord Hartington had an inter- view with Mr. Gladstone at the Premier's official residence in Downing-street on Wednesday afternoon. Supplementary estimates were issued on Wednesday for £1,000,000 for the army and £324,000 for the navy, to meet deficiencies caused by additional expenditure arising out of military operations in Egypt. Sir Thomas Brassey, Parliamentary Secretary to the Ad- miralty, speaking on Wednesday, at a dinner crf the ,Fish- mongers' Company, said he bad the greatest confidence in the present condition of our navy. Preparations for the Bechuanaland expedition are pro- gressing very rapidly. The Royal ,Scots left Gibraltar on Wednesday, in the Orontes, for the Cape. A draft of 200 men had been received from England. ALLEGED HORRIBLE MURDER AT OLDHAM.--hf 'ham, on Wednesday evening, Jane Healey died at Oldham Infirmary from the effects of a horrible assault. She lived with a man named John Heves, who, in a fit of passion, threw a poker at her. The poker penetrated the skull, and had to be pulled out. The poor woman had lingered previ- ous to her death in great agony. lieyes has been twice re- manded, and will now be charged with wilful murder. ATTACK ON AN IRISH POLICE STATlON.—lntelligence from Antrim states that at the hiring fair on Wednesday, ma a man being arrested for drunkenness, the police were attacked by several hundred people, and the windows of the police station smashed. The assailants were driven back at the point of the bayonet, but not before several constable* were injured with sticks and stones. A local gentleman, in attempting to allay the tumult, bad his head split open. div.head: EXAMINER, s A TURMAN. NOVEMBER 15, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, s A TURMAN. NOVEMBER 15, 1884.
FORI4:IGN NEW

EGYPT AND THE SOUDA.N. THE NILE EXPEDITION. Doemoree, SATURDAT.—Lord Wolseley inspected the field hospital, and expressed himself much pleased with the ar- raegements. There are fifty-six cases of sickness under treatment. The steam cutter of her Majesty's ironclad In- vincible has been brought here by a nuggar for Lord Wolseley's use. An Arab merchant, who has arrived here overland from Khartoum, via Shendy and Arnbukol, states that fodder and water are plentiful along the route. He also affirms that he saw Colonel Stewart, Mr. Power, and the French Consul. together with thirty other persons, embark at Khartoum for Berber forty-five days ago on board a steamer towing two nuggars. Two survivers of General Hicks's army who were taken prisoners after being severely wounded have escaped from El Obeid, and arrived at Don- gola. They say the Mandi is constantly fighting with the people of Jabeldair for loot taken from General Hicks. CAIRO, SATURDAY—Lord Wolseley, telegraphing from Dongola yesterday, stated that the Mandi with only a small following, was reported to be at Korshambet, to the north of Khartoum, where he went after his attack on Om- derman. Daring the fighting at Omderman many of the rebels were killed, All. the Kababash tribe are now stated to have left the Mandi. ALEXANDRIA, ThESDAY.—The Nudclea arrived here to- day from the Cape, having on board the railway plant or the use of the Nile Expedition. THE CHOLERA.—RAPID SPREAD IN PARIS. PAM.% SATURDAY.—It appears from the statement made by M. Camascasse, at yesterday's meeting of the Council. General of the Seine, that cholera appeared in that de- partment in July last, when about 100 deaths occurred at Aubervilliers. , PARIS, SUNDAY.—Four deaths from cholera occurred yes- terday at Nantes. One case is reported from St. Nazeire. In Paris, between midnight and noon, 48 cases and 12 deaths were recorded ; front noon to eleven o'el.eelt to-ngi ilB cleeeri ttiitera and 51 deathe have cccurred in Paris. PARIS, MONDAY. Cholera is rapidly on the increase. More than 200 persons have been attacked by the epidemic, and 60 have died within the past 24 hours. There have been 55 cases of cholera and 22 deaths in the city and the hospitals from midnight to noon to-day. The Municipal Council of Paris has voted a 'sum of 190.0001. for dish). fecting purposes and for the conveyance of cholera patient, to the hospitds, together with a further sum of 50,0001. for the relief of the families of the victims. Three death, from cholera occurred yesterday at Nantes and two at Toulon. PARIS, WEDNESDAY, 620 A.ll.—From midnight to eleven o'clock yesterday evening there wore 152 Cases and 56 deaths in Paris, not including the cases in the various hos- pitals. BRUSSELS, WEDNESDAY.—The journal La Reforms to day states that several cases of epidemic cholera, some of which proved fatal, have occurred at Brussels and at Hal. The Brussels Board of Health, on the other hand, declare there has been no case in this city. Doenama, Tnunsne.v.—Lord Wolseley, Major Wardrop, and Zobrad Bey have left here in the pinnace of WM. iron- clad Inflexible to inspect the depots and hasten the advance of the troops. THE MAHDI'S MOVEMENTS. CAIRO, THURSDAY. —A despatch from the Mudir of Don- gola, of yesterday's date, reports the receipt of a telegram from the Sub-Mudir of Muraio. The latter announces the arrival from Khartoum of a man belonging to the village of Tankassi, who states that the Mandi had arrived at Om- derman, where he had established himself. The Egyptian soldiers at that place were compelled to retreat to Khartoum four days before the man left Khartoum. The Mandi ordered one chief, with 12,000 men, to march upon Dane gola, and another 9,000 to advance against the Kabbabish tribe. The Mudir, in communicating the above, asks for a fresh supply of ammunition, as he has now only 192,000 cartridges left. He adds, however, that the news abont the two chiefs is possibly untrue, as a long time has elapsed, and the intelligence has not been confirmed. FRENCH RUMOUR OF THE DEATH OF GORDON.

PARIS, THURSDAY.—At a Cabinet Council held this morning M. Jules Ferry communicated despatches from ' which it would appear that General Gordon has been shot dead while on the way from Khartoum to Berber. [Nora —No confirmation of this assertion has been re- ceived by the British Government.] CAIRO, THURSDAY, 8-35 I'M—The Khedive has received a telegram from the Mudir of Dcmgola this evening con- firming the report that one of the Mandi's chiefs is march- ing noon Dongola, and another against the Kabbabish tribe. DONGOLA, THURSDAY, 7 A.m.—Lord Wolseley, Major Wardrop, and Zobrad Bey have left here in the pinnace of the iroeclad Inflexible to inspect the depots and hasten the advance of the troops. DowoorA, THURSDAY.—A deserter from the Mandi's forces at Berber arrived here to-day, after fifteen days tour- ney. He states that the Governor of that place' Mabomed el Keir, is much disliked. The inhabitants have been much harassed by General Gordon's steamers, and are willing to tender their submission on the arrival of British troops. He further reports that provisions and ammunition are very scarce in Berber. FRANCE.—THE CHINESE HOSTILITIES. PARIS, SATURDAY.—The Ministry of Marine has received the following from General Briere de Lisle :—" Hanoi, Fri- day.—Some piratical bands have been dispersed without loss on our side. The Chinese attempted to renew the attack upon Tayen Quan, but were easily repulsed, only one man on our side being killed." A despatch from Admiral Cor- bel, dated Kelung, yesterday, announces that on the 2nd inet a body of 1,000 Chinese attacked the fortified works , commanding the road to Tamsui, but were vigorously re- pulsed by the garrison of the fort, under the command of Captain Leverger. After three hours' fighting the enemy withdrew, after having eastained heavy loss. The French had only one man slightly wounded. In the Chamber of Deputies, Admiral Peyron. Minister of Marine, brought in a bill for a credit of 3,400,000 f, to defray the transport expenses to Tonquin. The Senate to-day rejected an amendment proposed by M. Naquet in favour of the direct election of Senators on the scratin de liste system and by universal suffrage. PARIS, MONDAY.—It is asserted that peace negotiations are actively proceeding in London with Marquis Tseng through the intermediary of Earl Granville. Howoxoso, WEDNESDAY—The Chinese have made an attack upon the French troeps at Kelung, but have been completely repulsed with heavy loss. The French loss was trifling. The French have captured the Chinese gunboat Feihoo.

ensued, from-which Whalley chalked the fourth goal, the ball, after striking Parry's knee, passim:, through the posts. The Cheshire men were now less formidable, and could offer but slight resistance to the heavy kicks of the brothers Green and Duxbury and Dagnail, and repeated corners fell to the visiti.irs, which, however, were unpro- ductive. After the home right wing had run the leather into the Earlestown quarters, the Argyle were again compelled to act on the defensive, and Ogden notched the fifth goal, which was soon followed by a sixth from Dagnall, the light being now very bad. Time, however, was soon announced, and after a very uninteresting game Earlestown were left the winners by six goals to one. Teams :—Earlestown—J. Appleton, goal; R. Green and J. Green, backs; R. Bowker, J. Duxbury, and J. Whalley, half backs; W. Rich and H. Holcroft, right wing; A. W. Dagnall, centre; J. Sims and J. Ogden, left wing. Argyle —I. Parry, goal; J. Hoare and W. Mumford, backs; C. Keegan D. Cheshire, and J. Preston, half backs; H. Mor- gan and F. Hodson, 4e-ft wing ; E. Elwards, centre ; W. Morris and S. Roberts, left wing.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to nate that rep ,rts of matches played on Saturday mu.t be sent to the head office. Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wedue.sday morning.
HAYDOCE TEMPERANCE 2ND T. ST. THOMAS'S 2ND.— Played at St. Helens, and resulted ia a victory for the home team by two to ore.

WARRINGTON TRUE BLUES V. BEDFORD.—PIayed at Bed- ford on Saturday, and resulted in a draw in favour of Bed- ford by six minor points to nil. EARLESTOWN.WHITS STARS V. EARLESTOWN ALBIONS.— Played on the ground of the former and resulted in victory for the Albions by one goal to nil. BROPKLANDS SCHOOL V. WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—Played on the ground of the former on Saturday. The home team won by 1 goal and 4 tries to nil. ST. PAUL'S RANGERS V. HOWLEY TEMPERANCE F. CLUB —Played on Saturday on the ground of the former, and ended in a victory for the home team by one disputed goal, dropped by A. Oxley, 1 try 2 minors to 3 minors, The try I was got by W. Oxley. The kick at goal filed. BOOTHSTOWN V. Sr. HELENS RuculkhOg.—These teams met at Boothstown, on Saturday, and a thoroughly well- contested game ertde. in a win for Boothetown by two tries e enu two minor points to one try and two minor points. Creppin, Healy, and Fox played well for the home team, while for the Recreation W. Parr, J. Parr, Crregson, Finn, and Dean showed their usual form. WARRINGTON V. WAVERTREE (2ed Teams). These teams met at Wavertree, the visitors being successful by 1 try (Whittle) and 2 minor points to 2 minor points. War- rington team : T. Hewitt, back ; W. Thomasson, J. Board- man, and T. Balshaw, three-quarter backs; E. Lightfoot and J. Whittle (captain) halt-backs ; J. Jones, T. Ashurst, J. Russell, W. Brimelow, T. Parry, E. Holbrook, J. Savage, R. Littlewood, and A. Appleton, forwards. WA'FF STAR V. Sr. JAMES'S, WIGAN.— This match, the first of the season between the above clubs, was played at Warrington, on Saturday, and a fair mus- ter of spectators visited the ground. A late start necessi- tated the latter half of the game being played in the dark. Hill won the toss and chose the jockey goal. The result of the game was that the visitors were defeated by two goals 1 try 3 minor points to nil. Sr. HELENS V. BOOTLE —These teams met for the first time on Saturday at St. Helens. The visitors turned up short-handed, but were ably assisted by R. Langley and Glover, of the St. Helens Recreation F.C. The game even- tually resulted in a win for the home team by one goal, three tries, and five minor points, to one minor point. Team :—Sr. Helens—Rogers, back; Gregson, Haseldon, and Tickle, three-quarter backs; Edwards and J. Langley, half backs ; Arnold, Borthwick, Basnett, Twist, Finney (captain), Halton, Harwood. James, and Kershaw, forwards. Bootle—lsherwood, back; A. Drewe, R. Langley, and Ken- dal, three- quarter backs; Fowler (captain) and M`Farlame, half backs; Elams, Riddock, Graham, Wickham, C. Drewe, Emmett, RI warde, and Glover, forwards. NEWTON-LE-WILLOV7S V. FAIRFIELD.—This match was played on the ground of the Fairfield dab, on Saturday, before a large number of spectators, and victory ended in favour of Fairfield by ene goal, two tries, and three minor points, to one minor point. Teams :—Fairfield—F. Foster, full back; T. Clements, J. B. Lonsdale, and W. Lonsdale, threelearter backs; W. Lloyd and F. Healey, half hacks; W. Kirkpatrick (captain), S. Harbour, W. Edwardson, J. Hamilton, W. Stringier, A. Shingler, C. Blain, J. Swann, and T. J. Winks, forwards. Newton—G. Egan, full back; G. Lane (captain), W. Lane, and J. Boardman, three-quarter backs; T. Egan, and H. Willis, half backs; H. Liptrot, S. Rimmer, T. Braddock, J. Naylor, G. M`Corrnick, W. Aitken, R. Ritchie, E. Williams, and T. Fairclough, forwards. WARRINGTON V. WAVERTREE.—The first teams of these clubs met at Warrinkton for the first time this season on Saturday. The visitors kicked off and even play was for a short time witnessed when Massey got in, but no goal resulted. Two other tries were also scored, but the home captain gave way. During the second half of the game Warrington had pretty much their own way, Barnes drop- ping a goal and getting a try, as did also Ashton. At the close the seere stood :—Warrington, 1 goal 3 tries and 8 minor points to nil. The following composed the Warring- ton team :—T. Walsh, back; S. Hough, T. Barnes, and J. T. Massey, three-quarter backs; W. Speakman and E. Gil- bert, half-backs: H. Ashton (captain), W. Poyey, W. Hayes, Frank Turner, F. Davies, J. R. Calvert, Fairfield Turner, 1. Robinson, and J. Jolley, forwards.

LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT ASSOCIATION CHALLENGE CUE'. Several important matches in the first round of the corn. petition for the Liverpool and District Association Chal- lenge Cup took place on Saturday afternoon, and reports, en far as local clubs are concerned, are appended : HAYDOCK TEMPERANCE; V. LIVERPOOL CAMBRIAN. These clubs met at Stanley Park, Liverpool. Notwithstand- ing the numerous counter-attractions (there being no less than three cup ties in the immediate vicinity) upwards of 500 spectators were present. During the first half no point of advantage was gained by either team ; some good pas- sing being displayed by the respective left wings, and Cam- brian's centre forward (C. W. Kettley) playing with great dash. At half-time both sides played with great determin- ation. A few minutes bad only elapsed when F. Jones (full back) scored the only goal made during the match for the Cambrian, the home team thus winning by one goal to nil. Messrs. E. Jones, T. Morris, and C. W. Kettley (Cambrian) and W. Knowles, J. Carter, and W. J. Blackey (tiaydock), deserve mention for their play. Teams —Cambrian : Roberts, goal ; F. Jones and W. Harri- son, full backs ; E. Corey, W. G. Griffiths, and T. Lewis, half-backs; C. W. Kettle), (captain) centre forward •, N. Roberts and J. Evans, left wing.; and T. Morris and T. Dykens, right wing. Haydock : W. Knowles, goal; T. Hatton and A. Picton, full backs; J. Carter and J. Barnes, half-backs ; J. Taylor and T. Wedgwood, centre forwards; B. Twist and J. Harrison, left wing; and W. J. Blackey (captain) and T. Allen, right wing. HAYDOCK, ST. JAMES' V. BOOTLE.—This match in the above tie was played at Bootle on Saturday amidst a large concourse of spectators. Bootle won the toss, and the leather was set in motion about 3.15. The home team, although with ground and a very strong wind in their favour, made little progress for the first 25 minutes, owing to the capital play of the visitors backs. Moran and Wil- liams securing the leather, and with a bit of fine passing, I managed to elude the Bootle backs, and Moran scored the ' first and only goal for the visitors. The ball being again set in motion the home forwards came with a dash into the visitors' territory, and Sloane passing the ball to Wood he managed to put it through, this making matters equal. After 40 minutes play—just on the point of half-time— Johnson managed to score another for the home team. Ends being changed, the wind dropped considerably. Although now in the visitors favour they were unable to 'ecore again owing to the superior speed of the home team, ant just before the call of time Bootle scored again, thus winning by 13 goals to 1. The visitors played a good game throughout, but were rather short of speed. Teams :—Bootle : J. Jack- I son, goal; Chis. Evans and R. M. Sloane, backs; F. Woods, J. A. Eyton Jones, and C. H. Allsop, half backs; forwards, J. Rogers (captain), J. E. Grayon. J. M. Mprray, D. Dixon, and J. Johnson. Haydock : S. 'King, goat; It. Rimmer (captain) and H. H. Anderten' full backs; T. King, G. Marsh, and T. Pimblett, half backs ; forwards, H. Mayhew, M. Arnold, A. Anderton, J. Moran, and W. Williams WARRINGTON V. WALLASEY.—& match between these two clubs, in the first round for the above cup, was played at Warrington on Saturday, and resulting in a victory for the Wallasey team by four goals, one of which was disputed, to two. For some time after the kick-off had been made the Warrington men had decidedly the best of the game, and it seemed as if they were to be more than a match for their competitors. After some smart play the Warrington men secured a first goal amidst cheers. a. start having again been made the Wallasey men soon showed that they were by no means disheartened, and in the course of some vigorous play in which they manifested a good deal of skill in passing ,they scored four goals straight away, two of them being gained cornparatively easily. One of these goals was, how- ever, disputed on the ground that it had been handed by one of the Wallasey players. The referee, whose partiality •for the Wallasey team was bitterly complained of by the Warrington players, refused the foul. On ends being changed the home tram seemed bent upon retrieving lost ground, and often carried the ball into the proximity of the Wallasey goal, but no goal was scored till just upon finish- ing time when Siddall run the ball up and paesed it to Pear- son, who put it through. For the home team the goal was very clearly defended by Webster, and the hacks Davies and Royston played a very good game. The teams were as fol- lows :—Wallasey : Goal, Brundrit; backs, Newton and Settee; half-backs, Sparrow and Owen; forwards, Berry, Williams, Cox, Walsh, Tetley, and Edwards: umpire, Mr, H. M. Bewley. Warrington: Goal, Webster.; backs, Davies and Royston; half-hacks, Walton Duckworth, and Parker; forwards, Siddall, Pearson, Matthews, Yonge, and Dillon; umpire, T. 0. Phillips. EARLESTOWN V. BIRKENHEAD ARGYLE.—The Earlestown team having to meet Birkenhead Argyle in the first round of the tup competition journeyed to Birkenhead to fulfil their engagement, and the match was played on the Chester- street enclosure, in the presence of a large number of spec. tators. The ground was very soft, however, and good play was out of question. The visitors' captain won the'toss, and Earlestown played downhill in the first half with a moderate breeze at their backs. Edwards accordingly kicked off for Birkenhead, but the Earlestonians rapidly secured the leather and the Argyle quarters became the scene of play. Following several ineffectual attempts to clear, Sines and Dagnall successively lowered the Cheshire team's colours. After the second point had been scored the Argyle forwards initiated a raid on the Earlestown quarters, the most prominent in which were Morgan, Edwards, and Morris ; but the relief to the Argyle fortress was only tran- sitory, as the silver medallists came again, and some smart shots by J. Green, Whalley, and Sims caused the Birken- head custodian to he on the alert. At length Dagnall sent in a screw shot, and the leather struck the post, and follow- ing up the rebound of the ball he successfully shot the third goal, Parry only barely missing banding the leather out. The Argyle left wing now showed up, and secured a corner I kick. The ball was dropped in front of the Earlestown goal. and Keegan securing it, passed well to Morris, the latter I enabling Morgan to head the ball through, thus scoring the first and only goal for his side. Before the leather was again started half-time was called, Eerlestsven being three goals to one. After crossing over the home 'club had the advantage of ground, though little use cored be made of it, as the silver medallists were constantly press- ing their opponents, and the game was principally in the home quarters, though Morris, Morgan, and Keegan several times cleared their lines. A. free kick to Earlestown next

div.head: MADAGASCAR.
div.p: MADAGASCAR.

TAISATAVE, OCTOBER 25.—The French war vessels Ga- ronne and Allier have arrived here with fresh troops. The blockade of the east coast of Madagascar still continues. The British Consul left here OR October 10th in her Ma- jesty's sloop Ospriev_f?r_the north-west coast.

div.head: BALLOON STEERING.
div.p: BALLOON STEERING.

PARIS, SATURDAY.-A third experiment in balloon steer- ing was made to-day by Captains Renard and Krebs at Meudon, and resulted in a complete success. The aeron- auts went as far as Billiancourt and returned to lArcudon, deceoding at the spot whence they started. The voyage oc- cupied three-quarters of an hour. THE VATICAN.—NEW CARDINALS.

ROME, MONDAY.—The Pope held a Consistory thissmorn- mg, at which nine new Cardinals were created. His Holi- ness delivered an allocution adverting to the painful posi- tion in which the head of the. Catholic Church was placed, and the trials which the church was passing through. At the same time the Pope dwelt upon the progress of the Catholic faith in all parts of the world, and particularly cited the United States, where a plenary council was now being held in the city of Baltimori,. New bishops had also been appointed in Australia, India, and throughout the East. The Pope referred with especial gratification to the re-establishment of the See of Carthage. COLLIERY EXPLOSION.

Moses, SIINDAY-.—An explosion of fire-damp occurred to- day at a colliery at Wasmes, in this neighbourhood. Twenty miners were killed and five injured. GREAT FIRES IN AMERICA. NEW YORK, SENDAY.—A. disastrous fire has occurred at Palatfla, in Florida, whereby the greater portion of the busi- ness part of the town was destroyed. The loss is valued at 800,000 dollars. Another fire has ()neared at Napoleonville, in the State ot, Louisiana, the damace from which is eati- mated at 200 WO dollars. THE PRESIDENTIAL, ELECTION. NEW YORK, SAYEIIRDAY.—The Republicans will demand an official count of the votes given in New York State, in order to finally determine the result of the Presidential con- test, but they generally concede that Governor Cleveland has been successful. The electoral vote stands—Governor Cleveland, 219; Mr. Blaine, 182; the number necessary to secure election being 201. A TOWN BURNED BY NEGROES. - -

PHILADELPHIA, MONDAY.—The Southern negroes are re- ported to be showing some alarm because stories are being circulated that their re-enslavement will follow the Demo- cratic success. They have been very restive at Palatka, Florida, where some of them started a fire on Friday night, which burned nearly the entire town. The loss is estimated at 5700,000. The negroes refused to aid in extinguishing the flames, and a riot being imminent, troops were called out. On Saturday, Napoleonville Louisiana, was also burned, with a loss of 5200,000. The cause of that fire is unknown. THE NEW GUINEA ANNEXATION. WELLINGTON, TIIESDLY.—The House of Representatives has passed a resolution expressing general agreement with the decision of the Sidney Convention, and has sanctioned the payment of £15,000 as New Zealand's share of the cost of the British protectorate in New Guinea. MEXICAN ELECTIONS—FEARFUL RIOTS. NEW YORE, TuEsnAY.—Severe rioting occurred during the Mexican elections on Sunday, details of which have to- day reached New York. At Nueva Leon, Coahuila, Saltillo, and Santa Catarina. severe rioting occurred, many being killed and wounded. At Sabiots troops were utilised to favour the return of the Government candidate. The citi- zens, becoming enraged, opened fir'e upon the troops, killing 24, and driving others from the polling stations. Many citizens were killed. The district judge was shot. THE ANARCHIST OUTRAGE AT CRACOW. CHACoW, WEDNESDAY.—The trial by jury has commenced here of the Anarchists charged with throwing a bomb against the window of the police barracks in this city with intent to kill the officials. The prisoners, sir artisans and one student, all of whom are Poles, are further charged with intent to stab the Police Commissary.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

A conference Of a selected committee of the English Foot- ball Association was held in Manchester on Wednesday under the presidency of Major Marindin, at which the sub- ject of legalising professionalism in football matches was considered. The meeting was private, but we understand that a report was ordered to be drawn up for presentation at the next general committee meeting in London sanctioning professionalism. The draw for the second round of the Liverpool and Dis- trict Competition took place on Monday, when the result was as follows :—Earlestown v. Liverpool Ramblers, Cam- brian or Haydock Temperance v. St. Mary's, Earlestown Wanderers v. St. Peter's or Stanley, Bootle v. Bootle , Wanderers, Tranmere v. St. Benedicts. Solari-Tort 7. ton, Colborne v. 6—iteitnersdale a bye. The first- named club in each tie has the choice of ground. The ties have to be played off on or before December 20th. The Earlestown club, opposing Birkenhead Argyle in the first round of the Lancashire Challenge Cup Competition on Saturday, pressed their opponents from beginning to end, and won by six goals to one. The Earlestown Wanderers fairly thrashed the Liverpool Linden club in the same com- petition, winning by no less than eight goals to none. The Haydock Temperance played a fast and even game at Liverpool with the Liverpool Cambrian. The Haydock men have protested against their defeat on the ground of having been hampered by the crowding of the spectators. Haydock St. James were drawn against Bootle in the competition, and though defeated they played a plucky game. St. Helens Recreation were beaten by Boothstown on Saturday, but the former club had the drawback of a weak team, and shortly after c3mmencement of play their full back bad to retire disabled by an accident. TEE EARLESTOWN CLUE; PROTEST AGAINST WIT.. TON —lt will be remembered that in the second round of the competition for the Lancashire Football Association Challenge Cup the Earlestown club met Witton, and the latter won by six goals to one. The Earlestown club afterwards protested against Harry Sharpies, one of the players with the Witton team, on the ground that he was not a bona fide member of the Witton club. At a meeting of the committee of the Lancashire Football Associetion en Monday evening, the protest of the Earlestown club was sustained, and the two clubs were ordered to play over again next Saturday at Blackburn. The committee of the Earles- town deb, however, have since decided not to play the Cup Tie with Witton on the ground that it would rob the Earles- town nub of one of their principal home fixtures: that with Birkenhead. The Earlestown club thereby voluntarily withdraws from this season's Lancashire Cup competition, and Witton gets a bye.
Dr. Lushington, Emeritus Professor of Greek, will be elected Lord Rector of Glasgow University in place of the late Mr. Fawcett.
It is stated that the Lord Lieutenancy of Durham, vacant by the death of the Marquis of Londonderry. has been offered to the Earl of Durham.

The Colston anniversary was celebrated on Thursday, at Bristol. The Earl of Kimberley was the chief speaker at the " Anchor " or Liberal banquet. Mr. Thomas Martin, the proprietor of an betel at Ply- mouth, was, on Thursday, fined £2 and costs for assaulting Mr. Albert Groser, editor of the Western Morning News. The defendant was agarieved by some articles which had appeared in that journal. Two STEAMERS AND 44 LIVES LosT.—The steamers Thames and Lightning, which left Aberdeen a month ago for Norway with coals, have not since been heard of, and are now given up as lost. Heavy gales prevailed about the time of their crossing the North Sea The Thames had a crew of thirty hands, and the Lightning carried fourteen men.

SHOCKING FATALITY AT A DYE WORKS.—Early on Thursday morning, a labourer named McLotighlan died from the effects of scalds received at the Irwell Spring Dye Works, Bacup, on Wednesday afternoon. The deceased, with several others, was engaged in filling a boiler with a dye, when he stumbled and fell into the almost boiling liquid. THE PANIC IN A GLASGOW THEATRE.—The man named Turner, who was apprehended for raising a false alarm of fire in the Star Theatre Glasgow, ten days ago whereby 14 persons were killed and 14 injure ' d, WAS on Thursday fully committed for trial on a charge of culpable homicide. He will be tried before the Glasgow Circuit Court, which meets about a month hence.

LONDON LOAD MAYOR'P SHOW.—One of the last, if not every iast, of the Lord Mayro's Shows in the City of Lon- don took place on Monday. There were elephants in it,-and camels and men in armour representing the knights of old, and men in uniform representing the troops who are doing duty for England in the Soudan. All the bands taking part in the procession, at the request of the civic authorities' played the Dead March in " " when passing the General Post Office. . . . .

- - THE TUBBERCURRY CONSPIRACY.—The trial of Patrick N. Fitzgerald on the charge of treason-felony has resulted in an acquittal. The jury expreised the opinion that the evi- dence was very untrustworthy. When the news of the ac- quittal was telegraphed to Cork and Limerick, there ahre great rejoicings among the populace. At Dub;in, on Tues- day, the Crown entered a izolleprosegui against all the Tub- bercurry prisoners, including Fitzgerald, who was on Mon- day acquitted. Prisoners were discharged. Woman's Sorramaa—The annual meeting of the Man- chester National Society for Women's Suffrage was held in the Manchester Town Hall, on Wednesday, the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Harwood) in the chair. Amongst those present was Mr. W. Woodall, M.P., who pointed to the various directions in which the movement had progressed. He be- lieved they were within measurable distance of victory. A similar feeling was expressed by other speakers, who also bore testimony to the great loss which the women of this country had sustained in the death of Mr. Fawcett. THE CROFTERS' REBELLlON.—Telegrams from Skye, on Tuesday, state that the Crofters are still determined to re- sist the arrest of any of the fellows of whom, it is said, the police have orders to arrest 20 at Uig alone. The Rev. Mr. Macdonald, of Inverness, addressed a conference of Crofters on Tuesday. but, the weather being stormy, there was only a limited attendance. The West Highland steamer Clay- more, which arrived at Oban on Tuesday evening from the North, reported having passed the gunboat Forester in the Sound of Mull, en route to Skye. A largely attended meet- ing of crofters on the Kilmuir estate was held at Uig on Wednesday, and was addressed by the Rev. A. C. M•Donald, of Inverness. After some discussion, a resolution was unanimously adopted not to offer resistance to the police, even should arrests on a large scale be made. THE ASTON DISTURBANCE.—At the Birmingham Police Court on Wednesday, before the Stipendiary (Mr. Kinners- ley), summonses against three men, named Larry Mack. Edward Reed, and Charles Smith, were heard, the sum- monses being taken out at the instance of Messrs. RC Jarvis (a prominent Birmingham Conservative), W. Barton (secre- tary of the Birmingham Conservative Association), and his brother, C. W. Barton. The defendants were charged with having made libellous statements in the affidavits relating to the disturbance at the Conservative demonstration at Aston, which were quoted by Mr. Chamberlain in the House of Commons. There was a counter summons against Mr. Jarvis for misdemeanour in reference to certain declarations which he had made. Great interest was manifested in the proceedings. Evidence was called as to affidavits sworn to by the defendant Reed. and the case was adjourned. STRANGE SHOOTING CASE.—At the Henley County Bench, on Saturday, a youth named Buckner was charged with attempting to murder Mrs. Lawrence, wife of a shop- keeper, living at Dogmore End, a village in the Henley police division. The prisoner is said to have gone to the shop masked, and on seeing Mrs. Lawrence he fired a pistol at her, the bullet entering her right side in a line with the heart. She told him he had shot her, and he replied, " I will shoot you again." He then decamped, taking with him the cash box, which contained about £4. Buckner was apprehended after a desperate struggle by a police constable in disguise, and a pistol and some cartridges were found on , him. He is the son of a shopkeeper and postmaster of a I near village. No motive can be assigned for the rash act. The prisoner is only sixteen years of age. The poor woman I lies dangerously ill. The bullet has not been extracted. The prisoner was remanded. THE LORD MAYOR'S BANQUET.— The Lord Mayor (the Right Hon. G. S. Nottage) and Sheriffs Whitehead and Phillips gave the usual Guildhall banquet on Monday even- ing. There was a brilliant gathering, which included peers, Cabinet Ministers, judges, members of Parliament, diplomatic and official personages, and members of the Cor- poration. Mr. Gladstone was compelled to remain away by pressure of public business. After the usual loyal toasts, Sheriff Phillips proposed the "Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces." In replying, Lord Hartington said his anticipa- tions of last year had been fulfilled so far as regarded a steady increase in the effectual strength of the army by most satiefactory recruiting. He expressed warm appreci- ation of the gallantry displayed by all ranks in the Soudan operations, and eulogised the military genius and adminis- trative talents of General Gordon, who, he hoped, would soon be released from his difficulties, and enabled to accom- plish the object of his mission. The Earl of Northbrook re- sponded for the navy, and commended the naval forces in Egypt for the manner in which they were co-operating with Lord Wolseley to ensure the suc- cess of the expedition. Referring to the condition of the navy, he said the Board of Admiralty was fully prepared to answer all hostile criticism, and had been gratified to find in recent discussiona a general acquiescence in their princi- ples of increasing the strength of armour-plated ships and the number of swift cruisers for protecting our commerce. Earl Granville responded at length on behalf of "Her Majesty's Ministers." After referring to the unfortunate failure of the European Conference on Egyptian finance, the noble Earl referred to Lord Northbrook's mission, the report of which had cot been considered by the Cabinet. His lordship regretted the language used in some recent speeches on our fiscal policy and the revival of old fallacies. It was not true that the Foreign Office had failed to promote commercial relations with Turkey, Spain, and Italy. This country had not the least jealousy of German colonisation, especially when it was accompanied by freedom of naviga- tion and commerce. Lord Granville t-eferred to the Reform Bill, and said Mr. Gladstone desired harmony and the rational co-operation of the two Houses of Parliament. He could not but think it possible for the Conservative party to indicate the principles they favoured, and be was sure the Government would desire to bring about such an accord as would settle the question on a broader and firmer basis than would otherwise be possible. Other toasts followed.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

It is stated that a scheme is on foot to build a Govern- ment hospital in Dublin on the plan of G-uy's Hospital, London. It is rumoured that the Government will grant £15,000 for that object. Mr. Healy, M.P., was on Monday called to the Irish bar. The Court of Chancery was dsnsely crowded with specta- tors anxious to see him, and when he emerged from the Court after being celled he received an ovation. The Mayor of Swansea laid the foundation stone of the new Public Library buildiugs in Alexandra-road, Swansea, on Saturday. The building, which is to cost £lO,OOO, forms ' part of the new improvement scheme promoted by the Cor- poration. A printer named James rearson was on Monday sen- tenced at the Nottingham Assizes to eight months' im- prionment for printing and circulating a foul print, in the form of a "funeral card," on the late Mr. Justice Wet. kin Williams. FATAL POACIIING AFFRAY,—A desperate fight took place on Sunday night, in a wood, near Nottingham, between a party of gamekeepers, employed by Mr. Finch, M.P., and six poachers. One of the poachers was killed, and three ethers were arrested. THE 'ma NATIONAL LAND Coarra.Yr.-In Dublin, on Tuesday.a conditional order was made for the re-sale of the Bodkin Estate, County Galway, purchased by Mr. Parnell's National Land Company last July, the purchase money not

having been paid. CHESS.—The return match between the Yorkshire and Lancashire Chess Clubs was played at Manchester, on Saturday. There were 80 players a side. Result—Lanca- shire 871 wins to Yorkshire 471 wins. Lancashire won the previous match by 84 against 36. THE DANGERS OF FOOTBALL.—During a football match on Saturday, in the Eton College playing-fields, Oxford, against a scratch team from Oxford University, W. .7. Cor- bett, K S.A., sixth form at Eton College, had his right leg broken be' a cross kick. Hsi@ progressing favourably. THE Cearseater AT £lO A NIGHT.—The Claimant, whose recent a4dresses in Leeds attracted very small audiences, has accepted a four nights' engagement with the management of a Leeds music hall, at which he will appear during the first part of next week. His remuneration, we hear, will be £4O for the four nights. DESTRUCTIVE FlRE.—Damage to the extent of over £lOO,OOO was done by fire, on Monday. on the premises ef Messrs. Stewart Brothers and Spencer, oil merchants, Stroud, Rochester, and on adjoining premises to which the 'flames extended. The greater part, if not the whole, of the dam- age is covered by insurance. TIIE LATEST LONDON 1147STERT.—An inquest was held in London, on Monday, on fragments of human remains found recently in Bedford-square. Fitzroy-square, and elsewhere. Medical evidence showed that the remains were these of a woman between 25 and 50 years of age, and that the body han been cat asunder with a hatchet. There was no evi- dence of identification. The inquiry was adjourned. SOUTH WARWICKSHIRE ELECTION.—RESULT,---The re- sult of tlee polling was declared at Warwick as follows:— Mr. S. S.'Lloyd (C), 3,09.5 I Lord W. Compton (L), 1,919 ; Conservative majority, 1,176. This is a Conservative gain. The figures at the General Election, when the late Mr. Leigh was returned, were :—Sir John Eardley-Wilmott (C), 2,6134; Hon. Gilbert G. Leigh ( L), 2550; Earl of Yar- mouth (C). 2,507. At the previous election the Liberals polled 2,170 votes, and were in a minority of over 600. THE TRADE OF BRADFORD.—Alderman Smith, Who was on Monday re-el, cted Mayor of Bradford, alluded to the trade of the berough. He remarked that the commercial cloud which had hung over the town had dispersed. He believed Bradford had never at any period of its history done as it was now doing. Not only were the whole of the operatives employed, but there was a scarcity of opera- tives, and machinery was now standing idle for want of hands. In respect of trade he believed Bradford stood as high, nay even higher than any other town in England or in Europe. ROBBING A CATHOLIC CHURCH FOR GUT FAWKES.—Twe boys, one seven and the other nine years of age, were charged on Saturday, at the Southwark Police Court, with committing sacrilege. With a large stone they smashed four panes of glass in the sacristy window of St. George's Reman Catholic Church, Southwark, and stole a large altar candle, with which to celebrate Guy Fawkes Day. The priest said that damage had been done to the win- dow to the extent of between £7 and £B. The boys were too young to send to a reformatory, and the magistrates decided to defer judgment. THE SENDING OF A DEAD CHILD TO THE HOME OFFICE. —The body of the child which was sent to the Home Secre- tary, under the circamssances already reported, was for- warded from Colsterworth, near Grantham, Lincolnshire. The churchyard at Colsterworth has recently been closed, and no proper place has been provided. It was in order to call the attention of the Home Secretary to this state of affairs that the body of the child was sent to the Home Office. Sir William Harcourt has sent down an officer to inquire into the'parentage of the child, and into the facts of the churchyard having been closed. FUNERAL OF PROFESSOR FAWCETT, M.P.—The remains of the late Postmaster-General were interred on Monday in the churchyard of Trumpington, near Cambridge. Of pri- vate friends and acquaintances there was a very large as- sembly, and representatives were present also from the Gen- eral Post-Office and the political and other organisations with which Mr. Fawcett was connected. Amongst his late colleagues in the Government who went to render their tri- bute of regret ware the Home Secretary, Sir C. Ditke, Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, Mr. Mundella, Mr. Childers and Mr. 11. Gladstone (representing the Premier), and a large number of members of Parliament. The f aneral arrangements were of an unusually simple character, and no black horses were harnessed to the carriages. A wheeled trolley was need in- stead of a hearse. Wreathes were sent from many represen- tative and private persons, including one from Indians resi- dent in England. THE PRINCE OF WALES AND HIS COTTAGERS.—The vil- lage of West Newton, which forms part of the Sandringham estate, and ie which the Prince of Wales has had erected a considerable number of model cottages for the labourers, was en fete on Saturday, consequent upon the opening of the Sandringham Club, which has just been established by the Prince for the men and boys who are working on the Sandringham estate. The club, which is established in handsome and commodious premises known as West New- ton House, is placed under the management of a committee, on which the workingmen element is largely, represented. The Prince of Wales, on arriving to open the club and hand it over to the president (the Rev. F Hervey). ;mg accompanied by the Princess of Wales, Prieces Albert Victor and George, Princesses Louise, Victoria, and Maud of Wales, Princess Louise (Marchioness of Lorne), and the guests of their Royal Highnesses. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Prince of Wales, on the motion of one of the farm labourers who has worked at Sandringham for 22 years, not only for the establishment of the club, but for the nu- merous and valuable improvements in the labourer's Cot- tages and surreuiedings on the Royal estate.

PRESCOT - CANARY Snow.—The eleventh annual exhibition of canaries and British birds was held in the Town Hall on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday last. There were over 270 entries, a less number than last year, but in point of quality the birds were the best ever seen in the exhibition, and in some classes the judge—Mr. J. Benson. NVardwick, Derby— had great difficalty in awarding the prizes. The exhibition I was fairly well attended, and there will be a small balance to hand over to the Prescot Parish Church Nurse Fund. BOARD OF GIIARDIANS.—The fortnightly meeting was held on Thursday, Mr. W. A. Meadows presiding. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Dobell, of Huyton, for send- ing a quantity of Graphic newspapers for the use of the in- mates. The sanction of the Registrar-General had been given to the appointment of Mr. Peter Chorley as registrar of births, marriages, and deaths for the St. Helens sub- district. In consequence of this, a similar vacancy occur- red in Prescot. There were four applicants, including Mr. Willoughby Gilbody, of Ditton, who resigned his position as Guardian for that township only three weeks since; and Mr. Henry Fogg, of Wartington-road, Prescot. The latter was appointed. A letter was read from Su- perintendent Barker, of Prescot, drawing attention to the fact that three of the male paupers had been selling chips in Prescot, having been sent with them from the workhouse.— The matter was left in the hands of the clerk.—Before separating, the Rev. T. Chambers asked if there was any favourable news respecting their chairman (Mr. J. L. Hall), who for some time has been seriously unwell, and was in Scotland —The Clerk regretted that the last report as to Mr. Hall's health was not very favourable.—With refer- ence to the charges against Union officials by a writer sign- ing himself "W. Law," the Local Government Board did not contemplate the institution of proceedings against Dr. D. M. O'Hara in respect of his refusal to give evidence.— The Chairman remarked that there the matter ended —The Rev. T. Chambers (Halewood) di4 not think it should end there. He considered it a very curt and unsatisfactory reply, and thought the guardians deserved more considera- tion at the hands of the Local Government Board. He was not satisfied, the outside public were not satisfied, the guardians as a body were not satisfied, and he therefore proposed that the Clerk write to Sir Richard Cross and Col. Ireland-Blackburne, their county members, who were always courteous aud obliging to their Constituents, and especially had they been kind to that Board of Guardians, and ask them to interview the President of the Local GOVeroment Board on the matter.—Mr. Dohell seconded the proposition. —Mr. Jackson remarked that be did not think Law Was worth troubling about.—The Roy. T. Chambers said that if nothing more was done by the department, and if any more complaints came down from them, he should move that : they either lie on the table Or be torn into pieces and thrown . into the waste-paper basket —The resolution was carrhd unanimously.
GOLBORNE.
MISSION SEnxtmcs.—On Sunday Mr. T. Worthington (Wigan), preached in the Independent Methodist Chap, Golborne, in aid of the Home :Mission Fund.

SACRED CANTATA. - On Siturday the sacred cantata, The Lion of Judah" was given in the Primitive Metho- diat chapel, Golborne, by the chapel choir and friends. Recitations were given at intervals by Miss Booth (War- rington.) The Rev. T. Morgan, resident minister, pre- sided.

TREAT TO MESSRS. SMITHSON'S GOLBORNE EMPLOYES.-- Messrs. Smithson Brothers, the new proprietors of the Bank Heath Mill, Golborne, entertained their employes on Satur- day evening to tea in the large room connected with the Legh Arms Hotel. Amongst the many additions and im- provements the firm has made to the Bank Heath premises must be mentioned a new horizontal engine, recently erected by Messrs. Peters, of R. >chdale, the driving power having hitherto been insufficient for the adequate working of the mill. To celebrate the completion of the engine, it WM resolved to give the hands a substantial tea, followed by an appropriate entertairiment. Upwards of 100 sat down to a spread which did justice to all concerned. Mr. John Hol- lows, general manager of the Facit Mills, presided, the firm being further represented by Mr. H. Darlington, Mr. S. Spencer, and Mr. J. R. Hollows, of the Manchester Yarn Department.—The Chairman said competition was now ea rreat that everything had to be done first-class, and hav- ing gone to great expense Messrs. Smithson now thought it was only right that the hands sh mid do all in their power to make Bank Heath Mill a success Mr. Spencer, who, judging from the hearty rece;,tion accorded him, is highly popular with the hands, alse ad- dressed the meeting.—Mr. Lowe (manager) said as renz, trds the hands he could say of late they had done very well. They were getting about two and a half per cent, more money, and about twenty-five per cent, less work —Mr. Hevworth moved. and Mr. T. Silcock seconded, a vote of thanks to the members of the firm for their generosity, which was acknowledged by Mr. Hollows.—.A miscellaneous programme was then introduced, in which the Brothers Jackson took an important part. Songs, &c., were also given by Mr. Berwick and a number of Messrs. Smithson s employes. Mr. J. R. Hollows and Mr. E. Jackson were the pianists.

div.head: SAD CASE OF SUICIDE.
div.p: SAD CASE OF SUICIDE.

A sad case of;ici-cle-W-as--di;c-o;eire-d-,lt Golborne on Thursday morning. The deceased, James Forster, grocer, Bridge-street, retired to rest on Wednesday night, and was soon I followed by his wile. The latter wakened about four o'clock, I and, missing her husband, at once raised the family, when it was discovered that Mr. Forster had left the house by means of the shop door, which was open. Mr. H. Thorp, son of the Golborne curate, who happened to be sleeping next door, went out in search, and at once made his way to Mill-lane, a favourite walk of the deceased, which is situa- ted within a short distance of the house,-and at the bottom of which there is a large running brook. Upon getting near the water, Mr. Thorp struck a light and discovered de- ceased's coat lying on the embankment. The family were apprised, and the police at once summoned. Police Con- stables Radcliffe and Whiting hastened to the spot, and commenced dragging the brook, with the result that the dead body of Forster was soon secured. Deceased was re- moved home to await the coronet's inquiry. He was about sixty-six years of age, an old and well-respected Golborne tradesman, upright in his dealings, and of a quiet and peace- able disposition. For some time, however, he has been in a low, desponding state of mind.

div.head: PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.
div.p: PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.

A monthly si.-e-et-iwn-g--e-f—thii C-Otia-r-caittee was held On Wednesday afternoon, in the Offices, Golborne. There were present Messrs. Wm. Mitchell (in the chair), Thos. Pier- point, Isaac Taylor, Wm. Garnton, and It. Bennie (stir. vevory, THE PROPOSED NEW OFFICE.—The minutes of a special meeting of the Committee, held on the 24th October, were read. It was stated that it had been decided on the propo- sition of Mr. Yates, seconded by Mr. Wm. Garnton, that the question of building a Parochial Office stand over for a while, and the surveyor was instructed to make further in- quiries as to whether money could be borrowed for the pur- pose.—Confirmed. THE CLEANING OF ASHPITS.—The Clerk said be had written to the clerk of the Leigh Rural Sanitary Authority respectisg the cleaning of the ashpits. The clerk to the Authority in reply sent a copy of a letter by the inspector of nuisances in which he said that be had always 'given the verbal notice to the tenants to empty their ashpits. There had freque .tly been great delay in emptying them, especi- ally in Leigh-street, Queen-street, Wood-street, Police- street, James-street, and East-street, and several cases in. High-street and Lowtos-road. His great complaint against ithe present system was that in nearly every instance the ;material had been sorted on the spot, and everything not suitable for manure left strewed about the premises.— Several members remarked that they could not see how the I Committee could do anything in the matter, and the sub- ject dropped. WATER CONSITMPTION.—The Surveyor reported that 1958,000 gallons of water had been consumed during the month. , This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: SKILFUL SURGICAL OPERLTION.
div.p: A SKILFUL SURGICAL OPERLTION.

The American Ambassador at Vienna, Mr. Basson, has lately forwlrded to his Government an interesting account of a re- markable surgical operation lately performed by Professor Bill roth, of Vienna, which, wonderful to tell, consisted In the remo vat of a portion of the human stoma-h, involving nearly one- third of the organ—and, strange to say, the patient recovered— the only successful operation of the kind ever performed. The idisease for which this operation was performed was cancer of the stomach, attended with the following sympt-ms :—The ' appetite is quite poor. There is L. peculiar indescribable die- tress in the stomach, a feelinz that has been described as a faint all gone" sensation; a sticky slime collects about the teeth, especially in the morning, accompanied by an unplea- ; Sant taste. Food fails to satisfy this peculiar faint Benga- l Mon; but, on the contrary, it appears to aggravate the feeling. The eyes are sunken, tinged witn yellow ; the hands and feet ; become cold and sticky—a cold perspiration. The suff mers feel tired all the time, and sleep does not seem to give rest. After a time the patient becomes nervous and irritable, gloomy. his mind filled with evil forebodings. When rising suddenly from a recumbent position there is a dizziness, a whistling sen- sation, and he is obliged to grasp something firm to keep from falling. The bowels costive, the skin dry and h,t at times; the bl od becoming thick and stagnant, and does not circulate properly. After a time the patient suits up food soon after eating, sometimes in a sour and fermented condition, some- times sweetish to the taste. Often-times there is a palpitation of the heart, and the patient fears he may have heart disease. Towards the last the patient is unable to retain any food what- ' I ever, as the opening in the intestines becomes close, or nearly 80.
