div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 15, 1884.

THE Ninth of .November is a red-letter day in civic annals as the day upon which each Municipal Corporation appoints its Chief Magistrate for the ensuing year. It some- times, of course, happens, as was the case this year, that the Ninth falls on a Sunday, which is a the: non for business purposes, and then the all-important election takes place on the Monday. It is a "tickle matter "—that of making a Mayor, for Aldermen and Coun- cillors are notoriously " kittle cattle." The old proverb has it that when two men would ride a horse one must ride behind; but the municipal mare, if we may be pardoned the metaphor, does not permit of more than one rider at a time ; and, where there are so many ready to mount, the difficulty is to determine who shall occupy the saddle. With a view to making a selection without, at any rate, any public exhibition of bickering and heart- burning, it is customary with most Corpora- tions for the members to meet privately as they did at Warrington on Friday night and at St. Helens a fortnight ago. It is then, as a rule, settled after such discussion as may be unavoidable, or deemed necessary, who is to be nominated on the Ninth. The op- position, if there be any, having had their say, if not their way, accept the decision of the majority, and the appointment is finally made with the seemliness and grace befitting the importance of the occasion. This pre- liminary meeting of the whole Council is therefore, all things considered, a judicious proceeding; but we cannot regard it as judicious to precede this gathering by a meet- ing of a section of the Town Council as was done at Warrington last week. It is known, as indeed no secret was made of it, that there was first a meeting of Conservative Coun- cillors who went the length of sending a deputation to Alderman HARRISON to solicit him to allow himself to be nominated for another year. His Worship prudently de- ferred giving an answer, not less, we trust, in

the belief that it would scarcely be decent to do so in view of the larger meeting to be held on the same question than on the ground of his great reluctance to occupy the civic chair for two years in succession. It is, of course, impossible to prevent the wire-pulling of small cliques, but it is a different mat- ter when a part of the Town Council seeks to anticipate the verdict of the whole. It is a poor compliment to a body of men to ask them to go through the farce of deliberating and voting upon a fore- gone conclusion; and we would suggest that, for the future, there should be no ',arty meet- ing as to the Mayoralty, or that, if one be persisted in, the opposite party should, when the preliminary meeting of the whole Council is held, make themselves, by way of prbtest, conspicuous by their absence. This year—to take the two incorporated towns in which this journal largely circulates —there has been a change at St. Helens, Councillor Trios. COOK being made Mayor on the retirement of Councillor BAXTER, who leaves office after winning "golden opinions from all sorts of people ;” while, at War- rington, Alderman JOSEPH HARRISON has been re-elected amid a shower of com- pliments which testifies to the excellent im- pression he has made by his year of office, and to the high esteem in which he is held by both political parties for his ability and kindly courtesy. Alderman HARRISON was, for many reasons, loth to take office for another year; and this being the case we trust it will not be regarded as ungracious, now that the appointment is made, if we direct attention for a moment to the question of a second term. Considering the matter in the abstract, it seems to us that it is not wise to encourage a second-term policy. There is much, of course, to be said as to the especial fitness for the office after twelve months' experience of its duties ; and it is not to be denied that when large under- takings or negotiations are in progress con- siderable risk is incurred by making a change, for we have it on good authority that it is dangerous to swap horses when crossing a stream. But, speaking broadly, the Town Council shapes, and the permanent officials carry out, the municipal policy. A change of Town Clerk, Borough Surveyor, or Borough Treasurer is of much greater moment than a change of Mayor. As the office of Chief Magistrate is the highest honour which a Corporation has to bestow, it appears to us that it should pass from one to another amongst those who take a fair share of the burden of the work of the town, and that without halting too long on the way. Regard of course must always be had to a person's fitness to discharge the dutiks of the office with credit to himself and the com- munity. Then again the Mayor of a borough is for the time pledged to set aside party I considerations, and he is so often called upon to exercise what judicial faculty he may pos- sess that he acquires a habit of looking at things from an independent stand-point, which cannot fail to be of service to him in after life. He undergoes training of the highest class, and it is just because this train- ing is high class that as large a number of citizens as may be convenient should be brought within its influence. Confining our- selves for the moment to Warrington, we venture to say that there need be no difficulty for some years to come, even on the single- term principle, of finding suitable men for the Office of Chief Magistrate. The Conser- vatives, having had pretty much their own . way in this matter, have not neglected to • look to themselves; but we may mention Dr. MACKIE and Major LITTON as Conservative ; Councillors who are fully as well qualified for the post as the majority of their predecessors. . On the Liberal side there are, still within the Council, Mr. E. MILNER, J.P., Mr. JoHN GREENING, and Mr. JOHN PLATT, while, out- side, we have Mr. F. MONKS, J.P., and Mr. Z. AamiTaGE, J.P., not one of whom has yet been elevated to the dignity of Mayor, though there can be no question as to their fitness for the post. It the "sweets of , office" are worth having, let them be fairly divided amongst all who are entitled to them. We urge our views, it need hardly be said, without wishing to cast any reflection on the present Mayor, or upon past wearers of the robe and chain; and trust that when the next Ninth of November comes round they will find acceptance amongst those who have in hand the important duty of electing the Chief Magistrate of the borough.

LAST week the talk in the House of Com- mons was of a settlement with the Conserva- Live riarty on the question of the Franchise Bill. This week they will not hear of yield- ing—they are "full of fight." The cause of this change of front is the result of the South Warwickshire election ; it is a win for the Conservatives, and they are jubilant over it. They are trying to persuade themselves that the nation may. after all, be with them, for they have lost sight. already of the election at Scarborough, which went dead against them. Like drowning men, they catch at straws, but they show their stupidity in the matter in that they might catch at some- thing which would be more likely to save them. They have exceedingly short memories, or they would not so soon have forgotten how they were misled by two or three bye- elections previous to the last General Elec- tion. They are bad logicians who rush to broad conclusions from very narrow premises. Lord SALISBURY IS just now in his glory; he can "make believe "that the stars in their courses are fighting for him, and as a conse- quence drag his halting followers along with him in his policy of war to the knife against Reform. The Franchise Bill has again passed from the House of Commons to the House of Lords; and just now the question with the arch-conspirators against the rights of Two Millions of their fellow-countrymen is to determine on the particular mode in which the Bill is to be "got rid of," strang- led, murdered—take which word you will, but do not, oh! do not, say " rejected," if you would spare the gentle bosom of Sir RICHARD CROSS. It is stated that the second reading of the Bill will be taken on Tuesday next, and that it is not unlikely that it will be allowed to pass that stage without even going to a division, the conclusion having been come to that it will be better to give the 'stab in the back" when it is brought into Com- mittee. It will probably be done something after this fashion; the majority of their lord- ships will proceed to shed over it crocodile tears of affection, after which they will pro- ceed to put the Rope of a Resolution round its neck, and hang it up until its brother—the Redistribution Bill—is put in their hands to be sacrificed, if they should see fit, in an equally genteel manner. All this they can do, if they have set their minds on it—that is if the Liberals are foolish enough to play their game. But the Liberals would be the simplest of simpletons if they walked into a trap which may be said to be gaping lat them. Let the Lords resist, if they

SUNDAY CLOSING AT RJNCORN.—A public meeting on the subject of the Sunday closing of public-houses will be held in Runcorn Public Hall on Monday evening. RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB —ln the Cheshire team selec- ted to meet the Lancaaliire 15 at New Brighton to-day (Saturday), Runcorn is represented by Mr. W. H. Broady, 'forward, with Mr. W. Hughes and H. Hughes, reserves. CHANGE RINGING AT HALEWOOD. On Saturday, a mixed company of ringers rang on the bells of Halewood Parish Church a peal of Kent treble bob major, consisting of 5,120 changes' in 2 hours 48 minutes. This is the first eleal in the method on these bells. MALIN'S TEMPERANCE HALL, WIDNES. Mr. Joseph Cooper, of New Mills, who is widely known as the "Derby- shire Poet," gave his popular temperance entertainments in this place on Tnesd ay and Wednesday evenings There were moderate audiences. Addresses were also delivered by local speakers.' ST. MICHAEL AND ALL ANGELS' CHURCH, RUNCORN.— A great effort is being made to raise the £1,500 required to build the chancel and transepts of this church. True avail- able funds will only permit of the erection of the nave, end as the endowment would be withheld and the rite of con- secration not performed under these circumstances, it is considered highly desirable that the edifice should be com- pleted whilst the builder's plant is on the ground. Dona- tions amounting to £lB5 have been received and a staff of Collectors is at work to gather the remaining amount. ACCIDENTS AT Iturecoaer.—At the works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company on Tuesday Harry Davies. of 9, Rutland-street, got his arm entangled in the shafting of some machinery, and the limb was fractured. On Wednes- day, at the Old Quay Copper Works, Samuel Deaken, aged 65, living at Stonehille, was engaged repairing some pipes on a scaffold 16 feet high, when one of the planks broke, and he was precipitated below. He was rather seriously in- jured about the spine, and his arm was fractured Both the injured men are doing well under the care of Mr. T. a Coath, assistant to Dr. Mauritz. WESLEYAN GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION, WIDNES.— The opening meeting of the season was held in Lacey-street school on Tuesday evening, when an excellent entertain- ment was provided. Miss i. Jones sang "True till death" with true and appropriate expression and she was loudly encored, whilst Miss Hudson also contributed a song which was loudly applauded. Recitations were given by Messrs D. alcCririe Johnson, and J. Balmer, and the choir of the mission sang several glees. Mr. C. Taylor acted as aocompanist. Ad- dresses were delivered by the Chairman (the Rev. R. Har- per), and Messrs J. R. Hudson and T. S. Swale. " GERRYMANDERING." With reference to this word, which has been pretty freely used during the franchise con- troversy, a correspondent writes us as follows :—" In your leader of this week you use the word ' Gerrymander,' and spell it with a J instead of G. Gis pronounced hard tie in Gertrude. The word is derived from Ellridge Gerry, a governor of Massachusetts, whe was charged, though wrongly, with ' Gerrymanderiag,' or wrongly dividing, his State for party purposes." We thank our correspondent for the correction. The impression we had of it was that it came from " jerry," to "scamp " a thing, as for instance, jerry-building. RE-OPENING OF CRONrON WESLEYAN CHAPEL—After undergoing a thorough renovation at the hands of the work- men of Mr. Thomas Sadler, builder, Widnes, Crouton Wes- leyan Chapel was re-opened on Sunday, when special ser- mons were preached by the Rev. li. Harper, superintendent minister, and the Rev. C. Bingant. The collections amounted to £Ct lie. On Monday evening the re-opening was celebrated by a tea party, which was held in the school- room. There was a large attendance. Subsequently a pub- lic meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. W Clarke, who delivered an approsei ate address. Speeches were also delivered by the Rev. J. Hotbersall, the Rev. C. Bingant, Mr. Robinson. and others. The total cost of the work of renovation is £llO, and towards this sum the Committee have received £lO5 from various sources, including the fol- lowing donations :—Mr. Jemeet Taylor, £lO ; Mrs. James Taylor, £5; Mr. Job Glover, £10; Mr. John Glover, £5; Mr. John Hewson, £5 ; and Mr. Barkis, £5. FRODSHAM AND FRODSHaeI LORDSHIP PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES.—The fortnightly meeting of the above com- mittee was held at the Town 'Hall, Frodsham, last evening week, when Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., presided. Plans of the proposed new Wesleycn Chapel at Five Crosses were ex- amined and approved. Mr. Thomas Lewis (Guardian for Frodsham Lordship) stated that he had shown Mr. Ban- croft's plan and report for dealing with Overton sewerage to several of the largest ratepayers, and they were in favour Of scheme No. 4 being carried out, by which all the sewage from Overton would be taken down Flinn-lane and join the Frodsham sewer near the old Wesleyan Chapel, the esti- mated cost of the scheme, including ten per cent, for con- tingencies, being £756. A letter wee read from Mr. B rncroft informing the committees that the sewer down Flinn-lane included in No. 4 scheme would cost £163, and in his opinion should be apportioned as follows :—Frodsham, £347 58. ; Frodsham Lordship, £ll5 15s. The committes re- solved that scheme No. 4 should be adopted, and that notice of apportionment be served upon their respective townships, and application made to the Local Government Board for sanction to loan required for proposed works. THE OPERA AT DILLON COLLEGE: POLICE PROCEED- INGS —Before Mr. W. Bliukhorn, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the Rev. Joseph Predeck, priest, in charge of Ditton Hall Jesuit College, was summoned for suffering a stage play to be performed in St. Mary's Catholic School- room without having a licence.—Mr. J. T. Moore, Warring- ton, appeared for the defendant, and plea led guilty.— Superietendent Barker stated that on the 18th October it was brought under his notice that it was intended to per- form in the school named an opera, in three acts, entitled " Rosithorne, or the Sleeping Beauty." He instructed In- spector Wood to visit tho reverend defendant, and tell him that he ought not to perform the play without having first obtained a license, and that if he did so he would render himself liable to a penalty of £2O, and the persons taking part to a penalty of £lO each. lie also forwarded to the Reverend Mr. Predeck a copy of the journal "Justice of the Peace," which contained a statement as to the law on the subject. The opera was, however, performed on two occa- sions without a license, but as the defendant had admitted his mistake be (Superintendent Barker) did not desire to prese the case, and he was willing to withdraw the summons on payment of costs.—Mr. Moore characterised the Act of Parliament under which the summons was taken as absurd; but there was no other course open for him to pursue than to plead guilty, and trust to the clemency of the Bench.— His worship permitted the CASO to be settled on payment of costs, amounting to 7s. 6d. BIRTHS AND DEATHS IN RUNCORN AND DISTRICT.—Dur- ing the quarter which has just ended there were registered in England and Wales 225,459 births, and they yielded an annual rate of 330 per 1,000 of the population, estimated to I have been 27,132.449 in the middle of this year. The births are thus more than a third of the inhabitants of Che- shire, which in 1881 had 622,365. The deaths in England and Wales numbered 131,678, and they were equal to a rate of 197. They comprise I 69,907 melee and 64,771 females.' After deducting the deathe from the births, there was a natural increase of 90.781. In the September quarter of this year there was a very great falling off in the health of the town and sub-district of Runcorn, for the deaths were 136, and these were equal to an annual rate of 272 per 1,000 of the population—estimated to have been in the middle of this year 20,070, showing an increase of 867 on the total enumerated at the census of 1881. That rate was a very high one, and it was 6 8 more than that of the 50 great towns in England and Wales. In fact there was only one of them with a higher rate.

' The Runcorn Rifle Volunteers, as will be seen from an advertisement in another column, announce a grand con- cert to be given in the Public Hall on Teursday, Novem- ber 27th. SALE OF WORE AT RUNCORN. A sale of work was opened in Holy Trinity Girls' schoolroom, Runcorn, on Thursday afternoon. Its object was to aid the fund of ' the Church Pastoral Aid Society and the Church Mis- sionary Society. There was a stall containing fancy and useful articles of all descriptions in charge of Mrs. Preston and the ladies of the sewing class, and a refreshment stall presided over by Mrs. Lea, Mice Martin, Miss Tyrie, Mies Woods, and Miss Leathwood. In the evening there was the added attraction of a waxwork exhibition. The sale was continued last evening. THE GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WIDNES.—" Cap- tain " Elmes, who formerly had charge of the Widnes branch of the Salvation Army, has returned to the towp, and has, upon his own personal respensibilty, organised a gospel temperance mission. Several of his old followers and friends have already rallied round him, and on Monday evening a tea party and entertainment was given in Hud- son's Temperance Hall, which has been engaged for the work of the mission. There was a good audience, and Mr. R. A. Nayler, of Warrington, presided. Songs, recitations, were given, and Mr. Jessop's fife and drum band played several selections of music. CONCERT AT BUNCORN.—The members of the Mereey Missions Fife and Drum Band on Tuesday evening gave a concert of vocal and instrumental music in Bethesda school- room to a good audience. Mr. W. Shaw. the missionary, presided, and explained that the proceeds of the entertain- ment would he added to the funds of the bend. Under the leadership of Mr. W. Cooper, the band performed several selections of music in capital style, while individual mem- bers gave songs and recitations in a manner elicited the ap- preciative plaudits of the company. 'The names of the vo- calists and reciters are Messrs E. Hobson, A. Parson, D. Howard, T. Sounders, and J. W. Holt. Mr. J. Lightfoot gave a violin solo, and Master Clifford Le Coutier a piano- forte solo. Miss Jukes officiated as accompanist. THE ALLEGED GLYCERINE NUISANCE AT RUNCORN.— An adjourned meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners was held en Thursday, to consider the above ques- tion. Mr. R. Shaw presided, and there were present—Messrs. Meadowcroft, Briscoe, Lake, Norman, Dobson, Williams, Fisher, Taylor, Fairhurst, Speakman, Timmins, Linaker (law clerk), and Brookes (secretary). Mr. Thomas Harris took his seat, and signed the usual declaration —On the proposi- tion of Mr. P. Speakman, seconded by Mr. T. Norman, it was resolved that the application of Messrs. Clolos and Co., for permission to lay a sewer from their works to the cm- ' pool in front of the Royal Hotel, and the plans thereof be approved ; and that the Law Clerk be instructed to prepare a draft agreement embodying the terms which he would ad- vise the Commissioners to require for the protection of the Beard, and submit the same to the Parliamentary and Legal Committee. And that the agreement specially provide for the work being done to the satisfaction of the surveyor, and that the work be completed by the 31st December next. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. P. Briscoe. There were also present Messrs Coleburn, Whittaker, Roger- son, and Sebald (ecretary.) The Secretary's report sta- ted that the interments for the seven months ending Oc- tober 25th, numbered 218 ; . corresponding period last year, 186; increase 32. The fees received during the same period amounted to £238 13e id; last year, £l9O 18s 2d; increase, £47 14s 111—The Finance Commit- tee reported that the receipts for the month amoanted to £4B 13s sd, and there had been £9 9s paid in wages, and £39 4s 5d into the hank. Accounts amounting to £2 Ds 6cl were recommended for payment. It was recom- mended that a precept be sent to the overseers of the poor for £l2O payable on the 3rd December, and that consuls be purchased for that amount, and the dividends in the bank amounting to £125 8s 2d on sinking fund accept. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr.Coleburn, seconded by Mr ii Whittaker.—There was no other business of public interest. DIORAMA. OF ..COTLAND AT BUNCORN.—DnYing the past week the Public Hall has been occupied by Birrell's diorama of Scotland, and the entertainment provided is well worthy of the patranage of all admirers of Sc•tch scenery and the Scottish giants of literature—Scott and Burns. The views, highly beautiful as representations ef the wild and weird scenery of the country north the Tweed, are also especially interesting from the historical events associated with many of the places pourtrayed, the whole forming a picture gallery at once instructive and pleasing. In addi- tion there are Scottish songs and Scottish music by a com- pany of accomplished vocalists and instrumentalists. Miss Griselda Wess sings several favourite ballads with much artistic skill and finish, her performance as the "Bonnie Fish Wife" being particularly noticeable. Songs are also contributed by various other accomplished vocalists, and Miss Jemima Wyse dances a Scotch reel in graceful style. The ventriloquial performance of Professor Voce is exceed- ingly clever and amusing, and altogether the entertainment is one of great merit and excellence. Last evening was under the patropage of Captain Hazlehurst and the officers of the 2nd C.R.V. GOOD TEMPLARY AT WIDNES.—" Widnes ,Samaritan" Lodge : This lodge held its weekly session at 96, Victoria- road, on Monday evening, when the following officers were installed by Bro. Webb, L.D. : W C.T., Bro. W. Pearson; W.V.T., Sister A. Hewson ; P.W.C.T., Bro. Machin; W.S., Bro. B. Fairhurst; W F.S., Bro. W. Hewson ; W.T., Sis. S. Howson; W.C., Sister Smith; W.M., Bro. G. Wid- dors ; W.G., Bro. T. Widders •, W.Stl., Bro. D. Widders ; W.A.S.. Bro. J. Lamb; W.D.M., Sister L. R Widders.— " Haste to the Rescue" : The above lodge held their weekly meeting on Tuesday in the lodge room Major Cross-street, when there was a good attendance of members and visitors. During the evening there was one candidate initiated. After the usual business a discussion on the order took place, in which several mambos took part. The room has been cleaned, painted, and comfortably furnished. An enjoyable evening was spent.—" Star of Widnes" Lodge: The weekly session of this lodge was held on Wednesday even- ing, when an illuminated address acid a handsomely-bonnd bible were presented to Bro. Turton, D.G.W.C.T., in recog- nition of his long and faithful Cervices to the lodge. The presentation was made by brother Greig, and in acknowledg- ing the gifts Brother Turton displayed mach feeling. A coffee supper was afterwards partaken of, and the proceed- ings altogether were of a very pleasant character. BOARD OF GUARDIANS. —The fortnightly meeting of this body was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, when the Rev. Canon Barclay presided, there being also present— Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs E. Aaron, W. Handley, J. Mclntyre, T. Norman, J. Ashton, J. Highfield, W. Whit- taker, J. Derbyshire, J. Weir, C. Rigby, E. Wallington, W. H. Linaker (clerk), and H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—A let- ter was read giving the sanction of the Local Government Board to the appointment of Inspector Roche to the office of assistant relieving officer for Runcorn, at a salary of £3 per year.—A letter was read, in answer to the Board's in- quiry, dated from the office of the clerk of the peace, Ches- ter, stating that the Quarter Sessions had made the grant of £1:000 towards freeing the Dee bridges from tolls by virtue of the power given to them by a section of the Chester Im- provement Act. An extract from the Act was enclosed, empowering the justices at Quarter Sessions to call for con- tributions towards the bridge from the county stock or rates. —Mr. Aaron thought it was unjust that such a call should he made on the poor people of Cheshire and proposed that a committee should be appointed to draw up a presentment to be forwarded to the authorities at Chester.—The propo• sitien was adopted.—Mr. Handley reported that the Finance Committee had passed bills amounting to £35 2s and sta- ted that the House Committee was informed that the appli- ances available at the Workhouse in case of fire were very defective. The action of the Finance Committee was ap- proved, and it was decided to appoint a committee to in- quire into the question of the fire appliances.—This was all toe business. DEATH OF MRS. MIDDLEBROOK, OF RUNCORN.—At the advanced age of 99 years Mrs. Middlebrook, widow of the late Mr. John Middlebrook, died at her residence, High. street, Runcorn, on Wednesday.. Up to a recent date the deceased lady had enjoyed excellent health, arid the fact of her great age was often cited as a proof that the emanations of the chemical works had no serious effect upon the lon- gevity of the people in the neighbourhood. For 90 yeare she had lived in High-street, in close proximity to two chemical works. Her father, when she was " quite a girl," occupied the house now used as offices by Mr. 0. Leak, solicitor, and on her marriage with Mr. Middlebrook, who was a leading tradesman in the town, she resided with him in the premises where Messrs. Lea and Son now carry on the business of Ironmongers. Subsequently Mr. Middlebrook retired from business, and went to reside in the house where Mrs. Middlebrook concluded her existence. The deceased lady was aunt to Mr. Thomas Hazlehurst, whose munificent gifts to Wesleyan Methodism are so well known, and this relationehip and her own good qualities ceused her to be highly respected by those who were acquainted with her. Her mental faculties were keen and active to the last, and nothing gave her more gratification than to speak of Run- corn and its inhabitants as they were in her younger days, and to describe the changes which had taken place during her long life. She had been a thorough and consistent Wesleyan from her early days, and her name appears amongst the subscribers to the Wesleyan Missionary Society as early as 1817. Her remains will be interred at the Parish -Church. EXCITING TRAP ACCIDENT AT RIINCORN.—On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Thomas Norman attended the Board of Guardians at Dutton Workhouse, and was returning home in his trap, driven by his coachman, when he picked up Mr. James ‘Vilson, contractor, of Greenway-road. After ascend- ing the brow at Rocksavage, the coachman drove the car- riage close to the railings which run along the side of the road to avoid the deep ruts. After going a short distance a wheel came in contact with an upright stomp ; the horse was thrown violently against the railings and the vehicle overturned, throwing all the occupants heavily to the ground. The horse took fright, and rushed off at a terrific speed with the broken shafts and swingletree behind it. It continual its headlong flight on through Moughland's-lane, where the swingletree came in contact with a tree and was broken off. With only a small portion of the shaft attached to it the animal dashed along, leaped a wall, ran along the fields behind Stanley-villas, and then got into Greenwei- road byjurnping a fence. On arriving at Savage's Bridge the horae fell on the kerbstone, but quickly regained its feet, and continued in its furious course along High-street. Mr. T. Handley's cart was standing opposite the Post Office, and the driver seeing what was the matter drew it across the road, and thus stopped the affrighted runaway. The animal, which was very much bruised about various parts of the body, was led to Mr. Norman's stable by P.C.'s Kelly and Wallace. Mr. Norman and his coachmen escaped with a slight shaking, but Mr. Wilson had a rather severe cut on the left side of the face, and one of his wrists was very badly sprained.

"A FAMILY JAR" AT WIDNES.—JAn Evres appeared before the Widnes magistrate on Wednesday to answer a charge of assaulting ar.d threatening his wife Mary on the 10th inst.—Tee wife stated that her husband " beat " her because she had sold some things out of the house.—The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months. IMPROVEMENT OF THE BRIDGEWATF.II CANAL. The Bridgewater Navigation Company, who employ an immense number of barges aud steamers in the Liverpool shipping trade, intend to immediately commence operations for widen- ing and deepening the Old Quay Canal so as to render it capableof carrying vessels of 600 tons burden. It is expected that a considerable impetus will be given to the trade of Warrington and Runcorn by these improvements. A DEATH FROM kCOLLIERS' CONSUMPTION AT RUNCORN. —The Coroner has been warned of the death of John Clarke. 46 years of age, who had been in the army, but had recently worked at the bone works of Mr. Hatfield Weston. On th 7th inst. Clarke became ill, but until Thursday, when he became very seriously ill, no assistance was ob- tained. On that day Dr. Baguet' was called in, but death occurred before that genternan's arrival. Tbe doctor states death was caused through " Colliers' consumption." SALFORD AND THE SHIP CANAL.—Following up the de- cision recently come to at a meeting of ratepayers. the Sal- ford Town Council on Wednesday resolved to become joint promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal scheme. The money required for the purpose will come out of the boron ah fund or borough rate, and it hasbeen arranged that the total con- I tribution shall not exceed twopence in the pound for one year upon the annual rateable value of the borough. It was explained by the Mayor and other members of the Council that the liability of the Corporation will cease with the pas- sing of the bill. Ginr. THIEVES AT RUNCORN. Yesterday at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. W. Baokes and Mr. James Hand- ley, Mary Jane Doyle (15), Mary Dowd (15), and Mary Lavell (13) were charged with stealing a blanket, value 2s, the property of David Jones, of Stone-street. From the evidence of Mrs Jones, Mr. William Marsh, and P.C. Kelly, it appeared on the let inst., the prisoners were at Jones' house, and next morning Mrs Jones missed a blanket from the room in which they had been. When accused of the theft the prisoners denied their guilt, but on the evening 61 the day mentioned, Doyle and Dowd pawned the blanket with Messrs Marsh and Smith. Subsequently P.C. Kelly arrested the prisoner Doyle who acknowledged that she committed the theft, and stated Liven knew nothing about it.—Superintandent Leah said the girls were cast adrift on the world without anyone to care for them.—Doyle and Dowd were each fined 103 and costs, or 7 days' imprison- ment. Lavelle was discharged. ROBBERY FROM A RUNCORN PAWNBROKER.—Mary Hod- getts, a married woman Hiring apart from her husbacd, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court yesterday, charged with stealing two shawls and a driss and singlet, the pro- perty of Messrs Marsh and Smith, pawnbrokers, Church- street, Runcorn. The evidence showed that one of the shawls was missed from the shop on the 13th September, and the other articles on the 10th inst. On the latter day a boy named James Shaw, living in Perry-street, sew the prisoner in the shop conceal a bundle under the child's petticoats. It was proved that the prisoner pledged the singlet with Mr. Craddock, Church-street, the dress with Mr. Horatio Syred, Widnes, and the shawl with Mr. E. Imison, Chuich-street, Runcorn. On Tuesday P.S. Walley apprehended the prisoner, and in bar possession found 37 pawn tickets, and amongst them those relating to the stolen property. The prisoner, who acknowledged her guilt, was sentenced to a month's hard labour. ALLEGED THEFT OF ROPE AT RUNCORN.—Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, Thomas Threlfall, a young man, was charged on remand with stealing 19 pounds weight of rope, the property of Thomas Barton, captain of the flat, Emily Mary. On the 7th inst. the fiat was lying at the Old Quay, and Burton left it t 3 go home to Hartford. On the 11th inst. Mrs Ann Jane Leicester saw the prisoner on board the fiat handling a piece of rope, and acting as though he were a " hand "on the flat. Later she saw him carrying the rope (produced) towards to Mersey-street. On Tuesday morning the prisoner offered to sell the rope to Alfred Sant- ley, marine store dealer, but Santley had his suspicions as to how the prisoner became possessed of the rope aroused, and declined to purchase it. He afterwards gave informa- tion to the police. Subsequently P.C. Thompson arrested the prisoner, who denied committing the theft.—Evidence was called to prove that at the time th'e robbery was stated to have been committed, the prisoner was at home.—The prisoner was committed to Knutsford Sessions for trial. SID ENDING TO AN OLD MAN'S AMOURS AT RUNCORN.— On Wednesday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. G. L. Davies, Eleanor Reynolds and Alice Hampson, women of ill-fame and convicted thieves, were charged with having, on the 11th inst., stolen a silver watch, value £5, and a purse containing 255. from the house of Thomas Inman, Cholmondeley-street, Runcorn.—Reynolds, who is 39 years ef age, was engaged to be married to Inman, who has reached the advanced age of 65, and the benne had been published at the Parish •Church. 'The necessary period to elapse between the publication of the banns and the mar- riage ceremony would have expired on Sunday next, but Inman anticipating the ceremony, took Reynolds to grace his hearthstone a fortnight ago. Everything went on as "merry as a marriage bell" until Tuesday, when Reynolds invited Hampson to visit her new home and take a cup of tea. After the meal was concluded they appropriated the money of the absent husband elect, and also took bis silver watch, which was hanging over the fire place. On arriving home for his tea, Inman found the house deserted, and dis- covering the loss of his property, he gave information to the police. Later in the evening prisoners were arrested by P.C. Wallace. All the stolen money hat been spent, and the women had taken sufficient intoxicating liquor to make their condition somewhat elevated. Reynolds protested that she only took the watch to be mended.—His Worship, con- sidering the relation that existed between the prosecutor and Reynolds, discharged the prisoners after giving them a severe caution.

dare; 'but let resistance be met by re- sistance. We know what the result will be when their antique " China" comes in con- tact with the iron mug; it will go to pieces at the first touch. Let there be no compromise which in the re- motest degree affects the principle at stake; -no presentation of the Redistribution Bill until the Franchise Bill is put of harm's way. The Lords have sounded the note of battle; let them feel its shock. It is the Peers versus the People—the Five Hundred against the Five Millions. It is true the contest is absurdly unequal ; but how can it be other- wise? If the spiteful dwarf will persist in spoiling the work of the good-natured giant, the time must come when self-protection and self-respect alike demand that he shall teach • the imp to keep out of his way. The Peers and the People now stand in that relation to each other, and if the People are wise they will strike such a blow during the present conflict as will do something towards repair- ing the mischief of the past, and render their pitiful antagonists helpless, and therefore harmless, for the future.

UNITED CHESHIRE AND LANCABUIRE PERMANENT BENEFIT BUILDING SOCIETY, RUNCORN. The annual meeting of this society was held on Thursday night in the Holy Trinity schoolroom. Mr. Bimister was in the chair, and there was a large attendance of members, includinc Messrs S. Taylor, .1. Littler, J. Poole, F. J. Nor- man, J. Unsworth, George Moss, A. Jordan, C. Johnson, Joseph Pritchard, W. Whittaker, P. Briscoe, F. A. Lake, J. Johnson, T. Stringfellow, and J. W. Lightbarn (secretary). The report showed that the profits for the year asnonnted to £2,170 lie 4d, and after deducting the working expenses of the society amounted to £1,999 Is 2d, out of which the Com- mittee have spent £207 8s 3d in ordinary repairs, and £540 Os 91 in improvements and extraordinary repairs to pro- perties in possession of the society. These deductions left a net balance of profit of £1,251 39. 21, one-tenth of which would be carried to the reserve fund proper, the remaining portion £1,126 Oa. 81, of undivided profit added to the re- serve fend of £5,162 19s. 31., save a balance of assets over liabilities of £6,414 2s sd, being nearly equal to one-fifth of the entire liabilities of the society. The report stated that the propriety of spending large sums in improvements and extraordinary repairs, combined with the stricter supervi- sion which had been exercised over the properties, could not be more clearly illustrated than by the fact that previ- ous to the spending of these sums the net rent of properties only produced £1,691 16s. 5d., whereas in the present year they had produced £2,041 4e. 41., notwithstanding that the properties in possession had been reduced to £968 12s. lid, which sum was included in the Redemption Account, and had been paid to withdrawing members. The Committee regretted that in the face of such a financial condition they Could neither pay a dividend nor make any advances on morNage in 'consequence of the number of withdrawal notices which had not yet been dis- charged, but trusted that with the earnest co-operation of the shareholders that difficulty might soon be overcome. The report was conaidered favourable, and, after a protracted discussion, the meeting was adjourned until December 11th, with a view of inducing withdrawing members tO) cancel their notices in the meantime, and el alloy the society to pay 3i per cent, to its members. It was stated that the society is legally unable to pay dividends allaile the withdrawing notices remained un-

satisfied, and the meeting was of opinion that, if the society succeeded in getting the notices cancelled, they would be able to pay 34. per amt. did that, after spending £540 in ex- traordinary repairs, a committee was, therefore appointed to communicate with the withdrawing members.—Messrs eSarn- nel Taylor, George Moss, and Tnoin is Stringfellow were re- elected members of the committee. Mr. Jabez Unsworth was appointed in place of Mr. George Rhodes, deceased. Mr, Jordan was appointed auditor in place of Mr. Rholes, and Messrs A. B. rouse and J. K. Digges were appointed Ste wards.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at Alforde Chambers on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were present Messrs. Wright, Midwood, Dutton, Carey, Gaskell, Houghton, T. Handley, Webster, Sadler, Dr. O'Keeffe, J. T. Allen (clerk), J. Carr (engineer), Iliggineon (survevor)., Dickson (nuisance inspector.) THE MANCHESTER SHIP Canal,. —The Chairman reported that the deputation appointed by the Board had met the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal, and had come to a better understanding as to what Widnes would require. Plans had been forwarded to the Board, and after several people in the town had been consulted, another interview would take place. THE NUISANCE FROM THE WASTE HEAPS.—Mr. Gaskell, jour. presented the report of the deputation that had met Mr. Fletcher and Dr. Aft:leek on the 23rd s October, and ac- companied them to the several waste deposits in the neigh- bourhood, Mr. Allen and Mr. Dickson also being present. The report stated 'The first heaps visited were those ad- joining the Widnes Central Station. On the south side of the line are old heaps, which in places were found to be hot and giving off a considerable quantity of gas, these heaps were laid in the old way without and will no doubt continue to be a nuisance for some time to cools unless the bad parts are either dug out or the face of the heap is 'walled' in such a way as to prevent further oxidation. On the north side of the line waste is being laid in consider- able quantities, and here the ' is being carried out, and is to a greet extent preventing nuisance, particularly where the waste has not been treated for the extraction of sulphur. The waste which has been so treated is always a source of danger, and special care is necessary with it. The deputation found waste of this description which had only been laid a few hours before their visit, ani which was al- ready hot. Still the deputation are of opinion that much greater care is taken in the laying of these heaps than was the case some little time back, and that as the bad places in the old heaps die out the nuisance will continue te The next deposits visited were those on West Each, where the 'welling is also being carried out. The two kinds of waste were found to be depositing here &so, and as was the case at the heaps previously inspected. The 'blown' waste was giving trouble. In conclusion the deputation are of opinion that there is a great improvement in the way in which the waste is now being laid, that the nuisance will further be diminished as the old heaps give up evolving gas. This improvement might be hastened by ' tne old heaps on the south side of the line near the Cen- tral Station, and the deputation are of opinion that the Board might suggest to Mr. Fletcher that this should be done. A further improvement might be effected by the use of water where practicable, and where necessary during the laying of the waste, inure particularly the waste which has been traded for the extraction of salphur."—Mr. Gaskell moved the adoption of the report, and that a copy be sent to Mr. Fleicher and Dr. Afileck, asking if they approved of the recommendations. Mr. Boughton seconded the pro- position, which was carried. THE ALLEGED POLLUTION OF SANKEY CANAL.—The Local Government Board forwarded a letter from the Town Clerk of St. Helens respecting the pollution of Sankey Canal. The letter stated that the Corporation had no pre- vious knowledge of the complaints by the inhabitants of Penketh, and an the Sankey Brook did not touch the town- ship except at the actual spot where it fell into the Mersey at a point 780 yards from any habitation, the Corporation did not understand why the Rural Authority spoke of this complaint as being the old question of the Sankey Brook. As to the statement that the canal became offensive after receiving the waters of Sankey Brook (41 miles from the boundary of St. Helens), it might be poiated out that this complaint, if well founded, might be permanently remedied by the London and North-western Railway Company con- structing a culvert to carry under the canal the brook waters which were believed to be of no importance to them for the keeping of the canal navigable —Dr. O'Keeffe moved that the clerk be instructed to make a record of the letter, se that next spring, or at the commencement of the summer, the matter might be referred to and the canal prevented from becoming a nuisance.—Mr. Gaskell asked whether there was any positive information as to the steps that were being taken to Cause the nuisance to cease. He thought the matter ought to be dealt with at present by the Health Com- mittee, and not shelved until next summer, when perhaps the nuisance would have occurred again and it would be too late to do anything. Cholera had already reached Paris, and it was extremely probable that the disease would visit England next summer.—Dr. O'Keeffe replied that he under- (stood that the London and North-Western Railway Company were taking steps to Wild a culvert, at the place where the brook entered the canal, to take the sewage under the canal into the river Mersey. He was willing that the letter should be referred to the Health Committee, and this course was adopted. THE RAINHILL SEWAGE FARM.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board stating that one of their inspectors had been instructed to visit Rainhill Sewage Farm, and report on the alleged pollution of a water course by sewage therefrom—The Chairman remarked that this was very satisfactory. THE 13vg-Laws.—A. letter was read from the Local Government Board with reference to the bye-laws, and Mr. Carey, in moving that it be referred to the General Purposes Committee, remarked that the committee hoped to be able to arrange the bye-laws shortly.—Dr. O'Keeffe seconded.— Carried. THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL.—The Clerk read a communication from the Local Goverement Board stating that the application of the Board to extend the term of the repayment of the loan of £670 for the site of an Infectious Diseases Hospital from 50 years to 100 years could not be acceded to. The Public Health Act precluded them from allowing a longer term than 60 years.—Dr. O'Keeffe pro• posed that the Clerk be instructed to apply for the term to be extended to 60 years —Mr. Handley seconded.—Car- tied. Trig NEW PUBLIC OFFICES.—The followirg letter was read from the Local Government Board :—" Whitehall 27th October, 1884. Sir,-1 am directed by the Local Go- vernment Board to advert to your letter of the 11th inst., transmitting copy application of the Widnes Local Board for sanction to the borrowing of £lO,OOO under their Local Act of 1875, for the erection of public offices and for the , repayment of loans, having regard to the recent practice of 1 Parliament and to Standing Order No. 173 a (C) of the House of Commons. At the same time lam directed to ask whether the proposed offices are merely rermired for enable. lug the Locel Board to transact their own business and that of their officers and servants under the Public Health Act, and if so whether they ought not be provided by means of ' money borrowed under that Act."—Mr. Handley proposed , that application be made to the Local Government Board ' for a provisional order under section 303 of the Public Health j Act, 1875, to amend the Widnes Improvement Act, 1867, I and the Widnes Local Board Act, 1875, by extending the time for the completion of the works to ten years from the passing of the provisional order; to confirm the power to borrow money for such works, and to specify the number of years for which such sum may be borrowed.—Mr. Gas- kelt seconded the motion, which was carried' MR. DUTTON ON GAS—This WATER SUPPLY.—The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee contained the monthly report of the engineer, who stated that the exhibi- tion of gas stoves, &c., wan in every respect quite a success. Order had been received for 31 cooking stoves during the past month, making a total of 60 now fixed. At the ex- hibition, and since, 17 heating stoves had been sold. The water in stock on October 15th, 1884, was 6,054,119 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had , averaged 1555 candles. On the 4th inst. the Widnes Alkali I Company, Limited, asked if the price of water to consumers - of 1,000,000 gallons per week would be further reduced, and to what extent. The Clerk was instructed to reply that the last reduction had only beers in force three months, but that it was hoped a further reduction could be made at the end of the financial year, March, 1885.—Mr. Gaskell moved, and Mr. Webster seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Dutton said he did not think the illuminating power of the gas satisfactory. He bad noticed recently that , it had evidently got the " blues "—(laughter) ;,-there was a very small part of the flame that was illuminating ; and if that was 15 candle light he thought it was quite time that it was 19 candle light. Last week remarks were ,:made about the moral darkness of Widnes, but be thought there was ample room for remarks about the phyical darkness of the place. The Board had the illumi- nating power in its own hands, and he did not see why they should not have gas with an illutninatingpower of 19, candles instead of 15. Referring to the application of the Vrrdnes Alkali Company, he said he believed that firm, had made several applications with respect to the price of water, and concessions had been made in a very liberal spirit. He had no doubt that if private consumers had the same privilege they would have considerable advantages which they did not now possess. He should be glad to know upon what principle the Gas Committee held out hopes of a further re- duction next year, if at present they were producing water for the manufacturers at an actual loss. He had visited the waterworks a few weeks ago, and he was very much pleased with the cleanliness and the internal arrangements of the place, and he congratulated Mr. Carr, the engineer, on the state of afiairs.—Mr. Gaskell, in reply,, said they could not supply gas with an illuminating power of /9 candles at the price of 15 candles. If the ratepayers were willing to pay an increased price for the gas, the committee would be pre- pared to make it of ieoreased power. The committee hopel to be able next year to reduce the price of water not only to the works but to alraonsumers of water. It was. however, a matter entirely dependent upon future conditions. Of course, as Mr. Dutton was well aware, there had been a falling off in the, supply of water from Stock's well for some time, and they were pumping an increased supply from Netherley in consq,uence.—The minutes wore adop.

ted. Hrouv.r.at l‘terrtas.--The Clerk had reported to toe Highway Committee that he had made inquiries respecting the blocking of the foothpaths from Moore-lane to Ditton, and had discovered that the Railway Company had pro- vided in their Parliamentary plans for an arch over the Old 13riae-road which had not been constructed, and that a footpath had also been diverted. He had written to the Riilway Company on the subject. The chairman (Nir. Nid.wood) awl tho Clerk were requested to see the company

and report. Instructions were given to report to Mr. Shaw, district manager of the London and North-Western Railway Company, that the gatekeeper at Anne-street crossing lead refused to open the large gates except for vehicular trainee —The following plans were approved :—Alterations to three 'houses in Kaladah-terrace for Messrs. J. Muspratt and Sons; two houses in Ryland-street for Mr. R. J. Hurst; seven houses in Gladstone-street and two housee in Dick- son-street for Mr. E. Seddon.—On the motion of Mr. Mid. wood, seconded by Mr. Sadler, the minutes were passed THE SEWERAGE .SCHEME.—The minutes of the Sewerage Committee contained the Engineer's report, which stated that the 'No. 1 contract sewerage works had been completed on the 25th ult. The total cost of the works erected by Mr. Evans under this contract was 7,323 4s sd. The engineer considered that the works under No. 2 contract would be completed in a fortnight from the 3rd November. The committee recommended that the offer of Mr. .1. Evans, the contractor, to provide a man to attend the flushing of the sewer so lone as the maintenance remained in his hands for the sum of £1 per week, be accepted. The committee bad inspected the defective portion of the No. 1 contract and the damaged portion of the Hutchinson's estate culvert, and re- commended that the defective portion of the brick culvert (about 40 yards) be reconstructed, and that the damaged portion of the estate culvert be repaired to thoreatisfaction of the utupir-( Mr. Radford) in the late arbitrrtion case as agreed noon; and that tenders for the work be at once ad- vertised for.—Mr. Carey moved, and Mr. Webster seconded, the cenfirtn ition of the minutes—Mr. Sadler said it seemed to him a great burden that a man should be employed at El a week to flush a sewer after an expense of upwards of £20,000 had been incurred. He wished for informationjon the matter.—Mr. Cetey replied that the Board must be aware that the mouth of the sewer could not be kept clean unless there was a certain flow of water through the sewer to wasla away the s ind banks which formed in the river. The flushing had to be performed until such time as there was sufficient water in the sewer to render flushing unneceasery. At the present time the sews.. was not being made Use of, but when the neighbourhood generally was connected with it it was expected there would be water sufficient. The Surveyor had suggested that they might get some overflew from Bower's Brook to assist in keeping the sewer clear. (Laughter.) He did not himself think there would be eneugh.—Mr. Sadler : A fine state of aft airs thet.—Mr. Carey : The sewer was constructed to drain a laree Area, and not one fourth of that area will be connected with the sewer.—The Chairmaa siid whatever the cost they would hive to keep the mouth of the sewer open.—la reely to Mr. Handley, Mr. Carey explained the minute referring to the damaged culvert, crating that it was dangerous in its present condition, sod that by the arbitra- tion proceedings the Board was liable to do the work.—Mr. Dutton considered this a sad state of things considering that they bad an eminent engineer to overlook the work.—The minutes were Adopted. THE HEALTH COoverrreg.— The Medical Officer repor- ted to this committee tilt during October there were 94 births, 42 56 per 1,000, and 48 deiths, 21 73 ner 1,000. There were 7 deaths amonget ctaildren one year and under, and 16 amongst children between 1 and 5 years. Zymotic diseases ceased 12 deaths—The Naieance Inspector stated that there tied been 10 cases of typhoid fever reported, and three had proved fatal. There bad been four deaths from measles, one from scarlet fever, and three from diarrhcea. He suggested that special attention should be at once given to the drainage arrangements of Bold-street," Robin Hood." Appleton-street, and the new property at Lowe Homee-lane. —The Market Insmetor reported that the receipts for Octo- ber amounted to £22 12s 101, being a decrease of 163 4d as compared with October, 1583.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Dr. O'Keefe, seconded by Mr.l Manley. FINANCE.—The Clerk had reported to the Finance Com- mittee that the S. and M. Railway Company, had paid 2276 5s 3d, b-ing mime half ef the costs if the Moos Brook Bridge litigation.--1 'he renewing accounts were recommended for payment :—Gas £349 I% 71, water £212 14s sd, highway £603, hospital £l4 las 6.1, sewerage £1,917 7s 11d, health £7O 85 44. finance £1,536 Os 54, and main sewerage £7 130 IL—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Wright, and the Board went in' 'emmittee.

RUNCORN SANITARY AUTHORITY. The esua.l fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held on Tuesday in the Board-room at the Workhouse, Dutton, under the presidency of Mr. .1. Ashton. There were also present Meserse J. Hiehfield, J. Mclntyre, E Aron. W. H. Linaker (clerk), H. Linaker (deputy cicrk), and J. Farring- ton (nuisance inspector.) THE QUESTION OF SEWAGE AT Wesruere—Mr. Aaron said that be thoaget the Clerk to the Authority should be em- powered to write to the Local Government Board for power to borrow money necessary for the completion of the new sewer at Weston. lie should ales propose that Mr. Charles Linaker go to Weston and prepare plans and speci- fications to be submitted to the Authority.—The Deputy Clerk read a letter dated from the Land Agency and Estate Office, Frodsham, and signed Charles Linaker, stating that he had seen the representative of the Mersey Salt and Brine Company, who had purchased from the Bridgewater Naviga- tion Company the field at Weston Point through which the old sewer runs, and that there woald be no difficulty in deal- log with them in arranging for a new sewer. At an inter- view at which Mr. Axton Was present it was arranged, sub- ject to the approval of the Authority, that the line of the new sewer should be as indicated by tracings enclosed. There would be no buildings constructed over the sewer in the line suggested, which was of some importance. The Deputy Clerk added that he, Mr. Aaron, and the Clerk had had an interview with the Solicitor, Manager, and Engineer of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, who had agreed to allow the new sewer to be constructed on condition that the site of the present sewer, which was useless, should be given to them—Mr. Aaron then formally moved that Mr. Charles Linaker be instructed to prepare the plane.—Mr. Mclntyre seconded the propesition, which was carried. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.— Dr. Adams, medical offi- cer' reported a further extension of the outhreaa of typhoid fever at Sweetman's Cettagee, Weston. The cases, he said, were at present doing well, the wall directions for preven- tive measures had been issued, and disinfectants had been freely used. ROCK SAVAGE FARM WATER St:Teem—Mr. Farrington stated that he had submitted a sample of the water supplied ' to the Rock Savage farm to the county analyet, and it was considered of a very good quality. MlSCELLANEGUS.—Communications were received from the Local Government Board signifying that it had been considered expedient to extend until JAnuary next several orders relating to the importation of rags from France and Italy.—lt was resolverdthat the sum of £l2O should be paid on account to Mr. E. Timmins for work done for the Au- thority under contract.—.& letter from the Local Govern- ment Board stated that the qnestion of the water supply of Frodaham parish was still under consideration. This was all the business of public interest.

EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT OF A WIDNES POSTMAN. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. elinkhorn, Roger Cusick, a youth living at Milton-road, was summoned for having on or about the 27th August un- lawfully and wilfully detained a letter to Inspector Wood, and divers other post letters the property of Her Majesty's Postmaster General.—Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted on be- half of the post-office authorities, and stated that if he proved the offence mentioned in the summons his Worship woulA have no alternative but to commit the defendant to the Assizes for trial. It appeared that the defendant was employed at the post-office as a telegraph messenger. On the 24th August the regular postman was away on his holi- days, and the defendant was put on duty as a temporary postman. On the 27th August the defendant was, handed several bundles of letters to be delivered by him. There were about 200 letters, and amongst them was one addressed to "Mr. Inspector Wood, Police Station, Widnes," and another to Mr. William 'Parton, Vine-street, Widnes, near Warrington." These letters were not, however, delivered, and they were not seen again until the 25th October. About six o'clock on the morning of that day a man named Golding was coining from his work at the Widnes Alkali Company with a torch in his hand, when he perceived in a manhole under the tunnel of the London and North- Western Railway Company &bundle of letters. Gelding is unable to read or write, and he took them home. His wife at once saw that they were post letters addressed to various people in the town, and she conveyed them to P.C. Almond, who banded them over to Inspector Wood at the police station. The constable then went to the place where the letters had been found and after a search he discovered ' hidden in several manholes in the tunnel a number of other letters, which were also headed over to Inspector Wood. The letters, numbering in all 120, were taken to the post- office and given to Mr. William Dandett, the postmaster. The Same day the letters were specially delivered to the proper addresses by Postman Case, who obtained.the en- velopes after the varioas persons had taken out the con- tents. The envelopes were placed in the possession of Mr. Dannett.—Three weeks afterwards the defendant was dis- charged from his.position.—Mr. Dannett, the postrnaste7,l William Golding, of Milifield-road ; Appleton, labourer at the Widnes Alkali Works; Phoebe Golding; William Turton, , foreman plumber at Messrs. Muspratt's works; Inspeator Wood, and PC: Almond gave evidence bearing out the ; above facteond the defendant was committed, to Liverpool . Assizes for trial. He was admitted to bail in two sureties of L2O each.

CHILD' MlGill)Bll.—At the Norwich Assiaes, on Wednes- day, before Mx. Justice Maniety, Edna Carter, 21, servant, was convicted of the murder of her illegitimate child,. aged two rears. whose body was found in a pond. The jury added a recommendation to mercy. Sentence of Joath 'MS

passed. . Ma. CGAMBERLLIN ON Tortvism.---Mr. Chamberlain,. writing, on the proposal to establish a Junior Liberal Club at Hereford, says the future is with the young. Liberalism Is the doctrine of progress and the trae religiez of humanity. Conservatism represents the instinct of self-preservation, old age a season of timidity, and youth one of generous 1 impulse. When an old man bscomes a Tory he follows natural instinct, but a junior Coaservative sins against the light, and prematurely accepts the creed of decrepitude and decay. AN ABSCONDING CLERIC.—i2,OOO D3FALCVTIONS.—It IS understood that a young man employed in a confidential position by a Liverpool firm, doing a considerable business in goods on which a large Custom duty is chargeable, has disappeared after having embezzled £3,000 of his orn- ployers' money, which was paid to him for the purpose of releasing goods from bond. It is said that he had re- cently won £1,500 on horse racing, and that he has made his way to New York with his winnings and the amount of his defalcations.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

Lodinoxr, THURSDAY. The rapid disposal of the Franchise Bill in the House of Commons has brought us within measurable distance of the real crisis in its history and in that of the House of Lords. The movements of the controversy during the past week have been truly kaleidoscopic. When I last wrote there was an appearance, amounting almost to cer- tainty, that the questeen would be amicably settled. What took place last Friday so greatly strengthened this view ' that a settlement came to be spoken of as if it were already an accomplished fact. But the result of the South War- wickshire election changed all that. That it should have done so is certainly not rebutting evidencs against the libel that the Tory party is the stupid party. Supposing South Warwickshire had been a Liberal constituency for fifty years and being now fought had been won over to the Tories, there would have been something encouraging in it. But, as everyone knows, the facts are exactly the other way. For fifty years South Warwickshire has been a Tory strong- hold. At the general election, largely for personal reasons, a Liberal carnedu second on the poll. Now this seat has returned to its hereditary owners the event has turned the heads of the Tories, who see in it evidence that, as they ate accustomed to say, the country is with them.

Nothing could be more strongly or dramatically marked than the change of front accomplished by the party. On Friday night we have Sir R. Cross in the House of Com- mons almost plaintively beseeching the Government to do something to deliver the Conservatives out of their dim. calties. Anything would do for them. If not a bill, then resolutions. On Sunday evening a little party informally met at Lord Salis:..ury's house in Arlington-street, where the situation, as illumined by the South Warwickshire election, was discussed. What passed was private. But it was sufficiently indicated by the appearance of Mr. James Lowther on Monday night. "Jimmy," as this sporting politician is familiarly called in the House, speaking from the very place at which Sir Richard Cross bad stood on the previous Friday, threw over that respectable and well- meaning person, even denouncing as "backstair intrigue" his suggested settlement of the difficulty by means of reso- lutions.

Such a "turn about" hat never heel seen since Jim Crow retired from business. There was no mistaking the seriousness and deliberateness of the movement. It might have been thouilit at first that ,lirniny had kicked over the traces, and was having a lark on bte own account, an enter- prise of which he is quite capable. Sir SteffordNorthcote sat neat to him as he spoke, and what the Leader of the Op- position would say was anxiously looked for. Sir Stafford Northcote did not leave the House long in doubt. He joined Mr. Lowther in throwing over the hapless Sir Richard Cross, whose overtures for a settlement he contemptuously dismissed as "an °biter di:tinn." If this were not enough, and with the object of removing any lingering doubt, Lord John Manners appeared upon the scene on Tuesday night, and went quite as far as Mr. Lewther had gone. Lord Salisbury had evidently -succeeded, with the help of the South Warwickshire election, in winning over nits visitcre of Sunday night, and the Conservative party that on Friday was beginning to deliver itself from the toils of the destroyer, was on Monday fully committed to a policy of suicide. • - -• •

---- -- There are some people who cling to the idea that even at the last moment common sense and or dinary prudence will prevail, and the House of Lords will be delivered from the destruction the shadow of which even now overcasts them. That is a view which lam lingeringly inclined to share ; but confess that it rests upon no basis of fact or reasonable probability. It is simply born of the conviction that ElO men Can be so absolutely mad as, with their eyes wide open, to take the course Lord Salle bury advocates for the House of Lords. Actual facts point the other way and seem to make a settlement impossible. What have the Lords and the Conservative party to gain by such proceedings as those of Monday and Tuesday nights ?Supposing they are merely a feint, the difficulty of drawing back is sufficiently oppres- sive without increasing it by, in the penultimate moment, suddenly assuming a "No surrender "attitude. • Lord Sal- isbury must to-day mean business. But the safety ef his order and the peace of the country may find deliverance through other agencies, at present seemingly inactive. The declaration of Mr. Ritchie, the Conservative member for Tower Hamlets, who protested that he had beard with dis- may the speech of Lord John Mannera, finds a wide echo among the Conservative party in the H4119e of Commons, and is doubtless not unknown in the House of Lords. Mr. Gladstone, whilst declining to jeopardise the Franchise Bill, has gone the fall length of concession. On this ground sixty or seventy peers, not represented in Arlington-street, on Sunday night, may take their stand, and even at the last moment Lord Salisbury may learn that the House of Lords is not yet prepared or inclinectto commit suicide. It is a remarkable coincidenoe that sickaess should simultaneously have removed, from their Parliamentary duties Mr. Christopher Sykes and Mr. Robert Spencer. They represent on one side and the other the sublimity of dandyism in the House. It seems when reading in the newspapers references to "the Hon. Robert Spencer" or "Mr. Spencer" that it can have nothing to do with the light-heirted youth whom everybody in the House calls "Bobby." Bobby is really half brother to Earl Spencer, and representative in the House of Commons of an impor- tant•county constituency. To meet him in Parliament-street anyone might think that he was one of the mashers from the Gaiety Theatre who had lost his way to the Strand. At one time it was said to be the height of his ambition to wear more collar than Mr. Gladstone. He did this in self-sacri- ficing form, too, whilst the Premier wore stand-up collars in the shape and something of the size of the foresail of a yacht. Bobby had his cut and stitched after the strictest masher fashion, closely binding his neck and constantly cutting the lower part of his jaws. Mr. Gladstone has recently abandoned his phenomenal collars, which had at- tracted embarrassing attention in Punch. But Bobby stuck to his to the last, and to tboee who have watched him wear- ing those instruments of torture the marvel is net that he is ill now, but that he was not ill long ago. He is a light- hearted youth of simple manners and not very profound views. He is a general favourite in the House, and his ill- ness is universally regretted. Mr. Sykes, who also repre- sents a county constituency, is of quite another type. Tall In figure, grave in face, taciturn in manner, he moves about the House and stares about as if be were constantly wonder- ing what other people did there. The height of his ambi- tion is to entertain the Queen at dinner. He has many times enjoyed that honour.as far as the Prince of Wales is con- cerned. The Prince likes a good dinner and knows he would get it when Mr. Sykes is his host. Like Bobby" Chris- topher" is much quizzed by his acquaintances, but takes the attention in a different way. Whilst Bobby gaily laughs. Christopher regards the untimely humourist with a grave stare that hugely adds to the delight of the compaay. It is a long tima since a promised book was looked for- ward to with greater interest than Edward Yates's account, of his Recollections and Experiences, which Messrs. Bent- ley place in the hands of the public toagay. There was a general idea that a good many people would catch Mr. Yates bee only just turned into his fifties ; but few men have lived a busier life cast among better known people, and from experience of a gentle rap or two he occasionally deals out in the Prorld it was expected that his book would. be what is called piquant. Searchers after this charm will be distppointed in the two handsomely printed volumes which contain the Recollections. Mr. Yates might, I, am not sure he wort}d. have made a more attractive book •by the use of a little of that pepper ha is well known to hold in reserve. So far from being captious or spiteful. there beams throughout the book the kindliest spirit of brotherhood, and, when Mr. Yates has to mention any person with whom he has come in contact he says the very best things possible of him. There are two allegorical illustrations in the volumes, the one labelled "Work, 184 T-1870." presenting a view 0 the Post Office, St. Martrins-le-Grand ; the other to a pretty scene on the river Thames, with a wolimppointed siaiarn launch in the foregroand. This is labelled" Leisure, I 883," It is from the deck of this steam lauaeh, surrounded by the luxuries of life, and encompassed by the beauties of the scaeery that Yates looks back on his busy, tile. No one who. reads the book can grudge him his possessions, for they have been well earned. Within a year after the founding of the World, he woke op and f ound himself wealthy, and his prosperity, he himself testi- fies, has since been steradily advancing. Bt before that we have a long record o 5 labour boldly faced,.cheerfully and skilfully grappled with. He has in his time played many parts. He has 1111 e/ an office in the postal department, he has written plays, edited books, founded journals and con- ducted them, is a aovelist and was a poet, has seen the world as special eorreepondent, and has made money by lecturing in the 'United States. The scenes of this varied and active life are jotted down in these two volumes with all the charm of Mr. Yates's literary style. He brings home in a few touches of consummatesart the personality of. men whose names are familiar to. the public, from the heights of Thackeray and Dickens down to James Hannay and Frank Smedley. The interest of the book is varied and abounding, and the story is tad in a way that would light.en up much drearier passages in life. I hear !roma fellow-actor a curious complaint about Mr Terries, who is now playing Romeo, with Misa Mary Ander- son as Juliet. Mr. Terries has always had a fenc.iag part wherever fencleg was to be dene, and has acqr,ired con- siderable proficiency in the art. But so strong is boa dramatic instinct that he throws himself with dangerous vigour into the business of the moment, and his adversary finds himself hardly pressed. One gentleinan whom the chancea of the stage frequently brings fase to face with Terris., in deadly mulct bears about oa his bo.aY many scan. It has come to pass that an oncennter with this vigorous actor is a matter that no man with a family can enter upon with a light heart. It lalts been taid, with great truth, that whatever disad-
vantages a war may have, it makes people acquainted

. . geography. It also conduces to accuracy in the pronuncia- of foreign names. Everyone will remember the varying pronunciation of Cetewayo's name, till the Colonial Secre- tary, who had been carefully coached, recited in the House of dommons the pronunciation now generally accepted. The recent controversy between Lord R. Churchill and Mr. Chamberlain is the House of Commons has raised the question of the pliper pronunciation of the word "deposi- tion." Mr. Gladstone persistently called this " deeposition," which, as far as my experience goes, is not usual. It would be interesting to know how the Premier would pronounce the root word "dep6t." In America this is always called" demo," with a strong emphasis on the first syllable. I never beard anyone in this country call it otherwise than " deppo." In the Memorials of Tekyl, now in the Pre, there is an illustration of his wit much needed far the hoformation of this generation. A Mr. Bankes, a terrible bore, wrote a History of Rome which somebody in Jelsyl's presence said was very bad. "Yet his Rome," said the wit, 'is better than hie company." It is necssaary to, explain that in Jesyl's time Rome was pronounced Room I think Henry Byron's rerbrtee on the same lines is better than this. Byron was at one time acting at Drury-lane, whilst Chat- terton was manager, the company being an• exceedinglV poor one. Chatterton, whagenerallv loosed after himself,. had luxuriously fitted up the managerial room. Byron looking in one night Chatterton showed biro round. " Nice- room ; isn't it?' be said. "Yes," maid Byrom in his moody way," its a good deal better thin your compactv%"

div.p: CADISHEAD.

SERISIONS.—The annual sermons on behalf a Wesleyan Foreign Missions were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel,. Cadishead, on Suuday, by the Rev. J. D. Tetley, of Man— chester. The discourses were listened to with deep.interest by the congregations. The rev. gentleman addressed the Sunday school in the afternoon. The public meeting on be— half of the above society was held on Tuesday evening,. Mr. J. Ward, of Altriocham, occupied the chair. The-report.. was read by the Res. R. Dillon. The deputation, the Rev. J. Hammond, late of the West Indies. delivered a speech on the claims of the world on the Christian Church,-com— pletely rousing the enthusiasm of the people. The choir rendered efficient service. The collections amounted to a little over £7. Imam CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The annual concert on behalf of the above was held in the tchool-room on Mon- day. The Rev. R. Martin occupied the chair. Miss Briggs opened the concert with a pianoforte solo, after which the Church choir sang a glee Mark the merry elves." Mr_ W. Sharpies sang Love's request," for which he was de— servedly encored. Mr. J. H. Patterson sang several comic songs. Miss Curtis sang "Dream faces " and " Going to market," for both of which she was encored. Other songs. were sung by her brother (encored), Mr. Geodier Mr. C. H. Patterson, and a topical and " local " duett by Messrs. F. Sharpies and C. Patterson, all of whom acquitted them- selves creditably. Readings were also given by Messrs. Farrell, J. H. Ashe, and J. Garner. Mr. Sbawcross recited: "The fireman's wedding." At the close, Mr. Martin an- nounced that the money obtained would be devoted to. giving the scholars a Christmas treat.
