THE INFIRMARY CONCERT AT WARRINGTON. The annual concert promoted by the Workingmen's In- firmary Committee was held in the Public Hall on Saturday evening, and was again attended by a crowded audience. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and prior to the concert commencing he said that concert was in aid of one of the best institutions of which Warrington could boast, namely, their noble Infirmary. (Applause.) He was de- lighted to find present that night their good friend Mr. Beamont, the chairman of the Management Committee of the Institution, which was so much indebted to him Incite present position. (Applause.) If there was any institution in Warrington of which they should be proud it was their Infirmary. (Hear, hear.) tie did not suppose there was a better managed institution in England. It was compara- tively a small one, but be was quite sure of this, that the good done by it to poor suffering humanity was more than most people imagined. (Hear, hear.) It was not long since they had no Infirmary, and when a poor unfortunate man met with a serious accident there was nothing for it but to put him in a train and convey him to Manchester or Liverpool, and they could readily imagine how much suf- fering the journey would cause him. However, at length a fund was raised to erect the building in Warrington with which they were all well acquainted and so thankful for; and it must be a source of pleasure to them to know that these conoerts, which were inaugurated three or four years ago, had been so pre-eminently successful in their financial results. (Applause.) On the last occasion the concert realised upwards of £6O; and if he were to judge from the splendid audience he saw before him that evening, he was sanguine enough to believe that the proceeds of the present concert would not be very much less, if any at all. (Ap- plause.) He then mentioned that Sir Gilbert Greenall (who was present) had given a contribution of £5. (Ap- plause.)—The concert, which was then commenced, was in most respects a very creditable one, see- ing that the services of all the local vocalists and instrumentalists had been given gratuitously. One of the best features of the proceedings were the performances of a large band composed of members of the Warrington Orchestral Union, who were under the skilful direction of Mr. C. H. Pigot. The arrangements for the concert had been again gratuitously undertaken by, Mr. G. Riley, who had been indefatigable in his efforts to make it as success- ful as possible. Mr. Riley also acted as an efficient accom- panist. The band having rendered an overtare " Teleia," the first vocalist to appear was Mr. Kennedy, who sang Mary of Argyll "in a very pleasing manner, and subse- quently was loudly applauded for his rendering of " The meeting of the waters," an Irish melody. Miss Holland at once won the favour of the audience by her treatment of the pretty song "Love not," and was rewarded by an encore, when she sung" Cherry ripe." In the second part Miss Holland gave " The silver Rhine," and was again well re- ceived. Mr. Cavanagh's two songs were " The desert" and " Thou'rt passing hence," for both of which he was very cordially applauded. The most successful artiste, however, as far as popular applause went, was the comic singer, Mr. Manogue, who was repeatedly recalled. A solo on the piano was very skilfully gone through by Miss J. E. Picot, and received the warm encomiums of the audience. Two songs were also sung by Mrs. Lane, which, however, were not so successful as most of those by the other vocalists. —After the concert, Mr. Roberts, chairman of the Working- men's Committee moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor. which was seconded by Mr. B. Rudge and cordially carried. Mr. Dunbobin moved, and the Mayor seconded, a vote of thanks to the singers and those who had to do with the get- ting up of the concert, which was also carried. On Tuesday evening a meeting of the Working-men's Committee was held in the Town Hall, Mr. B. Rude pre- siding. It was stated that the total proceeds from the con- cert so far as had been then ascertained (including a dona- tion of £1 from Mr. W. Crosfield) was £7O 9s ; the ex- penses had been £l.B 163 lid, thus leaving a net prodt of £5l 12s aid.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Sacunnev.—There was no business. MONDAY—Before Mr. John Fairclough and Mr. P. Stubs. DRUNICENI,TESS.—The following charges were dealt with: —Mary Nolan, fined ss, including costs; Thomas Garvin, 5s and costs, or seven days; James Kelly, 5s and costs, or seven days; John Flannigan, 53 asd costs, or seven days; Peter Lawless, 5s and costs, or seven days; Edward Wil- cock, 5s and costs, or seven days •, Thomas Matmion, 5s and costs, or seven days; and Annie Hodgson, 10a and costs, or 14 days. THREATENING LANGUAGE.—AIbert Harrison was ordered to be hound over in his own recognisances of LIO, and one surety of £5, to keep the peace for six months, or a month's imprisonment in default, for using threatening language to- wards his wife, Mary Ann Bardeen. A SUPPOSED LUNATIC.—John Minton, apparently a tramp, was brought before the Bench under peculiar circum- stances. On Friday evening he was seen at Wilderepool acting in a strange manner, and at the instance of Inspector Spinks waa sent to the Workhouse for the night. On Saturday, however, be was again seen to be conducting himself in a strange manner, and was consequently detained. —He was remanded to the Workhouse authorities for medi- cal examination. DISTURBING TICE PEACE—Albert Stokes and William Moran were ordered to be bound over to keep the peace, I themselves in £lO each, and two sureties each in £5, for ' fighting, the former in Bridge-street and the latter in Better- market-street. A NEGLIGENT CARTER—John Smith, carter, was sum- moned for being at too great a distance from his cart, and was ordered to pay the costs, Cs. GUNPOWDER PLOT.—John Lee, a boy, was summoned for letting off fireworks in Kendrick-street.—He was dismissed with a caution. TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. Broadbent and Monks. The only case is reported elsewhere. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Webster and Mr. John Fairclosgh. DRUNKENNESS —Patrick Hanlon was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly in floreemarket-etreet ; and Michael Gilligan, charged with committing a similar offence in Sankey-street, was dismissed on promising to leave the town. Turrasats.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. DnuNnatramss.—William Yates. charged with being drunk and disorderly the previous day, was dismissed with a caution. ASSAULTING A POLICEILAN.—Thomas Miskell (30th ap- pearance) was fined 5s and costs, or seven days, for assault- ing P.C. Turner, in Foundry-street, the previous evening. CRUELTY TO A PONY.—Thomas Oakes, a boy. and Mat- thew Booth Lowe, pig-dealer, Sutton, were charged with cruelty to a pony.—Mr. Browne appeared for the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.—On Wednesday Inspector Greenwell, of the Royal Society, met the defen- dant Oakes in Sankey-street leading the pony, which was weik and lame and unfit to work. He ascertained that it belorged to Lowe, and that person afterwards told him that he brought the animal to Warrington to sell to be shot, but was sending it back becasse he thought he could get more money for it at St. Helens.—Oakes was fined 5s including costs, and Lowe 103 and costs. Fatray.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), and Mr. John White. BEGGING.—Edward Mullin (16), a native of Roscommon, Ireland, and last from St. Helens. was brought up in cus- tody on a charge of begging in Church-street on the pre- vious evening.—He was dismissed with a caution. Misctusvors Boys.—Frederick Bird, Henry Cotterill, and Wm. Sutcliffe, boys, were fined 5s each, including costs, for doing damage to a brick field in Orford-lane, the property of Edward Bolton, on the Stla November.—Mr. A. Browne defended. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Elirlbah Powys was charged by Mary Griffiths with assaulting her.—The case was dis- missed.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. NONDAY.—Before Mr. William Bdnkes and Mr. James Handley. DRUNEENNESS.—Mary Ann Pearson, Elizabeth Santley, William Abrams, Thomas Ushin, Ambrose Bate. Jane Hicks, and Agnes Ford were each tined for being drunk and dis- orderly. BEGGING.—Joseph Simpson, an old soldier, was convicted of begging in Church-street, on Sunday, and was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. ScHoot, ATTENDANCE.—James Millington, of the Stone Hills, was summoned fer not sending his child regularly to school, and on the evidence of Mr. Bowyer he was fined ss.

NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. SATIIEDAY.—Bef ore COI. Geo. McCorquodale ; Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and A. C. McCorquodale. DRUNICENNESS.—WiIIiam Ronayne (for whom Mr. Moore, of Warrington, appeared), was summoned for being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on the 31st ult., and was fined Ss and costs.--William Bowser, for being drunk and dis- orderly at Earlestown on the 31st ult. was fined 5s and costs. --A like penalty was also imposed on Herbert Smith, for being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on the lot inst. --George White and John Harrison were together sum- moned for being drunk and disorderly at Haydock on the 7th inst., and were each fined 5s and costs.—James Heves was fined 5s and costs for a like offence committed at Havdock on the Ist inst.--James Jackson was also fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly on Oc- tober 24th, at Haydock,--Michael Owens, for being drunk and disorderly at Haydock on the 27th ult, was fined 5s and costs.

She was fined 5s and costs.—Joseph Gresty was summoned for being drunk and disorderly at Windle, on the 4th inst., and was fined 5s and costs. CHIMNET-FIRING.—The following persons were each fined 6d and 4s 6d costs for having the chimneys of their dwell- ing-heuses on fire :—James Buckley, Robin's-lane' Sutton; Wffl Thomas Whittle, Waterloo-street, hie ; and William Roberts, Randal-street, Windle. BREACH Of THE PEACE.—James Leyland and James Gerard were summoned for committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Bridge-street, Windle, on Saturday night—As there was a doubt in the case against Leyland the charge was dismissed, and Gerard was bound over to keep the peace. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. W. W. Pilkington and A. Sinclair.

DRENKENNESS.—James Flannagan, Wm. Barlow, Wm. Reid, Wm. Forbes, Dennis Maloney, and Joseph Waring were each fined Zs and costs for drunkenness. The follow- ing persons were each fined 7s 61 and costs for a like offence. —Ellen Armitage, Thomas Campbell, James Scarry, and Richard McCormick.

MISCELLANEOUS.—Jas. McCabe, Sutton, was fined 2s 6d and costs for using profane language at Sutton on the pre- vious Sunday night.—Peter Smith, a boy, was summoned for throwing stones at Sutton on the let inst., and was fined is and costs.—James Groves, of Eccleston, was summoned for allowing his horse to stray in Luesmore-lane, Sutton, and was fined Is 6d and costs.

WILFUL Droxitem.--James Banks. Eocleston, summoned for doing damage to the amount of 7s 6d to the door of a dwelling-house occupied by John 4cColeth, Peter-street, on the 2nd inst., was fined 10s and costs, and ordered to pay the damage.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

Cassell's fine art edition of Longfellow's poems sustains its high repute. Paq third to hand has for frontispiece a beautiful full-page illustration of the well-known " Hymn of the Moravian Nuns." The issue embraces also the poems on slavery, and a portion of" The Spanish Student." Part 10 of the lincyclopredic Dictionary does not get beyond the letter B, which is highly suggestive of the fullness of this really wonderful work. The two serial stories " Within the Clasp" and" John Ford" are both concluded in Cassell's Magazine for November. They are to be immediately fol- lowed by" A Diamond in the Rough" and "Sweet Chris- tabel," and, as some other new features are about to be in- troduced, it is a very suitable time for fresh readers to com- mence their acquaintance with this highly popular maga- zine. " The Quiver " for November has a striking fron- tispiece illustrating some lines on " The Return of the Pro- digal." The article occupying the first place is on " Clubs for Young Women," and is from the pen of Lord Brabazon. The new serial stories are " Mollie's Maidens " and "A Poor Man's Wife." George Weatherly contributes a poem (illustrated) on "Queen Margaret and King Malcolm." "Little Folks" is brisk as ever, and above the average this month in the way of pictures. " A Shipful of Children," being " Little Folks' Annual for 1885," is just out, price sixpence. It is full of lively stories, with the most comical illustrations by Harry Furness and other well- known artists. " Cassell's Illustrated Almanac for 1885" keeps its place as a sixpenny issue which is alike cheap and excellent. In addition to the stock topics, it includes a story by Mr. Cr. Manville Fenn. Part 7 of Popular Garden- ing leads off with a charming, coloured plate, representing% portion of the rockery at the Royal Horticultural Society's Gardens at Chiswick. Amongst the varied contents are papers (illustrated) on- Orchids, Florists, Flowers, Ferns, Rock and Wild Gardening, and Glass Structures and Appli- ances. "The Book of Health," which also reaches Part 7, deals with stimulants and narcotics and their relation to crime, lunacy, and pauperism, afterwards proceeding to treat of the effects of opium, chloral, tobacco, and tea. It need not be said that the number is a mine of ir.formation on these topics. "The English Illustrated Magazine " (Messrs. Macmillan and Co.) has for its leading article " A visit to Eton," illustrated by Mr. Herbert Railton and Mr. L Wain. Mr. Railton is an exceedingly clever young artist; nothing could be finer than his interiors. This month's issue is throughout all that could be desired. We observe that there is to be a double number for Christmas. The Rev. H. R. Haweis, M.A., incumbent of St. James's. Marylebone, bas issued a second edition of his "Key of Doctrine and Practice," price one shilling. The volume is a summary of over a score of sermons on the most interest- ing subjects, such as—to take the first half-dozen-Infidelity, Christianity, the Trinity, the Devil, Heaven, and Hell. The sermons are distinguished by the breadth of view and liber- ality of thought for which the author is noted; and not one of them is dull reading, which is a good deal to say under the circumstances.

"Trowel, Chisel, and Brush" is what it purports to be— "a concise manual of architecture, sculpture, and painting." It is .a neatly-bound volume, published by Messrs. Griffith and Earran at the price of one shilling, and is from the pen of Mr. Henry Grey, who has won a reputation by his "Classics for the Million," "A bird's-eye view of English Literature," Rzc. The book before us is as carefully finished as its predecessors, and will prove exceedingly useful as a book of reference for those who, in these days, want "much in little."

"Joseph and His Brethren, a Drama for Young People " by the Rev. R. Pitcher, WA., of Warrington, follows appro% priately upon "Alfred" by the same author. The old, and yet ever-new story of Joseph is treated with something of novelty and freshness. It is very dramatically presented, and yet highly suitable for the young folk of our Sunday schools. Mr. Pitcher has written in blank verse, which he handles on the whole effectively, though he sometimes takes more than "the poet's license." We give the following as a specimen of the finer passages of this excellent little work— _ _ _

Oh ! how caa I before my father stand Without his boy? For I stood surety ! I said, Lo! if I do not bring him safe Let blame be mine, as I shall blame deserve. Ah ! Sir ! have pity ! Kneeling at thy feet I ask to serve as bondsman in the place Of this, the youngest and the best beloved, And let him go lest the old man should die!

"The Printer's Devil " is a sixpenny brochure by " Anglo-Scotus," who will be pleasantly remembered as a former contributor to the columns of this journal. Indeed, a portion of the work has been before our readers in the shape of lettere. The additional matter gives evidence of wide re- search, and we need not say that it is lively reading. " The Printer's Devil" is brimful of fun, and should command a large sale. We have received a set of the Dramas and Dialogues published at twopence each by Mr. Abel Heywood & Co., 56, Oldham-street, Manchester. They are for the most part smartly written, and are admirably adapted for repre- sentation at schools and private parties, and ought to be in great demand during the winter months. For particulars as to titles, dr,c., we refer the reader to our advertising columns. Mr. Heywood publishes an "Amateur's guide to the law of musical and dramatic performances," which will be invaluable to those who wish to know their way about in these matters. He has also just issued" The Liberal Cabinet Photographic Almanac," which is illus- trated by portraits not only of members of the present Cabi- net, but of some other celebrities. Some of them are very striking likenesses. The accompanying letterpress gives information which will be valuable in the hands of wide- awake Liberals.

We have also to hand "The Season," and " Le Monitenr de la Mode," with their charmingly coloured plates and numerous original patterns and designs, together with " Myra's Journal of Dress and Fashion," and " Myra's Threepenny Journal ;" and an AB C Railway Guide for Manchester, which is exceedingly meritorious from its simplicity and clearness.

The Free Library Committee of the Chester Town Council, after trying the experiment of opening the free library on a Sunday for nearly two months, have resolved to close it on that day, in consequence of the small number of visi- tors:

The Hon. Charles R. Spencer, M.P. (brother of Earl Spencer) is seriously ill, having been obliged to take to his bed since lie returned home after the division of the Fran- chise Bill on Friday night. He is suffering from typhoid fever. - _

—A-Man named James William Pollard, who was stabbed in Soho, London, died irrithe Middlesex Hosoital on Tuesday night, and his alleged aisailant, James Walker, cdias Shaw- cross, who is in Custody, will now be brought up on a charge of murder:

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 15, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 15, 1884.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Boardroom at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. There were present—Messrs Cooper (in the chair), Harrison, Der- byshire, Appleton. Brown, Hunt, John Houghton, Forster, Mackie, William Houghton, Greenhall, Jeans Gibs. on, Owen, Rev. G. R. Roberts, Kilshall, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. 'Sutton (deputy clerk).

PROPOSED INCREASE OF SALARIES. The committee appointed by the Board to deal with the applications for increase of salaries recommended the follow- ing increases :—Miss Mackie, Workhouse school mistress, $5 ; Mr. Caldwell, inquiry officer, Newton district, £5 ; Mr. Basil Shearer, celiector, Warrington district, £lO. The committee further recommended the appointment of Mr. Samuel Sutton to the office of assistant clerk to the Guardians with an annual salary of £lls.—The CLERK said tbat as the committee meeting had only been held on the previous day it would be for the Board to decide whether they would deal with that report that day or at I their next meeting —Tie CHAIRMAN did not see why they ought to put it off to the next meeting.—Mr. HARRISON said there was a matter of great importance contained in the above recommendations, he would urge that their consider- ation be left over till the next meeting.—The CHAIRMAN : What is your reason for wishing to do that F—Mr. HARRI- SON : I think that a very important question will rise, and the Clerk himself suggests that it should be deferred.—The CLERK said he suggested that if it be deferred they should not discuss it —Mr. HARRISON said the fact that their chair- man was not there and that there was only a small atten- dance was a quite sufficient reason for adjourning it.—Mr. HUNT did not see why they should adjourn it, because the committee had carefully gone into the matter, and he was sure that if the whole Board had been present they would have done as the committee had done—Mr. APPLETON

thought that if the members of the Board had felt keenly on the subject they would have been present, they had all had notice. He, however, moved that the matter be ad- journed. The CLERK said Mr. Jolley had told him that he could not come, but that he con- curred in what the committee had done. Mr. FORSTER said that it seemed to him that one of the items they had before them meant the erection of a new office, and he wished to know whether it would be quite in order to rush :the matter through. He seconded Mr. Anpleton's proposaI.—Mr.DAREYSRIRE said none of the matters men- tioned in the committee's report came upon the Board as a surprise. They had been before the Board before, and the one alluded to by Mr. Forster had been laid before them so long as April last.—Mr. HARRISON thought the proposal of the committee practically meant the increase of the clerk's salary by £ll5, and he did not think it ought to be done hurriedly. If they resolved to go on with the question that day he had something more to say.—Mr HUNT said it was not correct to say the clerk's salary would be increased by £ll5, as his income had been lessened by £54 per annum owing to the triennial elections.—The CLERK said that Mr. Harrison's remarks were such as to convey a false impres- sion.—Mr. HARRISON: Oh, dear no —The CLERK said Mr. Harrison would not wish them to do so. but the facts were that in April last, before the whole Board, he asked for exactly that to be done which the committee on the previ- ous day after an inquiry recommended should be done.—Mr. HARRISON asked who attended the committee meeting.—The CLERK: Mr. Hunt, Mr. W. Houghton, Mr. Brown, and Mr. Darbyshire. Mr. Jolley could not attend, and Mr. Broad- bent was sitting on the bench that day, He (the clerk) wished to remove the impression that that was a matter which had come before the Board suddenly. In April last Major Cartwright had got up to support his (the clerk's) proposal, and two or three other Guardians did the same

The salary was now the same as it was in 1867, and was practically the same as his predecessor, Mr. Geddes, who was also Town Clerk, had received. At that time his (the cleik's) staff was one clerk, but he now had three clerks, who were paid by himself. He was appointed clerk to the Rural Sanitary Authority twelve years ago, and he bad never once asked for a revision of salary. He was appointed clerk to the School Attendance Committee, and he had never asked them to revise the terms of the appointment. He then pointed out the great increase ia the population and rateable value of the Union since his appointment, and the consequent increase of work to his office.—Mr. JEANS said that there were thirty elected members on the Board and fifteen ex-officio members, while there were only fifteen pre- sent that day. He thought, therefore, the matter ought to be adjourned till there was a fuller meeting. He did not think they ought to have an assistant clerk as tbe clerk should be responsible for all the duties of his office. The clerk ought to pay his assistant out of his own salary, and if his salary was not sufficient it ought to be increased—Dr. MACKIE thought the best friends of the clerk would vote for the matter not being settled that day. The clerk had such a complete case that he (Dr. Mackie) felt very little doubt in promising him his vote, at any rate on the lines suggested by Mr. Jeans. It was very undesirable that that matter should be settled in haste, and therefore be was in favour of

adjourning it.—lt was then unanimously agreed that the consideration of the subject should be adjourned, and on the motion of Mr. JEANS, it was decided that a committee meeting of the whole Board should be held next Wednesday to deal with it.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE thought the action taken by the Board reflected very much on the committee. ("No, no.") He did not see the use of appointing committees if their recommendations were to be treated in that way —After a little discussion, it was agreed that the ex-officio members should also be invited to attend the committee meeting to consider the increase of salary.

THE EAELESTOWN ANTI:VACCINATION SOCIETY. MISCELLANEOUS ENTENTAINMENT.—JUdging by the success of a miscellaneous entertainment held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, Earlestown, on Saturday evening under the auspices of the Earlestown Anti-Vaccination Society, the opponents of compulsory vaccination in Earlestown and district are still in strong force. The entertainment was in aid of the funds of the Anti-Vaccination Society, and it was in every respect a thorough success. The hall was crowded with an enthusiastic audience. During the evening Mr. George Wright (Earlestown) sang "The Village Blacksmith " with hie accustomed ability, and he met with a deserved recall. Miss Owen (Newton) beautifully rendered "Tit for Tat" and "Ever Faithfni," both songs being greatly appreciated. "The True Heart's Constancy" was given in an expressive manner by Mr. T. J. Gilmour, who was loudly applauded; and Miss Cameron (Newton), who in addition to accompanying the singers on the pianoforte, gave two excellent solos on the pianoforte, I cleverly performed her part. The principal feature of the entertainment was a selection of Lancashire sketches and readings by Messrs Butterworth and Travis,of Oldham. These gentlemen excited prolonged applause by their mirth-pro- voking recitations, ctn. Mr. Butterworth gave "Fast fleet at coortin ;" Mr. Travis, "William and Robber ;" and toge- ther they gave " Owd Betty and di' Census Chap," "Pop- ping the Question," selection from Fratchington's "Tim is cleonin' while Pegg is shoppin'," and "Tim comes whom drunk without coat, when Peggy gives him th' length of her tung." At the close the artistes were entertained with re- freshments, and were heartily thanked for their services by the committee.

div.head: EARLES TOWN.
div.p: EARLES TOWN.

A CARTER FINED. - James Woolley, of Warring- ton, was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions on Satur- day, for using his cart without a name at Newton on the 24th October. The case was proved by P.C. Jones, and the defendant was fined 5s and costs.

PHRENOLOGY. —On Thurscizy evening Professor T. Morris, the noted phrenologist and delineator of character, commenced a course of lectures on phrenology and charac- ter at the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street. There was a fair attendance, and the subject, "Heads, and how to read them," was treated in an interesting manner. CROW-LANE CATHOLIC CHAPEL.—In connection with St. Mary's Catholic Chapel, Crow-lane, an interesring lec- ture and entertainment were given in the Catholic Hall on Monday evening. The Rev. Father W. J. Byrne, of Gol- ' borne, spoke upon the "Humorous stories of the traits of the national character," and his address was highly appre- ciated. A programme of songs, recitations, &c., was after- wards gone through. DISCLTSSION AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB. The usual weekly meeting of the debating class was held at the Conservative Club, Earle-street, on Wednesday evening, when there was again a large attendance. Mr. IV. Mauds- ley occupied the chair. Mr. George Wright read an inter- esting paper on " Fair trade in comparison with our sba m Free Trade," and an instructive discussion ensued, which was ultimately adjourned until next Wednesday evening. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and also to Mr. Wright. GOOD TEMPLIRS MEETING. —The usual weekly ses- sion of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held on Monday evening in the Lodge-room, Bridge. street, there being a very good attendance. Bro. John Tay- lor, W.C.T., presided. A rehort was presented by Bro. Geo. Clarke, D.M., on the advisability of joining a proposed Temperance Union for Earlestown and Newton, and after some discussion it was unanimously decided to join the Union; and three representatives (Bro. Geo. Clarke, James Barnard, and E. Newman, W.S.) were appointed to repre- sent the lodge at a preliminary meeting. Other items of business haying been transacted, the programme for the evening was 'The Magic Post Office," the proceeds of which were in aid of the new banner fund. The meeting, closed at 9-45.

CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—Before Messrs R. Hough- ton, T. J. Gillespie, and A. C. McCorquodale, at the New- ton Town Hall, on Saturday, William Ellam was summoned for cruelty to a horse by causing it to be worked in an unfit state, and John Hightield was summoned for working the horse. Both defendants pleaded guilty.—lnspector Lock- weod, ef the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, stated that on the 25th ult he saw the defen- dant Hightield in charge of a bay horse attached to a cart. The horse was suffering from a canker, and matter was issu- ing from a wound en its body, while it walked very lame. —Mr. Moore of Warrington, appeared for the defendant Ellam and pleaded for a small penalty. He stated that as soon as his client knew the horse was unfit for work he had it stopped, and it had not since worked.—The Bench im- posed a fine of 103 an 4 costs on Ellam, and a fine of 2s 6d and costs on Highfield. THE EARLESTOWN EIBERA.L CLUB. —There was a large attendance at the Earlestown and District Liberal Club on Wednesday evening, when a discussion on the re- cent political disturbances at Birmingham took place. The chair was occupied by Mr. Thomas Howard. The question " Were the Radicals justified in the conduct they pursued ?" was introduced by Messrs. M. Birkhead and Joseph Stur- geon. Among the subsequent speakers were Messrs. P. Hall, E. Edwardson, C. A Luff man, W. Gilmour, Holyocke, and McEvoy. The general opinion of the speakers was that while the disturbance which had given rise to such discus- sion throughout the country must be deplored, it !had been caused by a fraud on the part of the Conservatives, who thus provoked the action which the Radicals adopted. The discussion was of an agreeable character, and concluded with a hearty vote of thanks to the chairman, on the motion of Mr. Gilmour, seconded by Mr. Edwardson. BILLIARD HANDICAP AT TEE CONSERVATIVE CLUB. The members of the Earlestown Conservative Club have this week manifested a keen interest in a billiard handi- cap which was commenced on Monday evening. The prizes are Ist, value £1 lOs ; 2nd, value £l. • 3rd, value 10s. About 60 members have entered, and the handicap- ping on the whole has given every satisfaction. Up to Friday the results were as follows :—T. Adams (23 points start) beat W. H. Shun (50) by 25 points; H. J. Dar- man (40) had a bye, T. Ashton (40) having with- drawn ; T. Owen (25) beat It. Harrison (20) by 25 ; J. Millington (45) beat R. Lythgoe (15) by 16 ; F. Jackson, (10) beat H. Rich (35) by 28; S. Leather (25) beat T. Kinrade (40) by 2; C. Singleton (25) beat N. Slinn (40) by 22; Cr. Slinn (35) beat G. Wright (15) by 24; J. Howe (50) beat John Gibson (45) by 16 ; P. Bent (owes 10) beat W. Baldwin (25) by 11 • J. Wrigley (35) beat W. Anhbury (30) by 4; J. Gray (40) beat J. Goslin (15) by 60; W. Blair (20) beat F. Emmett (15) by 26; James Gibson (50) beat J. Varley (45) by 9; W. Noss (20) beat J. Blakemore (20) by 10. PROPOSED TEMPERANCE UNlON.—Arrangements are being made for the formation of a Temperance Union for Earlestown and Newton, and as far as present appearances indicate the movement should meet with a great share of success. For a considerable time past the Bands of Hope and other temperance organisations have been nominally bound together by a united committee comprising represen- tatives of each society in the district. Their duty was principally to arrange for united demonstrations and gatherings, and to a certain extent this was carried out satisfactorily and with a degree of success. Many temper- ance corkers, however, have lately favoured the idea that a more active organisation, uniting the various societies in one common bond of sympathy and labour, and one to take a greater interest in the progress of each individual society was wanted in the neighbourhood. To attain this desired end, the suggestion has recently been brought before each of the temperance societies in the district, and so far as can be ascertained it has been well received. A meeting of the representatives of the various Bands of Hope and similar organisations will shortly be held, at which the question of forming a Temperance Union will be finally decided. TIIIS EARLESTOWN TUEATRE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs George McCorquodale, 11. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, and A. C. McCorquodale, George Bailey, of Earlestown, proprietor of the Alexandra Theatre, Market-place, Earlestown, applied for a renewal of his theatrical license for that building for the ensuing year. —The Clerk stated that Mr. Bailey had held the license for the theatre fer some years, and applied for its renewal. He asked if there was any objection to its renewal.—Superin- tendent Jackson : No, sir not at all.—The Chairman : Can you describe it to us. Is there plenty of opportunity for getting out in case of any fire or anything 7—Superin- tendent Jackson : Oh yes. You have only to put your shoulder to any part of it and push to bring the whole thing down, so that there is no danger to be apprehended from fire. Two years ago you asked me to look at it particularly and I found that the doors were ample; and all made to open outwards so that there would be no block in the event of anything happening. .It is only a temporary erection and could be shook down by any person putting his shoifider

against it.—The Chairman : Are you prepared to say that it has been properly conducted in time past ?—Superinten- dent Jackson : Yee, sir--The Bench granted the applica- tion, and Mr. B liley, with his two sureties, Messrs Henry Houghton and William Melling. were each bound over in the sum of £l.OO each for the good conduct of the theatre.
DIE EARLESTOWN BAPTIST Car: ANNIVERSARY
SERMONS AND TEA MEETING.—The anniversary sermons were preached in the Baptist Chapel, Market-street, Barks- .

. . town' on Sunday, and were largely attended. The morning and;af ternoon preacher was the Rev. J. Bennett Anderson, of Liverpool, and in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. W. C. Taylor, pastor, who selected as his subject "Hard work and bad pay." A collection was made at the close of each service in aid of the chapel fund, and the sum of £7 was realised. An enjoyable gathering was held in the some place on Monday evening, when the annual tea meeting was held. Some 200 persons sat down to an excel- lent tea, the tables being presided over by Mrs. Jackson, Mrs. G. F. Aveline, Mrs. Street, Mrs. Whiteman, Mrs. Adams, Mrs. Bradshaw, Mrs. Jones' Mrs. Walton, Mrs. T. Water- man, Mrs. W. Waterman, Miss Jackson, Miss Williams, Mrs. Phillips Mrs. E. Davies, Miss Aveline, Mrs. Evans, Mrs. Cooper, Miss Lambert, Miss Eckersley, Mrs. Mulreay, Mrs. Partington, Mrs. Mottram, and Mrs. Matthews. There was an increased attendance at the subsequent meeting. The chair was occupied by the Rev. W. C. Taylor, who was supported by the Rev. James Allatt, of Newton (Congrega- tional), and Mr. A. Pitt, of Liverpool. After the meeting had been opened with singing and prayer, Mr. G. F. Aveline read the annual report, which 'stated that during the past year five names had been added to the church roll, and they had lost two members by transfer, making a gain of three, the present number of church members 73. Mr. A. Pitt, of Liverpool, had kindly assisted them in their Sunday services, and the congrega- tions, though perhaps slowly, but nevertheless surely, were increasing in numbers. They had had a great demand for pews, and it was their intention to provide additional pews in a short time. Sunday school work was well sustained, there being at present 235 scholars and 17 teachers The various organisations in connection with the Sunday school were in good working order; the Band of Hope having 60 members, while there were 22 tract distributors under the direction of Mr. Thomas Howard, engaged in visiting 700 houses weekly; and the mothers' meetings continued to be well attended. With respect to the debt on the chapel, it had been reduced during the year by £2O, leaving it £390. They had had to build an additional class-room, estimated to cost £lOO, but at a great portion of the labour had been kindly given by members of the congiegation, It cost £53 only and that had been entirely paid off. (Ap- plause.) The amount raised during the year was £139, in addition to which was .215 from friends at Liverpool, and £l5 from the County Association of Baptist Churches. Mr. A. Pitt subsequently addressed the meeting, as did also the Rev. James Ailatt, who remarked that to some people the various churches and chapels in their midst were a sign of mere rivalry, jealousy, and everything that was unami- able and weakening. But to others they had a better and nobler suggestiveness about them—they bore witness,to the fact that in the hearts of mankind there was a conviction that man did not live by bread alone. He urged all present to try to lift up and elevate their fellow men. Addresses were also given by Mr. J. C. Farrie, of Liverpool; Mr. E. Mounsey, of Liverpool; and Mr. Adamson, Birmingham. The choir' under the conductorship of Mr. Holdsworth, sang "The Lord is my shepherd," Mr. E. Eckersley pre- siding at the harmonium. An instrumental duet by Messrs Holdsworth (clarionette), and Eckersley (harmonium) was warmly applauded.

div.head: TUE VACCINATION QUESTION.
div.p: TUE VACCINATION QUESTION.

The Clerk having submitted some vaccination returns, Mr. APPLETON asked what was the position the Board was now is with respect to vaccination.—The CLERK said he did not know whether the persons fined had paid their penalties or not. He contended it was the clear duty of the court to put the law into operation. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Buckton wrote to him to say that if the Guardians were to send to him the names of the persons against whom they wished proceedings to he taken, and the fees, proceedings should be taken. He (the clerk) wrote back to say that he could have no information as to who had paid, and that he (Mr. Buckton) must know who had paid and who had not paid, and he promised in the Guardians' name that if the penalties were recovered they would pay the costs. The truth was it had become exceedingly difficult to prosecute their business in the county magistrates' court, owing to the peculiar technical courses that were taken in a divided jurisdiction between two officers. He again repeated— whether it was policy or not—that it added to the difficul- ties of obtaining the due administration of justice in the courts of petty sessions within that Union. (Hear, hear ) Mr. JEANS thought it was the duty of Mr. Buckton and the police to enforce the orders of the magistrates. (Hear, hear, and a MEMBER: There is no doubt about it.) It was their duty, and it was not a question whether the Guardians would pay them or not. It was the duty of the magistrates and their clerk to carry out the law.—The CHAIRMAN said that owing to the law not being carried out the people were setting it at defiance. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. JEANS: I think It should be intimated to the clerk of the magistrates that he would be held responsible for the carrying out of the law.—This suggestion was understood to be agreed to.

div.head: CONTRACTS.
div.p: THE CONTRACTS.

Mr. OWEN brought forward a motion for the appointment of a committee to consider the best and fairest means of dealing with the contracts sent in to the Board, and in the course of his remarks he condemned the present loose sys- te.n of dealing with contracts.—Some discussion took place on the subject, from which it seemed to be the opinion of the Board that there should be some alterations in the way of looking into and deciding upon contracts.—After a short discussion, however, the subject dropped.

THE BOARD AND THE INFIRMARY. Dr. SPINES, who was present, complained of a man who bad broken his leg the previous •night having been sent to the Workhouse from the Infirmary. The man was not a pauper and had a home in the town. He (Dr. Spink9) ob- jected to being called out of bed at midnight to attend to these cases.—Mr. HARRISON asked if Dr. Spinks thought they had had no spare beds at the Infirmary.—Dr. SPINES : I cannot say, but there shonld be an explanation.—Mr. HARRISON said that before they judged the In- fimary they should be satisfied whether there had been accommodation for this person.—The RELIEV- ING OFFICER stated that the case had not been brought to his notice at all, and Mr. MACKIE, Workhouse master, said he had known nothing about it till the man was brought to the Workhouse in a cab.—The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS said it was simply a question for inquiry.—Mr. BROWN said it was not the only case, as about a month pre- viously there had been a,similar case—lt was agreed that the Clerk should inquire as to the cause of the man being sent to the Workhouse. This was all the businem

div.p: IIUYTON.
Co..

CHDRCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. The Huyton branch held their fortnightly meeting on Monday evening in the infant school, and it was the best attended meeting of the Reason, several persons being unable to obtain admission. The Rev. Canon Penrhyn presided. Addresses were given by Messrs James Davis, of Farnworth, and Mr. MacArthur. of Liverpool. A number of songs, readings, (Sze., enlivened the proceedings. ENTERTAINMENT AT HUTTON QUARRY. un Friday evening a most successful entertainment was given in the RO9O Cottage schoolroom, on behalf of th'e Wesleyan Chapel Fund. The artistes were principally from Stoneycroft, Liverpool, and an admirable prograikime was efficiently ren- dered, several encores being the result. Mr. J. B. Leach was the chairman, and Mr. David Kilshaw accompanied the several pieces on the pianoforte. The room was well filled, and the proceedings closed with the usual votes of thanks. _ -

HUTTON TEMPERANCE ASSOCILTION.---ihe above held their usual meeting in the Huyton Park schools on Tuesday evening. The Rev. J. W. Walker, B A., occupied the chair. and in his opening address congratulated the association on their being the means of diminishing the consumption Of intoxicating drinks in the neighbourhood, a public-house in Huyton Quarry having been obliged to close its doors owing to bad trade. Addresses were given by 'Mr. T. Smith and Mr. J. McCracken, of Liverpool. A pianoforte duet was well executed by Misses C. Williams and F. Leach ; songs were rendered by Messrs H. and P. Coppers; and a Yorkshire reading was given by the chairman. The room was well filled, giving evidence of the growing popu- larity of the meetings.
Lord Granville on Thursday unveiled a bust of the late Archbishop of Canterbury which has been placed in West- minster Abbey. There was a large gathering of members of both Houses of Parliament.

div.head: EARLESTOWN RATEPAYERS AND WARRINGTON
div.p: EARLESTOWN RATEPAYERS AND WARRINGTON
GUARDIANS. MEETING AT NEWTON.

On Thursday afternoon, a meeting -oll:atepayers, called by handbill, was held at the Town Hall, Newton, " for the purpose of taking steps to secure the election of a suitable ratepayer to fill the vacancy of Guardian caused by the death of the late Richard Walinsley." The meeting was announced for three o'clock, and at that hour there were some 30 or 40 ratepayers (principally from Earlestown) present. Among them were Messrs. Henry Hilton (over- seer), George Appleton (overseer and guardian), Thomas Hunt (guardian), Henry Houghton (assistant overseer), E. T. Evans, George Owen, James Woods, John Prescot, and other tradesmen, with a goodly number of working men. The proceedings might be described as short, sharp, and decisive, and of a lively character. After Mr. H. Hilton had been nnanimously elected chairman, Mr. Houghton read the notice convening the meeting. Mr. William Gilmour then rose and asked by whose authority, and why, the meeting had been called at three 'o'clock in the afternoon. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Appleton said he could reply te that. He suggested three o'clock in the afternoon to suit himself, for it was inconvenient for him to come in the evening, say six or seven o'clock.—Mr. Gilmour: Well, gentlemen, it has always been at seven o'clock.—The Chairman (interrupting): We never had one before.—Mr. Gilmour: We have had our ratepayers' meetings. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman: This is a special one.—Mr. Gil- mour: That is no matter, whether it is a special one or not. If itis a special meeting it strengthens my view of the matter. If there is something very special about it, the whole of the township should have an opportunity of being present. (Hear, hear.) He went on to say that to attend a meeting at three o'clock in the afternoon working-men had to sacrifice half a day. It might be suitable for shop- keepers and overseers, but it was not suitable for the general body of ratepayers. All they wanted was a fair, honest election. Be begged to wive "That in the opinion of this ' meeting the action recently taken by the Warrington Union Board of Guardians in refusing to fill the vacancy on the Board caused by the death of the late Mr. Richard Walmsley is out of place, and especially considering that about 18 months of the time is unexpired, and also at a time when there is so much agitation for a larger represen- tation; and further, that this meeting of ratepayers is strongly in favour of the vacancy being filled up, and calls upon the Warrington Union Board of Guardians to take steps that the vacancy be forthwith filled up." (Hear, hear.) He added that the reason why he pet the resolution was be- cause the Warrington Board of Guardians twice by resolu- tion had refused to fill the vacancy. Their (the ratepayers) representative, Overseer, and Guardian, as soon as the va- cancy occurred intimated very strongly to one or two of his Earlestown friends that the vacancy ought to be filled up, and said if they would only move in the matter and give him a few names to strengthen his hands be would nominate a candidate. But when the discassion took place at the Guardians' meeting the same in- dividual, he believed, never produced the requisition which had been signed by about 20 of the most influen- tial ratepayers of Earlestown ; and the Guardians never saw it, he believed. The individual he had alluded to was so inconsistent as to say that the ratepayers of that dis- trict did not want the vacancy filled up. He (Mr. Gil- mour) would appeal to the ratepayers present—that meet- ing at three o'clock in the afternoon showed very clearly that the ratepayers wanted it filling up, and were not go- ing to have the feather drawn over their eyes by one of the Guardians. Something had come out about the med- icine costing them 53 6d per 1,000, while in Warrington it only cost them 6d and that proved to them the neces- sity of having someone to look after the interests of the ratepayers of Earlestown and Newton. (Applause.) Mr. John Prescot had great pleasure in seconding the motion. He must say he was greatly astonished at his friend Mr. Appleton and the way he had acted in that matter. He and Mr. Appleton had been very friendly for a long number of years, and he never be- lieved that Mr. Appleton would have treated them as he had done. Mr. Appleton had confessed that that meeting had been fixed to suit his own convenience, and it was a candid confession of selfishness which was not to be found any- where else. (Hear, hear.) The Local Government Board wished to know the feelings of the ratepayers, but that meeting bad been called contrary to every precedent and the law of tbe land for a time when scarcely any of the rate- payers could attend. They ought to have someone on the Board of Guardians who would represent them, for they were not at present being represented. Some of the Guar- dians might represent themselves, or their own particular views or crotchets, but they did not represent the wishes of the ratepayers, who wanted someone to look after their interests in preference to his own. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas Hunt said the petition which had been allu- ded to was duly presented to the Board of Guardians, for he was present, and it was fully discussed, with the result that the Guardians came to the conclusion that there was no necessity to fill the vacancy. In reference to the charges far medicine he did not think the doctor had ex- ceeded his duty, but he had been too kind, for he had not only given medicine, but he bad given nourishment. He did not think the ratepayers of Newton were so uncharitable and inhuman that they would not give to their poor neigh- hour assistance and charity. He agreed with the doctor's proceeding, and they could not say anything against him.— Mr. Ratcliffe : That is not the question. The question is 'whether we want a guardian or not. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Hunt replied that he was only giving an explanation of what Mr. Gilmour had alluded to.—Mr. Ratcliffe thought they had enough to pay with their own rates without being bmevolent with the public money. (Hear, hear.) Whatever was just and due to the poor he was willing to pay without scruple, but they must be sure that the poor got it Mr. Prescot : They don't get 3d. out of the shilling.—Mr. Hunt stated there would be an expense in having an elec- tion.—Mr. Ratcliffe said he did not think it would make a single sixpence difference between electing a Guardian and not electing pne. He was in favour of having the vacancy filled up. (Applause.) The Chairman said they were rambling from tbe subject. They were met to consider the desirability of filfing the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Walmsley, and they ought to speak of nothing else at present —Mr. Hunt: I beg to propose there be no election without a just cause for it being shown.—Mr. Appleton, in seconding the motion, said the Guardians had refused to fill up two vacancies that had occured by deaths simply on account of the extra ex- pense that would have to be incurred by the respective town- ships. Whatever it cost the ratepayers would have to find the money, and if they thought it advisable they were per- fectly justified in having an election. He explained that he had called that meeting at three o'clock as a matter of con- venience to himself and others who were corn- ' palled to attend the weekly distribution of re- lief in the Newton township on Thursday afternoon. He did not think they could charge Dr. Watkins with in- consistency, for he was a honest, conscientioes, and per- severing man in the positien he held. No doubt if they decided to fill the vacancy they would nominate an anti. vaccinator. (Loud cries of" Order" and " Question.")— The Chairman: Order, gentlemen.—Mr. Prescot : I rise to a point of order.—Mr. Appleton : It is all right, I want to say— (Cries of "Question.")—Mr. Presoot : Some few moments ago--The Chairman (Interrupting): Mr. Appletor is in possession of the chair, I believe. You will have an opportunity of replying.—Mr. Present: Some few moments ago you asked us to keep to the point, and I heartily endorsed all you said. But Mr. Appleton in referring to the doctor and the anti- vaccinators is wide of the mark and wasting the time of the meeting. I have not Come here because I care a straw about the election, but to resent the fixing of the hour at three o'clock. (Applause.)—Mr. Appleton : And you have done that.—Mr. Gilmour: Therein another point. —Mr. Appleton: I did not interrupt you, and do not want to interrupt you.—Mr. Gilmour :, Keep to the point then. (Applause.)—Mr. Appleton : If you nominate a The Chairman (interrupting) : That is not in order.—Mr. Appleton: I will come to the point. I will second Mr. Hunt's amendment that the vacancy be not filled up.—Mr. Gilmour wished to correct Mr. Appleton upon one peint Tne Chairman: We are again departing from the point.— Mr. Gilmour said he was willing to keep to the point if be (the Chairman) would keep Mr. Appleton from throwing out insinuations and insults. Though he (Mr. Gilmour) did not mean to throw out insults he could do so if he wished.

W. Watkins (who had just entered) then asked if that meeting had been lezally called, without any notice having been sent to the Vicar or wardens of the parish.— The Chairman quoted a portion of the Act upon the point. Prescot : I say this is not at all necessary. Our friend the Doctor was not present when the notice was read. It was read legally at the commencement of the meeting, and I submit it is out of place to turn back now. (Hear, hear.) I move that we proceed with the business, and if there is anything illegal done here let the worthy Doctor take it lo the civil court or some other court. (Hear, bear.) The Chairman proceeded to put the amendment, where- upon Mr. Ratcliffe remarked that it looked bad it s hould have been moved by one Guardian and seconded by another Guardian. (Laughter.)-31r. Appleton; We are bath rate-

payers.—The Chairman: It shows there has been no collu- sion between the ratepayers and the Guardians. (Laughter.) —For the attrendment there voted only Mr. Appleton and Mr. Hunt, and the original resolution was carried with only these dissentients,'amid loud applause. Mr. Prescot then moved that future meetings of the rate- payers should be held at seven o'clock in the evening.—The Chairman said he personally would have been glad if that meeting had been called at that hour. (Applause.) After some further discussion he suggested that the point be raised at the annual meeting of ratepayers in March next, and Mr. Prescot withdrew his motion on that under- standing.
On the motion of Mr. Prescot, seconded by Mr. Ratcliffe, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and tke meeting concluded.

DARING BURGLARIES AT ST. HELENS AND EARLESTOWN. A clever capture was effected on Monday afternoon, when P.C. Gilligan succeeded in taking into custody, at St. Helens, a young man named George Eckersley, who was " wanted " for various robberies at St. Helens, Earlestown, Leigh, and Tyldesley. He was brought up at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday, before Alderman Mcßryde, and charged with burglariously breaking and entering the dwel- ling-house and shop, 91, Herbert-street, St. Helens Junction, some time between 10-30 p.m. on the sth inst. and 4-30 a.m. on the 6th inst, and stealing therefrom a black coat and quan- tity of groceries, value £1 Os 6d, the property of Joseph 11ilton. A second charge was preferred against him of breaking and entering a shop in Bridge-street, occupied by Thomas Harris, pawnbroker and clothier, Bridge-street, St. Helens,some time between 10-45 am, on the Bth instant and 7 a.m. on the 9th instant, and stealing therefrom eight over- coats, three dress coats, four pairs of trousers, two vests, two singlets, two shirts, and eight mufflers, value £l3 10s. Pri- soner was further charged with breaking and entering the bookiag office at Gerard's Bridge Railway Station, on Mon- day afternoon, and stealing therefrom 19s in silver and cop- per, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. From the evidence given, it appeared that the prisoner had gone about his nefarious practices in a cool and systematic manner. In the case of Mr. Hilton, he broke a pane in the scullery window, opened the sash, and entered, packed up the groceries in a basket, put on the coat over his own, and made off. Police-constable Mather met him walking down the railway in the direction of Rainhill. Being asked where he was going, he replied, 'lam going to St. Helena; I have COMA from Tyldesley, and missed my train at Newton." When he saw the officer approaching he had put the gro- ceries down under the railway bridge ; and on the officer taking him to the place he said he hail got them from his sister at Tvldesley. Mather and prisoner turned to go down the railway embankment, but the latter suddenly sprang back and made off, the officer being unable to catch him. Three nights afterwards he is said to have gone to the rear of the shop of Mr. Harris, in Bridge-street, forced the win- dow, wrenched away an iron bar, and entered. The shop was ransacked, and the prisoner carried off a large quantity of clothing. He had apparently tried on some clothing, and finding a coat that fitted him better than the one he had taken from Mr. Hilton's, he left the latter behind. When apprehended by Police-sergeant Gilligan' at nine on Monday night, he was completely attired in the stolen property. The other articles were found at hie lodgings Island's Brow, Merton Bank-lane. During Mon- day, and while the police were close upon his track, he turned up at Gerard's Bridge Railway Station, and while the stationmaster, Mr. Peter Hewitt (to whom he had spoken, saying he was a shoemaker from Wigan, and wanted to go to Earlestown), was away for a short time ha forced the booking office door open with a spade, and entered and took 19s. from the cash drawer, which also he had forced. —Prisoner, who appeared quite unconcerned whilst the evidence was being taken, bad nothing to say in reply to the charges. He was committed to the assizes for trial.— It may be stated that the prisoner's apprehension took place under singular circumstances. Daring Monday a number of constables in plain clothes were told off to watch for him. About nine o'clock Police Sergeant Gilligan re- ceived information that he was near the fair ground, and on proceeding there prisoner took to his heels, and a most exciting chase was witnessed, prisoner running through the principal streets of the town for about three-quarters of a mile before be was captured. THE PRISONER'S DOINGS AT NEWTON. On Wednesday morning the prisoner Eckersley was brought up at the Warrington Occasional Court, when he was committed for trial at the Assizes on three charges of burglary, viz :—(1) Breaking into the Liverpool Farm Re- formatory, Newton, on the 2nd November, and stealing three pairs of trousers and other articles; (2) breaking into the shop and dwelling-house of Mr. Siddeley, 8, Earle. street. Earlestown, on the 2nd November, and stealing various articles; and (3) breaking into the shop of Thomas Cooper, watchmaker and jeweller, 25, Market-street, Earles. town, on the sth November, and stealing jewellery valued at £25. He pleaded guilty to all the charges and manifested no concern at his position. The evidence showed that the burglaries were carried out very skilfully and with con- siderable daring. Prisoner was apprehended on Monday night at St. Helens for burglaries there, and when in cus- tody he was taxed with these other crimes, which he ad- mitted, telling the police where most of the articles could be recovered.—Mr. Eldridge, assistant schoolmaster at the Reformatory, deposed that on the 2nd inst he entered his bedroom and noticed that three drawers in his chest had been broken open and several pairs of trousers and other articles had been removed. The prisoner was formerly an inmate of the school and left about fours ago, since which time witness had not seen him.—P.C. Gilligan said he ap- prehended the prisoner at St. Helens, when he found the articles produced at his lodgings—P.S. Commins deposed that he received the prisoner in custody from last witness, and in reply to the charge, he said, "I did," and gave an account of what he did with the articles, adding that he would point out where they were. At one o'clock on the following morning prisoner took witness to a pit at Newton, where the trousers and other articles were found.—ln the second case, Nathaniel Siddeley, grocer, 8, Earle-street, said he found his premises had been broken into by the smashing of a pane of glass. All the drawers in the shop had been burst open and their contents scattered about the fleor.—ln the third charge Mrs. Cooper gave evidence to finding the shop having been broken into and the missing of 30 gold rings, 22 silver rings, 8 silver thimbles, 12 pairs of earrings, and other jewellery.— P.C. Gilligan said to the prisoner when he was apprehended "This is a caution—these goods have been stolen from Earlestown." The prisoner replied that they had been along with a portion of other property lying in an old stable near the railway station and in his lodgings. The sergeant afterwards went to the stable alluded to, where he found some of the articles concealed in a flue. On being charged by P.S. Commins the prisoner replied, " Yes, I took the pro- perty, and he (referring to P.C. Gilligan) has got it except what I lost when I was running away, or some stolen from where I had planted' it."—As previously stated the pri- soner was committed for trial on each of the charges. ocienortern : THE POLICE FIRED AT. The Golborne and Lowton districts have lately been in a state of excitement in consequence of several daring rob-, beries having been committed. Towards the end of last week several well-known houses in Lowten were visited. In one case a drawer was ransacked, but fortunately only Os was discovered. Had a paper been overturned which was lying at the bottom of the drawer, a considerable sum m gold would have been secured. An attempt was made to enter the Hare and Hounds public-house, pear Lowton Church, through one of the bedroom windows, but Mr. Churton (the landlord) had not retired for the night, and hearing his approach, the thieves ran away. Three farmers have since reported their premises to have been plundered, and more than 40 pigeons, hens, and ducks missing. But the most extensive raid was made early on Tuesday morn- ing, when some half-dozen men visited a farm between Lowton and Golborne, occupied by Mr. Hart. Here no fewer than twenty-nine hens, &c., were killed and " sacked " ready for carrying off, when the police (who were on the look-out for the thieves) ap- peared on the scene, and disturbed them in their work. Unfortunately the officer was single handed, but he at once whistled for two companions who had only just left him. Hearing the whistle answered the roughs took fight, but OR6 stopped and discharged a gun at the officer, who escaped in- jury, the shot flying over his bead. The police followed in pursuit, but failed to overtake any of the men. The rail- way company's coal office, which is rented by Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Co., was also broken into during Monday night, but there was nothing found that the thieves considered worth carrying away. The police are keeping a vigilant watch, and they are hopeful that this stete of things will oon be stamped out.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.
&nom, ATTENDANCE.—WiIIiam Shenton and Elias Top- ping, of Haydock, were each fined 5s at the New- ton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, for neglecting to send their children to school.

NEW POOR RATE.—The magistrates sitting at Newton. on Saturday last, sanctioned a poor rate at Bd. in the to meet the expenses for the half-year ending 25th March, 1885. Mr. Edwin Jackson, assistant overseer, made the application. THREATENING LANGUAGE,— At the Newton Petty Sea- Mons, on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie and A. C. MoCorquodale, two brothers named Thomas Pilling and James Pilling were summoned for using threatening language to Henry Low at Haydock on the 25th October.—The defendants, who were represented by Mr. Moor, solicitor, of Warrington, pleaded not guilty.-- The complainant stated that he lived next door to the defen- dants. On the date named the defendant James Pilling commenced to curse and swear at him. He (the defendant) said "You --- thing I should like to break your neck, and I will do some day." Complainant took no notice, whereupon the threat was repeated. The second de- fendant, Thomas, then interfered and threatened to run a drill through complainant. He was afraid of the defen- dants causing him some harm.—They were subsequently bound over to keep the peace.

FRIGHTFUL COLLIERY EXPLOSION.

-- - FIFTEEN LIVES LOST. A fatal explosion, involving the loss of fifteen lives, te°_,/r place at ten minutes past nine o'clock on Saturday eveninls' at the Hochin Colliery in the Sirhowv Valley, about W.: miles from Tredegar, and which belongs te the Tredege.; Coal and Iron Company. The shock was felt at a sign; box at Bedwelty pits about a mile away, and as soon as tu,", situation was realised, the officials of the London and Nat," Western Railway placed an engine and a van at the diepeer, of the colliery officials, in which Mr. Colquhoun genet manager, and others proceeded to the pit's mouth,t;undree' of persons hurrying thither from neighbouring cottages! It was known at the time that there were fifteen men in the pit engaged in repairing the pit roads, in addition to an en: gineman working half-way down the pit. The cries of tb latter were heard, and he was after some time rescued by exploring party, which was organised under the direction 0' Messrs Stratton and Reynolds. The force of the expleeiell had blown the engine-house and the ventilating fan at the pit's mouth to atoms, some heavy piecee of timber beinga found a hundred yards away. The cage was closely jarnin against the top, and the zinc roofing was scattered in ever, direction. The exploring party were only able to penetrate a little way into the workings owing to the absence of vee: tilation by the destruction of the fan' and they only fennel four bodies in their first descent, Three of these were iden' ' tified as Gwilym Owen, Evan Griffiths, and John Danis% but the fourth body was mutilated beyond recognition. A painful fatality occurred about two hours after the egdir sion. Ropes had been placid rourd the pit's month to keg) back the crowds of the friends and relatives of the unforte; nate miners; but one of these, a man named Pugh, state° to have been under the influence of drink, proffered assic tance but was prevented from approaching the pit's meet by the officials. He, however, rushed forward again, eyed; jog them, and approaching too close fell down the pit. ti was subsequently found at the bottom a mangled corpse' The result of the sad catastrophe has spread entire Ow!, over the neighbourhood. Great confidence was placed ir the safety of this colliery as being one of the best yen?' lated pits in South Wales. Had the explosion occurred 11;1., the daytime, or on any other night except Saturday nigh., the consequences must have been much more disastroaS• eis between three and four hundred men are employed. T,ljt, cause of the explosion is not i'et clear. The ventilating was restored about mid-day on Sunday, and the explofieg party again descended, and four other bodes were recovere all in a dreadfully mangled condition. Forty-three horses which were in the mine at the time 1:)f the explosion were killed, and a large body of men bee! been employed during the day in digging a hole near ti pit in which to bury them. The exploring party is still lt; the mine, and the ventilating fan is now working mecca! fully; they are expected to recover the remaining bodie? during the night. Several of the bodies already recovero were found in the main level, making it appear as if tbd were trying to escape. The rescued engineruan is progreer ing towards recovery. The inquest was formally opened at Tradegar on Tuesdale . and adjourned until the 24th inst. The explorers are still at work, but have been unable to recover the two bodies yet in the pit. Work will, it is hoped, be resumed in a fell days.

HOTEL-KEEPER AND COOK.—An hotel-keeper named dal* land was fined £3 by the Luton magistrates, on for assaulting his cook. It was alleged that, not being satin' Saturdalo fled with the plaintiff's services, he entered her room early' in the morning, and having pulled the clothes off the bed, threw over her, among other things, a jug of water. MASONARY AND TEMPERANCE.—A new Lodge of Fr,ey. masons was consecrated at Leeds on Saturday. by Deputy Provincial Grand Master of West Yorkshire (Lit Tew), to be conducted on temperance principles. Th 1"; was a large attendance of the members of the craft. Mayor of Leeds (Bro. E. Woodhouse) was installed as iira.Z. STARTING A WIFE TO DEATH.—CharIeS Briggs, -1 chemist, Clee, near Grimsby, indicted at the Notts an, Lincoln Assizes, on Saturday, for the murder of his wife bl starving her to death, was found guilty of manslaughle_l and was sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude. The mottl°. of the prisoner, who was also indicted for murder, tvae quitted. I SAD ACCIDENT TO CHILDREN —Three little children, t,be eldest of whom is six and the youngest two years old, on Tuesday playing with a can of gunpowder at Brad well,; village in Derbysihre. They had some matches, with WhiC they set fire to the powder, when the can exploded, and the children wore dreadfully injured. 'lwo of them are not 'e%. pected to recover. WIT AND HUMOUR. Charles Lamb said of a clumsy girl who was always pinning against things and breaking them, "I believe that girl would break the Bank of England if she should run against it!" "Doctor," said the grateful pati. ent, seizing the physician's hand, "I shall never forget that to you I owe my life !" " You exaggerate," returned the doctor mildly; "you owe me only for fifteen visits. That is the point which I hope • yon will not fail to remember." At dinner one evening a well-known actress was most amiable to a very young subaltern who sat next to her. He was mightily pleased at being on such good terms with a live actress. Suddenly she said, in her artless pretty man- ner, " I am to take a boy's part in a new play, and I have been watching you ever since we were introduced. You don't mind, do you ?" A sculptor recently produced the likeness of a celebrated personage, in whose biography it was mentioned that he regarded architecture as a very secondary art. The son of this personage visited the artist's studio for the purpose of examining the bust, when, after considering it with the air of a connoisseur, he inquired, " Could you not express more clearly his contempt for architecture ?" "You ask me," wrote Douglas Jerrold once to a young man, "to supply you with a list of books, that you may purchase the same for your private delectation. My dear boy, receive this, and treasure it for a truth—no wise man ever purchases a book. Fools buy books, and wise men— borrow them. By respecting and acting upon this axiom you may obtain a very handsome library for nothing." Proof was being given as to the fact of a Mr. Jones having been on board an American steamboat when her boiler ex- ploded, Mrs. Jones, who lost both her husband and trunk, having brought an action for damages. A German witness, on being asked if he had seen Mr. Jones on board, replied, "I didn't see him aboard de boat de last time." "You didn't ?" said the company's lawyer, who thought his case , was now safe. "Where did you see Mr. Jones last ?" "Veil," said the German, " vhen de schmoke-pipe and me vas going up, ve met Jones coming down." WHY HE WAS SO VERY LITIERAL.—SOMe European ladies passing through Constantinople paid a visit to a certain high Turkish functionary. The host offered them refresh- ments, including a great variety of sweetmeats, always taking care to give one of the ladies double the quantity he gave to the others. Flattered by this marked attention, she put the question through the interpreter, "Why do you serve me more liberally than the rest ?" "Because you have a larger mouth," was the straightforward reply. PRINCELY STRATEGY.—Once, when visiting a small town in one of the smallest German States, the sovereign prince was received at the gates by 20 young damsels in white. As a piece of cunning strategy, the ten prettiest maidens were placed in the front rank and ten less pretty ones in the second. Charmed with the attractive appearance of the van- guard, his serene highness did what comported itself well with his sixty years and his princely dignity—he kissed every one of them on their beautiful foreheads. At the end of the front rank he made a sudden pause—only for a couple of seconds, however; then he beckoned to his adjutant. " Sparrenholz, here—go on with the rest." SPEAKING FROM EXPERIENCE —" They say that fish makes brains," remarked Mrs. Yeast to her friend, Mrs. Crimsonbeak, with whom she was dining the other day. "I don't believe it" replied thesmart hostess,who generally liked to have her own way. "Well, I do," said the visitor rather emphatically. "Well, I guess I ought to know," sharply exclaimed Mrs. Crimsonbank, losing her temper; "I've been eating it for the last 46 years !" WITHOUT ARGUMENT.—He was a young lawyer, and was delivering his maiden speech. Like most lawyers he was florid, rhetorical, scattering and tedious. For four weary hours he talked at the court and the jury, until everybody felt like lynching him. When he got through, his opponent, a grizzled old professional, arose, looked sweetly at the judge and said: "Your Honour, I will follow the example of my young friend who has just finished, and submit the case without argument." Thew he sat down, and the silence was large and oppressive.
