div.head: Tetterg to the editor.
div.p: Tetterg to the editor.

- CHURCH AND STATE. Sir,—Permit me to bring before the notice of your cor- respondent "Populi" the fact that a society has recently been formed. which has f. its objects "the discussion of matters of social and polit'lal interest (to the exclusion of purely party Illations), and the giving of lectures on pop- ular subjects.' The subject upon which he addressed you last week is clearly within the above objects, and I would suggest to " Poi:mil" that he should join the society, as be- ing the better way of arriving at an understanding on the points raised by him—upon which points I must candidly say that he has been misinformed—than opening a discus- Mon through your columns. I should be glad to add your correspondent's name to the list of members, after which I would set a night at Hs disposal for the discussion of the 'questions in which he seems to take interest. Or, if be does not care to become a member, I think I could make arrange- ments for him to give us a lecture should he feel so dis- posed. The society meets every Friday evening at eight o'clock. Any other information I shall be glad to supply.— Yours truly, H. J. WESTBROOK, Hon. Secretary of the Holy Trinity Literary and Debating Society. Stockton Heath.

div.head: RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.

Sir,—On perusing The Examiner about three weeks ago, my attention was drawn to a letter reflecting open the ser- mons which have been delivered in the Parish Church of Runcorn for the past two months or so, and coupling with one of them the name of the Rev. Mr. Madden. I was in- deed very sorry to observe that the writer, who signs him- self " A Churchman," should have sunk to the level of personalities. I think he might have had the good sense to have left.eut the name of the reverend gentleman, whom I don't suppose had done him any harm in h'e life. If that is the spirit in which Churchmen enter the .use of God, to "Criticise" and "sow dissension," I for one world advise them to discontinue ceming. People go to church to hear the word of God, to confess their sins, and to give thanks for the mercies vouchsafed unto them, not to expose and ridicule ministers of the Gospel, and I was very pleased to hear the Rev. T. M. Armsos, in an eloquent extempore ser- mon allude to these facts last Sunday evening. I guess the writer of that anonymous epistle, if he were present, most have felt stung to the quick upon hearing the clergyman exhorting the congregation to concentrate their thoughts upon the services of the Church, and not upon distant objects or trivialities. In conclusion I may say that the before-mentioned -"Churchman" mast have had very little respect for the "worthy vicar," as he designates him, or he would have refrained from wounding his feelings by drawing public attention to the manner in which the scriptures had been recently expounded in the church of which he has had sole charge for upwards of 36 years. ID&
STONJAHEG.
THE MAYOR'S DI
ER AND THE TOAST LIST.

reading your report of the proceedings referred 'to, I was very much astonished to observe that while the usual toasts were duly honoured, including that of the ex- member for the borough, what ought to have been one of the principal toasts of the evening, viz., the health of the member for the borough (John Gordon McMinnies, Esq.), was absolutely omitted. This is all the more inexplicable -seeing that only a week or two before the Mayor and the members of the Town Council had dined with Mr. McMinnies at Summer House. Such a piece of gross dis- courtesy is in my opinion unequalled in the annals of War- rington. and the question naturally arises, "Who is to blame for it?" The Mayor certainly had no toast list printed, or 'the omission of the one in question would quickly have been fresented by the Liberal members of the Town Council, but at the same time I do know that the propriety of seeing that the toast was drily submitted was considered by his Wor- ship, and why it was not carried out I am entirely at a loss to understand. Possibly the omission was accidentally arranged for in order that the ex-member's feeling might 'not be unduly harrowed, although I have observed that he has saved himself from as much of this as possible by care- fully absenting himself on every occasion from public gatherings in which it was probable that our worthy mem- ber would take part. It was also noticeable that whereas the invitations were ostensibly only to include the members of the Town Council and Corporation officials, they were se extended as to bring in a few prominent Tory outsiders, but not a single Liberal of note or Dissenting minister was •honoured (?) with his Worship's favour. Straws serve to show the way the current flows, and it is matters of this character which incline one to think that only a portion of the mantle of neutrality which was so graciously worn by his predecessors has fallen upon the present Mayor.— Yours, , A DISGUSTED LIBERAL.

div.head: PARISH CHURCH CHOIR.
div.p: THE PARISH CHURCH CHOIR.

Sir,—ln your last impression I read with pain a letter from Mr. C. E. Rowley, late organist at the Warrington Parish Church. Well, sir, lam not going to dispute any of the points he has raised, but will content myself by saying that I am surprised at his ungentlemanly conduct towards the Rector; and that he, Bimini" the liberal hospitality of the latter, and, I believe, hie private purse, should now in a tit of passion (which, no doubt, hereafter he will regret) divulge to the world what no doubt was told to him pri- vately and confidentially. If confidence is to be betrayed in this way, then those betraying it must no longer be called what most men prize—gentlemen. That is the opinion of many of Mr. Rovley's friends here. It further goes to show the Rector and all other rectors and incumbents the great desirability of not placing too much confidence in paid ecials of the church.—Yours respectfully, A FORMER C.W.
November 13, 1834. Sir,

Hurrah! the strike is o'er The battle's done. The choir's defeated The Rectlr's won. Bravo, Rector, for you are like the judge in Gilbert and Sullivan's "Trial by Jury" who says "Though all my law is fudge, yet I'll never never budge." etc., and budge you have not, but persisted in ignoring the whole body of your late choir. You might have known that, it you had kiceed several of the members out of one door they would have scome in at another, and trusting to this, and the popularity of the organist you had appointed you have again come off victorious. But what can, and do. the parishioners think of those members of the late choir, who pass a resolution to absent themselves from their place in church, until such time as the Rector should meet and consult them, and then eat their own words, and efface themselves before all men. After passing their resolution to absent themselves from the ser- vices of the church, until such time as the Rector and war- dens should meet the members of the choir, and passing it unanimously, what happens? They all absent themselves for "one Sunday," bat this, we are told, bad such an effect on one member's health, that he had to seek the invigora- ting air of Wales. and'was thankful when be returned home an the Saturday night to find an invitation for him to-join the new choir. What a chance ! Talk about honour" what is honour to being in the Parish Church choir ? But the Rector, forgetting that he ever had a choir, inserts an advertisement in the Warrington papers for tenor and bass singers. What a' blow; it:made some of the old members -twitch and tremble all over as though they had been seized with some kind of a stroke. What about our annual pic- nic now, and the supper that the Rector gives "ones " every " three years" when Gilbey's claret and Walker's 'XX are in abundance? Why did we ever •" t ome out?" But that is not the question now—how must we get in again is the question. The Rector won't have some back at any price. What excuse can we give to leave these out who will not eat the Rector's leek ? We most say, that to show our disapproval of the affair getting in The Exam- -iner, we have determined to "go in" and will never ven- ture to have an opinion of our own again. Now, air, these creatures who will be snubbed, insulted, -and ignored by our worthy Rector, have begged on again, after having committed the serious offence of exercising ,their own opinion. They are, to my mind, extraordinary freaks of nature, and I should advise your readers not to miss seeing. them in their stalls, at either morning or even- ing service ; they are perfectly harmless, as their past his- tory shows,—Yours, etc., ANTI-HUMBUG.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
Sir,—lt seems to be thought by some people that the Ship ,Canal will take away all the ills that the British working- man is heir to. Whilst it is being made, a golden shower of

sine or ten millions is to fall upon him, and when it is made it is to bring back the halcyon days of British 'industry. Your correspondent, "Clifford Dix," is apparently ,one of those who indulge in these, I am afraid, deluding visions. lie assumes that the canal will put our manufacturers in a position to compete successfully with foreign manufac- lurers. Now, sir, I had always thought that, owing to the superior skill of the workmen and the improved appliances they had at command, English manufacturers were more than able to compete, in almost every branch of industry, with their foreign rivals. What they cannot fight against is foreign tariffs; and how will the Ship Canal help them to .do this? at may perhaps reduce the freightage of goods so much a ton, but the foreign protectionists will meet this move by the simple but completely effective counter move Of raising their tariffs by an ectuivalent amount. Looked at from this point of view the canal will brifig anything but blessings to English working-men. At present the dues which are paid to the railway companies go into the pockets of English shareholders and English workmen; construct ' the Canal, and the saving in freightage at the home end to be secured at the exnense of these shareholders and workmen will be lost at the other end in order to enrich foreignexehequersrl am, air, tflc. CIVIS.

TEE SHIP CANAL POLL. Sir,—The poll which it is supposed will show the feeling of the owners ond ratepayers in respect of the proposed rate to help to pay the expense of getting s Ship Canal Bill through Parliament is to be taken at the end of nest week, and the result may be described as a foregone conclusion. The Ship Canal promoters are paying as agent of the Liberal party, and (I assume from their advertisement) the poor-rate collector for Warrington, to carry oat the work of :fling-up personally and by their assietants the " proxy " and " owner " claim forms of all who will allow them to fill them up in favour of the rate. Opposing owners have been left to procure as best they could the necessaty forms, and in some cases their representatives have been referred from the Town Clerk's office to the Ship Canal Agent's office for such forms, and there refused them. The owners and ratepayers are being waited upon and told that the Quanfacturore who memorialized the Mayor against the ate

div.head: have withdrawn their opposition; that practically everybody is now eager to support the rate and itching to fill up
div.p: have withdrawn their opposition; that practically every- body is now eager to support the rate and itching to fill up
MR. DIGGLE AND THE SHIP CANAL

ANOTHER SCREAMING FARCE. On Tuesday evening, Mr. William Digele, who is well known as a determined opponent of the Manchester Ship Canal Scheme, again appeared before the public of War- rington in the capagity of a lecturer. In accordance with an announcement, he addressed a meeting in the Co-opera- tive Hall, at which about 200 persons were present, having paid an admission fee of threepence each to "see the fun." That they would not be disappointed was well assured, as, on a previous occasion when Mr. Dingle delivered an address in the same building, the hilarity was extreme. Had there not been a counter attraction in the town in the shape of a circus that was performing on the fair ground Mr. Diggle might have obtained a still larger audience, as his peter of repartee and charming frankness in dealing with the chaff of his hearers are known and appreciated. A synopsis of the subjects with which Mr. Diggle would deal had been circulated, but it was generally understood that his remarks would chiefly be in opposition to the levying of a 2d. rate in aid of the promotion of the Ship Canal Scheme. For some time before the lecturer made his appearance a small table placed in the middle of the platform was the subject of much speculation. On it were placed several bottles of considerable proportions, a similar number of or- dinary tumblers, and a small phial fearfully suggestive of poison. Mr. Diggle, punctually at 7-30, made his entrance on the platform from the side door with an air befitting the importance of the occasion. He was greeted with la"ghter and ironical cheers. Probably bearing in mind the warmth and "unpleasant pleasantries" of a recent similar occasion, he informed the audience that it was not his intention to reply to any offensive remark that might be made. A minister preached his sermon, and he did not see why he should not preach his. This remark was received with laughter, and Mr. Diggle rather precipitately forgot his in- tention expressed in his opening remarks. He would, he said, far rather give "those lads " their money back and let them go out; he had hoped that the price would have kept them out. (Renewed laughter, and cries of "Nam,i a chairman.") The desirability of a chairman had been over- looked, and as Mr. Diggle did not appear to have made a selection, Inspector Spinks, of the borough police force, was nominated by the audience with much laughter. To this, however, Mr. Diggle objected, and in no complimentary manner. He had rather, he said, not have a " bobby " as chairman, although be hid to go to home under their pro• tection from two meetings. (Laughter.) Asa sweetener to the pill, however, he added that there was no one for whom he had more respect than "bobbies." (Renewed laughter.) Finally, Mr. J. L. Wilson was elected by the audience to take the chair this time, which he did, in spite of the feeble remonstrance of the lecturer, who pathetically re- marked that Mr. Wilson seemed more incliaed for fun than business. Mr, WILSON, however, announced that he should occupy the position in such a way as to please both the company and the lecturer. He should insist upon good order, and appealed to all not to interrupt in a frivolous manner. But if both lecturer and chairman were inclined for business the audience were more inclined for fun, and during the eubse- squent proceedings did not fail to manifest the inclination. A suspicious quietness having been obtained, Mr. DIOGLE prepared to give his address. He said th it it might seem strange that be should entertain views that differed so mach from those of a great number of his fellow. townsmen in reference to water and the canal. That night he should endeavour to show them why he took that course. They would perceive that reporters were present, so they Must let him go on. He was a ratepayer and a property. owner. (Laughter,) It was not a frivolotte matter that forced him to the coarse he was taking. He was a managing dyer, and had much to do with water. (Cries: "Sup," and "Speak up, Diggle.") He had got their money, and he would turn some of them out. He had been in business 22 years, and no one had suffered more agony—(laughte-) and suffered more pecuniarily from bad water than he had. (" What water," and renewed laughter.) It would be his endeavour to leave his hearers better thin he found them. (A Voice: "Who gets the Dickey up, Dingle ?" a remark having reference to the lecturer's display of shirt front, which caused roars of laughter.) They had in Warrington lost many trades, and he would show the way to regain them. It was a most serious matter. He had been in the cotton trade 15 years, and had seen about six panics. (" Good lad, Diggle," and laughter.)—The Chairman : Please speak to your point, Mr. Diggle. (Laughter, and cries of "He has none.")—Mr. Diggle : If they will not listen to my pre- liminary remarks how can I expect them to listen to my ad- dress. (Cat-calls and laughter.) He then commenced to read a list of different trades which had been carried on in Warrington, when he was interrupted by general disorder. Some chaff ensued between the audience and Mr. Diggle, after which he proceed( Ito say that Warrington was once noted for pinmaking.—(A Voice : "What, rolling pins ?" (laughter)—and another Voice : "Has tha sold thi houses yet r and laughter.).—Mr. Diggle : Tha's nooan to sell, I'll bet; if the had tha'd make less noise. (Laughter. )—The Chairman said that he had looked over the programme, and there were several items that woald prove of interest. —Mr. Dingle said he had thought that if he had hid anything to spare after payment for the room he would have had his address printed in pam- phlet form, but if they bad had threepennvworth he would go away. ("So, no," and laughter.) Pin- making had almost deserted them. Fustian cutting had been more successful, but it was dependent on the fashions. (A Voice : " Amen, Diggle.") Mr. Diggle: Tha should ha browt thi mother Wi this. The nest is pile-cutting and tool-making. (" What sort of tools," and laughter.) The next is cotton manufactures. We have had about eleven cotton mills in Warrington. (Cat calls, and a voice : "Shut up.") I say, officer, keep that lad quiet ; that foolish. thing, rake him to the fair and buy him a ha'-penny whistle. (Laughter.) What is the reason that we should only have two of these mills, and used to have eleven ? (" No reason, Diggle," laughter, and interruption.) I will not put up with all this trouble and thought on this mat- ter to be laughed at by a lot of boys. I don't care about being laughed at, but there are some here who want in- formation, Well, what is the reason ? (Renewed laughter.) Now, just don't laugh while I get through this, because it is important. (A voice " Go on, old Shylock," and laugh- ter.)—The Chairman: Will you quietly allow him to go on with the cotton business; he cannot keep on when you interrupt him.—Mr. Diggle again attempted to speak, and was again interrupted by derisive laughter and cat-calls, and he sat down. (A Voice: " Let's have a redistribution of seats.")—Mr. Diggle: Tha'll never be elected to a seat. (Liughter) I'll just do a bit of sitting down. (Laugh- ter.) Warrington with all its advantages—(interruption, and cries of "Stand up, Diggle.") You are not worth talking to, I'll talk to these: gentlemen (the reporters). Warrington with all its advantage—(Cries of "No whis- pering." " It is a public meeting." " Stand up," and " Don't be afraid.") I never am afraid, because I believe I have a good cause, and I want to do you good. (" Very good," and hear.) You had better bring your fathers here. (Laughter.) Mr. Diggle then endeavoured to show that the loss of trade was caused by bad water, and the puzzle of the bottles and glasses he endeavoured to explain. The water from the first bottle he said was Warrington pump water, and into a tumblerful of it he poured part of the contents of the suspicious-looking Phial, which he said was " stuff to discover lime in water." The water immediately assumed a " chalkish " tint. The second bottle, which he said con- tained water that descended from heaven—(" oh, heaven," and laughter)—but had fallen upon a house and gone into a tub. (" Tubby or not tubby," and laughter.) A third bottle was similarly dealt with, and Mr. Diggle, producing cakes of what purported to be lime, en- deavoured to shew that therein lay the reason of bad trade—because Warrington had no water fit for manu- facturing purposes. The not very lucid explanation was constantly interrupted and the speaker again appealed to the reporters to learn if his audience was worth addres- sing. (Cries of "Give us a song, William" and " General Booth.")—Mr. Diggle: I've generalled thy money out o, thi pocket. (Laughter.)—The chairman said that the' object of the meeting was--(a voice : "Imposition "and laughter)—to consider the desirability of contributing a rate towards the promotion of the Ship Canal scheme, and he asked Mr. Diggle to proceed to that subject.—Mr. Dig- gle : "Why has not Warrington made more progress " ? ("Just so, Diggle" and "why.") That is the first on the programme, and if you will not allow me to show that I'll shut up. I'll have a meeting and charge a shilling. (Lauah- ter.) Am I to go on with this important question—(a voice: "Have a jujube, William")—l think there's a bit of Jew about thee. (Laughter and a voice : "Throw it from thi chest.") It appears to me that you do not want to know anything about trade in Warrington and I'll leave that question (A voice : "Unfold thi bosom, William," and laughter.) If you don't get pure water there will be no more mills here. ("No more, Diggle?" and disorder.) I think I"l turn round and talk to the wall. (Laughter.) Mr. Diggle proceeded to severely condemn the pollutioe of the Mersey by Manchester filth. He was born on the banks of the river. ("Shame !" and laughter.) He proceeded to advocate the purchase of the waterworks, when Mr. W. Roberts ascended the platform and informed .the audience that up to that time Mr. Diggle had obtained their money by false pretences ars, he thought, it was generally under- stood that he would give his reasons for opposing the pro- posed Ship Canal rate, a subject he had not yet mentioned. —Mr. Diggle. pointing to his placard, said he had not men- tioned the rate. H 3 condemned the Ship Canal scheme as a speculative one and asked how they would like a private firm to make a similar demand upon their pockets. He in- stanced the Hull and Barnsley Railway Dock Scheme as having been a failure, but was prevented from' a full ex- planation of his views by constant interruptions. If the promoters of the Ship Canal scheme got the £l,OOO they would come and say "We are in a bole again "—(laughter) --aa did a neutral editor not a thousana miles from War- rington, who had got £l,OOO in and wanted others to help him out. They had got the greatest sheet of a newspaper in the country and the windiest editor he kaew of, and they had also a baby Guardian but it had got the "ricketts " and had never thrived. eLaughter.) If the promoters of the scheme could not get money for preliminary ex- penses how could they raise money to carry the affair out? Mr. Diggle now changed his subject and spoke of the sewage at Longford, bat returned to the Ship Canal ques- tion, asserting that the recent meeting was an illegal one as a great many non-ratagpayers held up their hands in favour of the rate. Ultimately, amidst disorder, he proposed "That all ratepayers and property-owners in Warrington decline to pay the rate of 2d in the £ for he assistance of the promotion of the Ship Canal."—The

his voting paper in its favour. Will you allow me through the medium of your next issue to assure all concerned that anybody who tells them that the leading manufacturers have e ithdrawn their oppo- sition to the rate says what is not true. The opponents to the rate—who include all the men who are likeliest to know and to sapport what will benefit Warrington; who have done more in the past, and are doing more now than all other men in it to create and sustain and develope its Indus- tries; and whose enterprise has given it its standing and reputation as a commercial centre—are not the men to offer an unwarrantable or vexatious opposition to any sensible and sound scheme for the promotion of the interests of Warrington by the cheapening of carrying between it and Liverpool and Manchester, or by any other means, nor are they, the men who, having put their • hands to the plough (in this instance the plough of opposition to a rate which has not been justified, which cannot be justified, and which it is admitted by its public supporters in Warrington is without a precedent) are likely to look back. And who are the supporters in Warrington of the pro- posed rate? With scarcely an exception, they are men who have done little, if anything, for Warrington ; who have at the best an ieconsiderable stake in the town, and without an exception they are men who do not profess to have the technical knowledge which is requisite to enable them to judge of the merits and prospects of such an un- dertaking as the proposed Ship Canal. On the vital point as to whether the Borough Funds Act empowers such a rate as they propose to be levied, they dare not speak, and in respect of the illegitimate and dangerous invasion of in- dividual liberty by the unheard of proposal to force unwil- ling parties to find funds for the promotion of a work which these parties think and with every reason will never be consummated, they coolly admit there is no precedent, and as coolly suggest that Warring- ton can make the necessary precedent. The Town Clerk of Ashton has just advised the Council of that town that a rate cannot legally be laid in promotion of the canal; the Manchester Corporation have just been called upon by the Local Government Board to justify their proposal to levy such a rate; and the Warrington Corporation will shortly have the same ordeal to face. I will not anticipate the result. In the meantime, the poll is to be taken. Does anyone in Warrington believe that the canal will ever be made; that the necessary walla can be had without the expenditure of millions over and above the proposed capital outlay on the canal; or that in view of such consideration the capital will ever be raised ? If so, let him come forward and give reasons for the faith that is in him; if not, then (knowing the £l,OOO proposed to be contributed by rate will be lost if the capital is no traised) let him joie with those who believe that the end does not always justify the means, and who horn higher motives are determined to oppose the levying of the rate by every means In their power.—l am, yours, &c.. LIBRA.

resolution was seconded by a person in the audience, who 1 gave the name of "Sam Blank."—Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS proposed as an amendment," That this meeting approves of the levying of a 2d rate in support of the Ship Canal, and expresses the hope that the ratepayers will ratify it by a large majority." WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ELECTION OF MAYOR. A. meeting of this Council was held on Monday for the purpose of electing a Mayor for the ensuing year, the ap- pointment of committees, and the transaction of other buei- ness. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, Davies, Thewlis, Webster ; Councillors Broadbent, Platt, Roberts, Ridgway, Ashton, Barker, Bolton Brown, Burgess, Dixon, Francomb, Fleming, Hutchinson, Litton, Mackie, Marsh, John Pierpoinr, Wm. Pierpoint, Sutton, Taylor, Tinsley, Whittle, and Wright; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), and Longdin (surveyor.) There was a larger attendance of the public than is usual at Council meetings. ELECTION OF 015.1011. The Tower CLERK read the return of Councillors elected on the let November, after which The MAYOR said the next business would be the election of Mayor, and he asked that some one might be appointed in his place. Alderman HOLMES said that following up a practice which had been adopted by the members of that Council for a great number of years a meeting of the members of the Corporation was held in that hall on the previous Fri- day evening, and it was concluded with entire unanimity that the Council should proceed to ask the Mayor to return to the office which he had so well and so graciously filled during the year which had just closed. He had therefore much pleasure in asking him to accept the appointment for another year. He might see' that the Mayor's presence on all public occasions and his attendance at the meetings over which he had been called upon to presid,ss had been very gratifying, and he (Alderman Holmes) was sure that all of them looked back with very great pleasure to the manner in which lie had endeavoured to carry on the proceedings in that Council ; and the great affability and urbanity which he bad displayed to all the members of the Corporation with whom be had been brought in contact had been greatly appreciated by all. He then formally moved that Alderman Harrison be re-elected Mayor. (Applause.) Alderman WEBS TER seconded the nomination. The pro- posal, bethought, needed very few words of recommenda- tion from him or anyone else, for they had had the Mayor's conduct for the past 12 months before them, and that was quite sufficient to warrant them in asking him to continue in office for another year. He need not tell the Mayor the personal esteem he had for him. That of itself went for nothing on an occasion like that ; but he could only again say that he had great pleasure in seconding the nomination of his friend, Alderman Holmes, and to express a hope that the ensuing year would be as agreeable to him (the Mayor) as the past had been, and that he would have no cause to regret having decided to remain in that office for another year. (Hear, bear.) Councillor Surrox supported the nomination. Alderman DAVIES, in also suPporting the nomination, said they were called upon at that meeting to consider as to what was to the best interests of the town. (Hear, hear.) He believed that the desirability of re-electing a Mayor at that stage of the history of the Council of this borough was very great. Because be was bound to say, indeed all of them knew, that matters of the vastest importance as affecting that borough would come before that Corporation during the present year, and therefore it was very necessary that one WIG) was well in the saddle—he didn't want to play upon the word Mayor—(laughter)—should be able to continue in office, after fortifying himself in the position he oc- cupied rather than that a new man should take his place. He was bound to think that the Mayor, having had the ex- perience of the pest year, would be able to steer through the many difficulties he saw in the coming year. (Hear, hear.) Alderman THEWLIS having complimented the Mayor on the manner in which he had conducted the business of the Council, Alderman ilimagas put the resolution that the Mayor be re-elected to the Council. The resolution was carried unanimously, and, after having subscribed to the usual oaths, The Mayon thanked the Council for having a second time reposed their confidence, in him by electing him to the honourable office of Mayor of this good old town. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they would not deem it to be ungracioue of him if he said that, instead of being the recipient of the honour himself, he had simply been there in his place par- ticipating in conferring it upon some other member of the Council, of whom there were several who could discharge with undoubted ability the honours, the duties and the responsibilities of the office with grace and dignity—if such had been the case he could assure them he should have left that Council after witnessing the proceedings with feelings ;of unalloyed pleasure and satisfaction. However, it had I pleased them to do otherwise. They had been pleased to ask I him to take it again and had brought some considerable pressure to bear on him. He hoped he should be able to discharge the duties to their satisfaction, and he would en- deavour to deserve that success which it was not in mortals necessarily to command. (Applause.) APPOINTMENT OF MAYOR'S CHAPLAIN. The MAYOR said he begged to appoint the Rev. W. Que- kett, rector of Warrington, as chaplain for the year. THE MEETINGS. The MAYOR moved that three quarterly meetings of the Council be held on the first Tuesday in February, May, and August next at six o'clock in tha evening, Councillor BROADBENT moved that the meetings be held at four o'clock in the afternoon instead of tfix o'clock in the evening. He thought that owing to the meetings being held at six o'clock a good deal of the business was often hurried over as members wished to get away—(hear, hear) and he also thought that the change would be convenient for several members of the Council. Councillor FLEMING seconded the amendment, which was opposed by Councillors SUTTON and BURGESS. Alderman DAVIES believed that all married men would vote for six o'clock, and as there was a majority of married men in the Council he was inclined to think they would carry the motion. (Laughter.) If the meetings were held I at four o'clock their wives would naturally expect them to I go home at a reasonable time; when the Council met at six o'clock there was a very reasonable excuse for going home late. Therefore he should support six o'clock on those grounds. (Laughter and applause.) Alderman Thewlis supported, and Councillor Platt and Alderman Burgess opposed the amendment. Councillor BROADBENT mid he should have been tempted to withdraw his amendment, but that their weak-kneed I brethren like Alderman Davies—(laughter)—might fall into I temptation—(laughter)—and he should be sorry if some ' gentleman like Alderman Davies would not go straight home, but spend the midnight hours somewhere where it would be better not to go. (Loud laughter.) A MEMBER: You don't speak from experience, I hope. Alderman DAVIES : He knows all about it. (Laughter.) The MAYOR having expressed an opinion in support of the motion, the amendment was put, when there voted for it :—Aldermen Thewlis, Councillors Broadbent, Mackie, W. Pierpoint, and Fleming. All the rest voted against it, and the original motion was carried. The monthly meetings were fixed to take place as hereto- fore, viz., six o'clock in the evening on the first Tuesday in each month.

div.head: CONTRAST.
div.p: A CONTRAST.

Sir,—l am led to ada-re;W:f-e;;o-ids to you on the posi- tion taken up by two gentlemen well-known to Warringto- nians. The Rev. G. S. Heaney, in the current issue of " To. Day," takes up the position of Christian Socialist, and in an able paper tries in a very earnest fashion to solve the "Bitter Cry" problem. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, at the recently held Liverpool Diocesan Conference, launched forth a series of most unjustifiable charges against what he was pleased to call the "dominating class." Ties positions assumed by the two rev, gentlemen might well form a study. The one represents all that is offensive in the Church Hier- archy. With a mind of the narrowest and most intolerant kind, he would, by fair means, or fool, make us all subject to his obsolete and worn-out "Dozy." Speaking at Liver- pool, he advised his listeners to beware of "exaggeration" when speaking of " modern forms of unbelief." That "their danger did not arise from philosophical scepticism, and that we lived in times singularly free from assaults upon Christian religion." When I read this I thought of the fable of the ostrich. Does Mr. Carleton, then, hide his bead in the time of danger and advise his friends to do likewise? He knows as well as Ido that he can scarcely enter a gentleman's drawing-room without seeing on the table books of a decided Freethought tendency, written by men who have not:only thrown off tha trammels with which his church surrounded them, but who are determined, to the best of their ability, to help the people to throw them off. He may take some comfort from the fact that "Supernatural Religion" was published "anonymously," but the real, the underlying, reason for this was self-protection. He may scoff at this reason, but all Freethinkers know what Mr. Carleton does not know, viz, what the history of the past teaches. There is no need now for martyrs ; the ball is set rolling, and it will certainly roll over him, and through his church, unless they clear out. As in religious, so in politicil matters; he would fetter the mind and limit it to pabulum that would "spread sound and accurate information upon church matters." Let him accept this statement, that most sceptics could teach him not only a few lessons on church matters, but what is of vastly more importance—how to speak respectfully of his fellow-men.

In the rev. gentleman's speech I find two or three state- ments positively insulting to working-men. First: "A peculiarity of a certain section of working-men was to delight in doing what might shock their more decent neighbours." How dreadful this, that a section of work- ing-men should shockltheir decent neighbours. But what section is referred to? Certainly not an Atheistical sec- tion, because "there is but one really professed Atheist in Warrington." Nay, question the section referred to, and they will repudiate " the idea that they are Atheists." Our rev, friend having rope enough makes good use of it before he finishes. The fact is, he sees no difference between Atheism and Liberalism. After the above sensible remarks, he adds another equally lucid and brimming over with truthfulness. "Some political leaders thoroughly under- stood this habit of the working classes, and traded upon it in order to get up those barbarous productions of the 19th century, namely, demonstrations against the institutions of the country." Our rev, friend here evidently refers to the demonstrations recently held by the people in support of Mr. Gladstooe ; they are "barbarous," ergo, the people are barbarians. I thank thee, priest. for teaching me this word; and, if I can do anything towards keeping its memory green it shall be done. One more word, and I have done with this filibustering pilot of the sky. "He admitted they might find a vendor of Atheistical pullications skulking in some back street." Yes; this is partly true. You buy the twelve and sixpenny "Supernatural Religion" at the big shop in Sankey-street; a carriage brings the purchaser to the shop door, and no reference is made to Atheistical literature; but the twopenny trash has to be bought and sold under the dread of the landlord's displeasure. Mr. Carleton's special forte is truthfulness. "An Inde- pendent minister," Mr. Samuel Pearson, is charged with ignorance of Church matters because he told his hearers "that at the time of the Reformation the property of the Church of Rome was taken away and given to the Church of England." In this case a mistake only is made as to where the ignorance is. Should Mr. Carleton study Church history afresh he will know better where to locate it. But let us leave this ecclesiastical drummer, and get to a more congenial theme.

The Rev. G. S. Reaney in " To-Day " resumes the "Bitter Cry" question. At various times the question has been raised, should the parsons take an interest in politics? Should they take an active part? I should most emphati- cally answer yes, for in that direction lies their only pos- sible chance of doing good. I have had occasion before this to draw attention to the work Mr. Reaney was d oing amongst the poor of London, and for his speeches delivered at the meetings of the Congregational Union I tender him my thanks. Writing "against a narrow creed and a narrow life," he allows the manly part of his nature to protest against a resolution that meant nothing more than shelving the question that, to him, lay at the root of all our social misery. To pass a resolution embodying nothing more than entering "into prayerful counsel with one another" did not meet the difficulty. Mr. Reanev at once moved that the words, "to assist as far as possible the endeavours of thousands of the poor to obtain fairer wages and shorter hours of work." Thousands of working-men will thank Mr. Reaney should he be successful in his efforts to benefit their poorer fellows. Mr. Green, of Ashton-under-Lyne, "a born wit," was selected to deal out the "dismal science." The consequence is not until May, 1885, will the subject of "Horrible London" be dealt with by the members of the Congregational Union. To those who care to give time and serious thought to the labour question, it must be very ap- parent that we are now at the parting of the ways, and in the article to which lam referring Mr. Reaney makes it quite clear that a dual life is not possible to the Christian. "To make money under the laws of political economy, and spend it upon the lines of Christian principle." receives none of his support. Verily the Socialists may be proud of their convert. Mr. J. G. Rogers, a name well known amongst Congregationalists, insists upon the inevitable char- acter of the laws of political economy. "But in season and out of season Mr. Reanev will push the poor to the front. May success attend his efforts to better their condition." I am afraid he will find that if he becomes too persistent he will become a bore to his friends. In that case I recom- mend him to seek the Hall of Science; there he will find colleagues. Speaking of the land question, he says," Reform the land lawsby all means, and give thelard to the men who work it," and that it is quite clear that the "cause of the poor being underpaid and overworked is to be found in the depleted English villages." Strange that these things should only jest be perceived by these leisured and well-educated men. Is it that they perceive when almost too late that we mast arouse " A public opinion beneath which no Christian man shall be able to live and make a million of money out of the very life of the poor." Well may Mr. Reaney wince when told at the city Temple—"lt is the well-to-do who entertain us, give us money, and pay for our sermons, and subscribe to our chanaies." Well may hie self-respect be shocked when he has to confess, as he does, that the "masses " still "curse the parsons ;" and allow me to tell him with all respect that the feeling is spreading; that a large and useless army of so-called teachers are being sup- ported out of the bard earnings of the poet, and they see no return. With him they kuow too well that" the gentleman with the black cost' is honoured amongst the parsons, and that the rich man is canonised." The Carletens that swarm o'er the land must be swept away; they are eating into the very vitals of the poor.
CAPTAIN CUTTLE.

ORANGE MEETING AT WARRINGTON. The Warrington Lodge of toe Loyal Orange Institution of England held a soiree on Monday evening, in the large lecture room of the new Conservative Club, in aid of the district benevolent fund. The room was decorated with flags and bannerettes, and in addition to various Conserva- tive mottoes that adorned the walls a banner was placed in the recess at the back of the platform, the centre-piece of which was a representation of William 111, mounted, his horse standing between two trees, on one of which appeared the words "Boyne—Enniskillen," and on the other" Derry —Aughrirn "; surmounting the representation were the words " Loyal Orange Institution of England, True Blue Lodge 359, Warrington." On one side of the room was placed the motto " The Earl of Enniskillen. Our Imperial Grand Master. Viscount Crichton, M.P., our D.G.M." and 'opposite it the one "The Protestant religion and the liber- ties of the people I will maintain." Mr. W. Bloomfield, D.W.D.M., occupied the chair, and amongst those on the platform were the Rev. G. Carson, deputy grand chaplain of England, Messrs W. Touchstone, Grand Secretary of England, J. Egan, Deputy Prov. Grand Master, H. Thomas, Prov. Grand Secretary; Lang, Prov. Grand Treasurer; J. Roberts, J. Mather, W. It Arnold, W. F. Arnott, T. Egan, junior, J. Dobb, and Parker. Letters of apology for absence were read from Sir Gilbert Greenall, Sir A. B. Wal- ker, and others. After a few introductory remarks by the Chairman Mr. TOUCHSTONE rose to move the first resolution. It was :—"That this meeting is of opinion that the home policy of the present Government is deserving of the gravest censure; because, neglecting the trade interests of the country, it ha gone out of its way (as witness the cases of Lord Rossmore and the Parnellites) to discourage and in- timidate the loyal, while truckling to disloyalty, sedition mongers, and conspirators for the disintegration of our em- pire. This meeting further desires to express its confidence in the loyalty and devotion of the House of Lords to the bast interests of our gracious Queen and religion, and the people of this country." They were, he said, met at a period when their anniversaries were deeply interesting, but the sth of November was the real anniversary day ; the date was changed, however' to suit the convenience of lo- calities. Having traced the history and failure of the plot of the "fifth," and also referred to the landing of the Prince of Orange, Mr. Touchstone said that when James II was fairly seated on his throne he ceased to act on constitutional grounds, and did everything that a king could do to ruin his country. He did precisely what was being done by the Government of Mr. Gladstone to-day. He tampered with the army, removed officers who were known to be trusty to the constitntion, and put creatures of his own in their stead. He removed the magistracy precisely as the Gladstone Government removed Lord Rossmore and others (cheers) —and in every way possible did that which would ultimately have been destructive to the protestant liberties of tbe country. Speaking to the resolution, Mr. Touchstone said that in 1879 and 1880, Mr. Gladstone and others blamed the late Lord Beaconsfield and his Govern- ment for the state of trade that then existed. Before the Tory Government came into office in 1874 trade had begun to decline, and during the time it was in office there were many sources whence bad trade must of necessity arise, bad harvests, famines in India, changes in the silver currency, and the lending of money for speculative purposes on the Continent. Another reason of the bad trade was what was called free trade, which they never had had and had not got at present. When England was so taxed by other nations, she ehouldltake care to keep what markets she had open. The late Lord Beconsfield's Government never allowed a market to be closed if it had the power to keen .it open, but the present Government had deliberately closed some of the markets. Mr. Touchstone, in conclusion, dealt with the question of reform. Mr. Tames seconded the resolution. Mr. EGAN supported the resoltttion, and said that in Ire- land, under the boycotting system, the Government were powerless until the loyal Orangemen said that the thing must go no further. By their exertions that system was now almost stamped out. The Gladstone Government de- served no credit for that. At the first opportunity their loyalty had been snubbed, and it was, he said, their duty as faithful and loyal subjects to do all in their power to get rid of the present Government, and return a patriotic one worthy of the name of England. (Applattee.) The resolution was carried unanimously. The Rev J. Ceatecne proposed "That this meeting of loyal Orangemen disapproves of the foreign policy of Mr. Glad- stone's Government, and is of °pintos that it has brought humiliation and disaster to this country, and its brave and loyal defenders." The British lion had now, he remarked. degenerated into a cur, and foreign countries could now tread—not upon the lion's tail, because it was between its legs and they could not get at it—but upon its toes, and might heat it also, for the poor brute bad not the power to defend itself. The foreign policy of the Government had raised the blush of shame upon the face of every true Eng- lishman. Mr. W. ARNOLD seconded the resolution, which was also carried unanimously. Mr. HAWTHORNR proposed, and Mr. LANG seconded, the third resolution, which was carried. It was—' That the best thanks of the Orange brethren be given to the direc- tors of the new Conservative Club for their kindness in allowing them to hold their anniversary in the lecture room belonging to the club." A hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman closed the busi- ness Dart of the proceedings, and dancing was afterwards indulged in until an early hour next morning, the music beisg supplied bye band under the conductorship of Mr. Randall.

TEN BIRTH AND DZATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday, November Bth, 1884.—The mean temperature was 448 Fahrenheit, and therefore a little warmer than the preceding week. The maximum temperature, 61 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 2nd inst., and the minimum temperature, 28 Fahrenheit, en the 3rd di 4th insts. The rainfall measured 1.00 inches. The general direction of the wind was westerly. During the week, which was the 45th of the current year, 36 births and 28 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 303 per 1,000, against 23.8 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 21.2 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 3 from measles, 4 from diarrhoea 2 from hydrocephalus, 4 from brain disease, 1 from heart disease, 6 from lung disease, and 1 from kidney disease. One case of scarlatina was reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament. —Rum H. GoRNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

Cumons AFFILIATION CASE—At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday, Mr. J. C. Sutton on be- half of the Board of Guardians and Jane Isabel Miles, applied for an affiliation order against a young NUN named Joseph Hill, a fitter, alleged by Miles to be the father of her illegitimate child.—Mr. Percy Davies, who defended, objected to the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), who was on the Bench, taking Dart in the case as he was a member of the Board of Guardians.—The Mayor thereupon withdrew. —Mr. Sutton said that as an objection might be raised by Mr. Davies, he Would explain that the applicant Myles some three weeks ago applied in her own name for an information against the defendant, but the summons was refused on the ground that the case had already been tried on its merits. He mentioned this, as he understood that the child was now twelve months old, but that it was not so when she made such application, and he should ask the court to recognise the claim that she then made to lay an information as be- ing still in existence, so that an order could legally be made.—Mr. Davies, in a lengthy speech, submitted that the case was heard upon its merits twelve months ago, and the defendant then produced evidence that caused the magistrates not to make an order. He thought it was monstrous to bring a man before the Court from time to time in that way.—The Clerk (Mr. White): As the parties making the application are the Guardians, I think the case should be beard, but I'll take a note of the objection. I hold that this is a new application.—Mr. Sut- ton then explained the circumstances, remarking that at the first hearing of the case the plaintiff was not legally represented, and was no doubt confused, 80 that she might have omitted to give some material evidence. When an . order was made against a man for affiliation he had the right of appeal, but if it was refused the woman could not appeal against the decision, and he contended that the case should be re-tried in common justice to her.—The Bench de- cided to hear the case, and the plaintiff deposed to an engagement between herself and the defendant, and to an improper intimacy after promise of marriage. She also, in the course of a protracted cross-examination, denied having conducted herself improperly with any other person. or having kept company with other persons.—A number of other witnesses were called, and the case occupied the time of the court for several bout-N.—The Bench ultimately made an order of 2s 6d a week, and Mr. Davies gave notice of appeal. The magistrates on the _Bench were gr. J. Mite and Mr.Z. Armitage.

div.head: LATEST NE WS.
div.p: LATEST NE WS.

Shepherd's timber yard at Chiswick caught fire on Thurs- day night. It will prebably burn three days. The Garmoyle breach of promise case will probably be tried next week, perhaps on Tuesday or Wednesday. The strike of revetters at Napier's shipbuilding yard, Govan, Glasgow, terminated on Friday on the submission of the men.
Three men were committed for trial at Oundle, on Friday, for murderously assaulting, an Irishman without provocation.

A bulletin, issued at 6 o'clock last evening, states that Mr. Spencer, M.P., has passed a fair day, and has main- tained his strength. The failure is announced of Messrs. Spartali and Co., 25, Old Broad-street, London, with liabilities between £500,000 and £600,000.
A Lloyd's telegram frem Capetown, says :—The British brigantine City of St. Asaph, of Swansea, has been burnt at sea. The crew were, however, saved.

_ In consequence of the outbreak of cholera in Paris, travel- lers from France are not allowed to land at Jersey until they have undergone medical examination. A Lloyd's telegram from Capetown on Thursday evening says the British brigantine City of St. Asaph, of Swansea, has been burned at sea. The craw were saved. The execution of Edwards, convicted at the Exeter as sizes last week for the murder of his two children at Ply- mouth, has been fixed for the 26th inst. A petition for a reprieve is being signed. It is now definitely settled that the Queen will leave Bal- moral on Wednesday next instead of Friday as previously arranged. Her Majesty will travel over the usual route with as much privacy as possible. HUNTING ACCIDENT.— Mr. Wickham, who was married to Lady Ethel Beata only a month ago was on Friday thrown from his horse on to his head, whilst hunting with the Cottesmore hounds near Peterborough, and sustained very serious injuries. _ _ _

ICIEW RAILWAY —The cutting of the first sod of the pro- jected Barry Dock and Railway, near Cardiff, was per- formed on Friday by Lord Windsor, chairman of the com- pany. The dock, which is to be forty acres in extent, is in- tended mainly for the coal trade.

SHOCKING FATALITY AT A RAILWAY STATION.—Tbe up Manchester express to London, on Friday, killed a porter while passing through Hathem Station, on the Midland Railway. It appears that a porter named Letts ran out of the cloak room to cross the line and fell right in front of the express. His body was carried a considerable distance and terribly mangled. Death must have been instantaneous. It is supposed that the deceased had failed to notice the express approaching. FURTHER NEWS FROM GENERAL GORDON.

The Government have received a despatch from General Gordon, dated August 26th, stating that Khartoum was at that date provisioned for five months, and that he intended sending Colonel Stewart and the French and English Con- sul to the relief of Dong)la after destroying Berber,

Ike House met at four o'clock.

Quasnotss,drc.—Sir G. CAMPBELL gave notice that on Monday he should ask whether it was the intention of the Government to introduce a bill this session to provide for the appointment of Secretary for Scotland to attend to tar. gent Scotch affairs.—Mr. MusrDELLA, replying to Mr. Salt, said it was not legal for Guardians of the Poor to order a parent when making application for payment of school fees to send the child to a board school, the parents net desiring to do so.—Lord EDWALD FITZMAIINICB, replying to Sir G. Campbell, said Sir E. Baring's report on the tentative work- ing of the representative institutions in Egypt would be circulated during the present session if possible. The circular referred lo in the Times stating that the Egyptian Government had determined to collect taxes In arrear, and seize land and crops in default, only referred to the deficien- cies of rieh landowners able to pay,and had had the desired effect. He could not answer the question on Egyptian finance as the whole subject was under consideration.

THE RUMOURED DEATH OF GmeartaL GORDON—Lord FITZMAURICE intimated that a telegram had been received from Sir E. Baring, dated Cairo that day, at ten past two, stating that he had received a telegram from Lord Wolseley's private secretary, at Bongola, affirming that nothing was known of the reported death of General Gordon, and the rumour was generally discredited there. EGYPTIAN AFFAIRS.—SiT S. NORTILCOTE intimated a de- bate on Egyptian aff Aire would be raised, next Monday, on the Chancellor of the Exchequer making his proposals.—ln Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. GrAnsToNg slid he would state some day next week what was to be done with regard to Lord Northbrook's report. CONDITION OF THE CROFTERS.-011 the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. MACFARLANE called attention to the condition of the crofters in the Isle of Skye. He said the poor people deserved the utmost sympathy, as their state was deplorable,without in the slightest justifying their resort to violence. He hoped something would speedily be done in order to satisfy the wretched population of the Islands that their distress was not disregarded. Re- ferring to the habitations of most of the unfortunate people, he said they were such that English gentlemen would not keep their dogs in. He moved a resolution stating that it is the duty of Her Majesty's Government to give effect to the recommendations of the Royal Commissioners upon the condition of the crofters and cottars in the Highlands and islands of Scotland, or to apply such other remedies as they mizht deem advieable.—Mr. MACKINTOSH secon- ded the resolution.—Sir W. HARCOURT expressed his deep sympathy with the sufferings of the crofters, and with respect to the resolution moved it generally had his appro- val. He said it was with deep regret that be bad had to send a force to Skye, but the preservation of peace was of the highest importance, and to have shown weakness on the subject would have been a most dangerous way of dealing with the matter. He pointed out that the military force had not been sent in order enforce notices of removal. He said that the great diffi- culty was that it was not clear that the recommendations met with the approval of the crofters or their friends. As regarded the application of the provisions of the Irish Land Act to Skye, the evils that existed there, he said, were not the same ; therefore the remedy would not be identical. The Government accepted the responsibility of endeavouring to find some adequate remedy for the present state of things, and it was not for the unhappy occurrences at Skye to have taken place to satisfy the Government of the necessity of dealing with the question. He hoped the assurance of res- ponsibility which the Government felt, and of their readi- ness to discharge that responsibility would be accepted, and that it would not be necessary to press the resolution to a division.—Mr. D. CAMERON advised the Government not to confine their efforts to the preparation of a Land Bill, but to consider recommendations of the Royal Commissioners. —Mr. Picrow suggested the introduction of a suspending bill to put a stop to evictions.— Mr. A. BAL- FOUR did not think manipulation of land laws I was the remedy for the existing difficelty. Mr. WHITBREAD thought assistance might be given to voluntary emigration, but, whatever was done, required to be done quickly.—Mr. M. FERGUSON also wished the matter dealt with speedily.—Mr. WANTON complained that the Home Secretary had given countenance ta doctrines antagonistic to the rights of property.—Mr. DICK PHDDIB supported the amendment.—Sir H. MAXWELL, from what had occurred in the South of Scotland, questioned the benefit of 'stereotyping the race of crofters.—Mr. JESSE COLLINGS did net think mach benefit would arise from the debate beyond aiding the agitation now going on both in England and Scotland against the land laws.

ASSAULTING A, SISTER.—A young woman named Margaret Daley was brought before the Warrington Borough Magis- trates, on Wednesday, charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in the Old-road, Latchford, and violently msaulting her sister. On the previous afternoon prisoner got drunk, and when she went home struck her younger sister on the head with a quart can, inflicting a wound which bled pro- fusely. As the sister did not press the charge of assault, prisoner was only fined lOs and costs.

" PRACTISING.'" ON A POLICEMAN. —At the Warrington Borough Police Court. on Thursday, a young man named Wm. Yates, last from Manchester, was charged with assault- ing P.C. Turner, a borough constable.—lt appeared that the constable was in Foundry-street and saw the prisoner lean- ing against a doorway, apparently in a state of intoxica- tion. He requested him to move on, but prisoner said he would not move for a "young puppy" like the constable. Turner asked him what he meant, and gave him a slight push, upon which the prisoner struck him a violent blow. The two then struggled, and Turner was severely handled until the arrival of a second constable.—The Chief Con- stable said that Turner was a young policeman, and the prisoner was a man who was in the habit of "practising " on young policemen who attempted to correct him. The constable was justified in giving him a push, as that some- times induced people to be quiet without their having to he taken into custody. Turner seemed to have been very severely treated.—The prisoner was fined 5s and costs, or even days.

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.—A sitting of this court was held on Thursday, before Mr. W. ttiyanne Ffoulkee, judge. There were no cases of public interest. VIOLENT ROBBERY IN A PCBLIC•HOUSE.—At the Warring- ton Police Court, on Tuesday, three young men named Martin Griffin, William Mulcairn, and Thomas Farrell, described as forge labourers, were charged with having stolen a purse containing 4s 6.1 from the person of Lucy Barlow, a charwoman—lt appeared that on Monday after' noon the prisoners went into the Old Crow public-house. Fennel-street, in company with another man, who, however, left before the robbery took place. They there partook of a quart of beer, and after they had been in a short time Lucy Barlow came in for a glass of beer. She took out her purse, containing 4s 6i, to pay for it, when Mulcairn seized held of the purse anti the others held her till he took it from her. The landlady, Mrs. Bell, beard the scufre, and went to the room where the prison,rs and prosecutrix were, and on learning what had taken place, said she would not let prisoners out till they returned the purse and money, Mal- caira and Griffin, wha were also charged with assaulting Mrs. Bell, however, pushed her roughly aside, and left the house. Information had in the meantime been sent to th! police, and tney were apprehended. It was further stated that prior to this robbery and assault Mulcairn had asked 3 man who was in the public-house to lend him his knife, and had then refused t) give it back.—The Chairman (Mr. Broadbent) said the Bench was of opinion that all the pre. soners were guilty, as they bad all taken part in a cowardly and dastardly robbery; and that Mulcairn and Griffin were also guilty of haying assaulted the landlady, who had be- haved with very great spirit and proper feeling. The evi- dence, however, against Farrell was not as clear as against the other two, and therefore Griffin and Mulcairn would have to be committed to gaol for three mouths' hard labours and Farrell for two months.

IN PA.IILIAMENT. SESSION 1885. RUNCORN GAS. (Additional Capital, Application of Funds, Consolidation of Capital, Additional Lands, Construction of New and Maintenance of Old Works. Manufacture and Storage of Gas and Residuals on old and new sites, Limits of Sup- ply. Sale of Lands. Breaking up of Streets, Supply of Gas Meters, Stoves. Price of Gas and Dividends, Sliding Scale. Purity, Quality, and Pressure of Gas, Public Lighting, New Provisions respecting Regulation of Company, Rates, Rents, and Charges, Patent Rights, Incorporation and Amendment of Acts.) NOTIOE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that application is in- tended to be made to Parliament in the ensuing year, by the Runeorn Gas Company (hereinafter called "the Com- pany "), for leave to bring in a Bill (hereinafter called "the Bill ") for all or some of the following amongst other per- poses, that is to say, To authorize the Company to raise, for the purposes of the Bill and the general purposes of their undertaking, additional capital by the creation and issue of new ordinary and prefer- ence shares and stock, mei by borrowing and by the creation and issue of debenture stock, or by any of such methods, and to attach to any such shares. stocks, or loans any pre- ference or priority of dividend or Interest, and to apply to the 'purposes aforesaid any capital, funds, or money now belonging to or authorized to be raised or borrowed by the Company, end to consolidete and arrange the shares and stocks l of the Company. To authorize the Company to purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire by agreement, and to hold and use for the purposes of their undertaking, and in addition to the lands which they are empowered to purchase and hold by the Runcorn Gas Act, 1847 1 (hereinafter called "the Act of 1847 "), the following lands (that is to say) : ; First. Apiece of land, containing 4 acres 19 perches or there- 'shouts, known as Culvert Meadow, situate in the township of Runcorn, in the parish of Runoorn, in the County of Chester, and lying on the south side of and adjoining the Bridgewater. Canal, and bounded on the north or nerth west side thereof by the said canal and property belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited; on the west side thereof by property belonging, or reputed to belong, to the trustees of the Duke of Bridgewater; on the south side thereof by the public highway known as the Halton-road, leading from Runcorn to Warrington ; and on the east side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the execu- tors of the late William Henry ockleaton. Secondly. A piece of land containing 2 rods and 12 perches or thereabouts, with the building thereon, known as Highfield House, situate in the said toweship of Runcorn, and parish of Runcorn, and county of Chester, and lying on the north side of the said Bridgewater Canal; and bounded on the south aide thereof by the road adjoining the towing path of the said canal, and leading from Canal-street, Runcorn, to Bate's Bridge, Halton; on the west tide thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the trustees of the Duke of Bridge- water; and on the north and east sides thereof by land belong- ing, or reputed to belong, to the trustees of Mrs. Eliza Ann Kirkham. And to authorize the Company on those lands, or part or parts thereof, to erect, construct, Make, and maintain, and on the lands hereinafter described as the site of the Company's ,existing gas works, to maintain and continue, and as regards all such lands from time to time extend, enlarge, and Improve gas works, and works for the manufacture, distribu- tion, storage, and supply of gas, and for the manufacture, con- version, utilization, storage. and distribution of materials used in and about the manufacture of gas and of residual products resulting from such manufacture, and to empower the Corn pany on and from all such lands to manufacture, store, and supply gas, and to manufacture, convert, utilize, distribute, and store such materials and residual products as aforesaid, end to extend and make applicable to, and to enable the Com- pany to exercise, in respect of the before-mentioned lands, and of the supply of gas therefrom, all or some of the provi- sions of the Act of 1847 as altered, amended, or enlarged by the Bill. The site of the Company's existing Gas Works consists of the pieces of land hereinafter described, that is to say : First.—A piece of land containing 1,785 square yards or there- abouts, situate in the said township and palish of Runcorn, in the county of Chester, on the east side of Gas-street. and bounded on the westerly side thereof by that street, orr the southerly, or seuth-easterly side thereof by the towing path of the Bridgewater Canal. on the easterly side thereof by a street known as Stonrestreet, and on the northerly side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Marquis of Choi- mondeley Secondly.—A piece of land containing 2,609 square yards, or thereabouts, situate in the said township and parish of Run- corn, on the west side of Gas-street, and bounded on the north side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the said Marquis of Cholmondeley, on the east side thereof by Gas-street, on the south side thereof by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Runcorn Smelting Company, and on the west side-thereof in part by Sutherland-street, and on the remaining parts by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Trusters of the United Methodist Free Church, and by land belonging, or reputed to belong, to the Trustees of the Duke of Bridgewater respectively. To amend or repeal section 7 of the Act of 1847, and to alter and define the limits within wMch the Company may supply gas such limits to include the town of Runcorn, otherwise called Higher and Lower ILuncorn, the township of Runcorn, and the townships or hamlets of Halton, Astmore, otherwise Astrnore-with-Halton, Norton, Weston, Weston Point, and Clifton, otherwise Clifton-with Recksavage, in the County of Chatter, or such of them, or such par:a thereof as may be speci- fied in the Bill. To empower the Company, from time to time, to sell, ex- change, let on lease, or otherwise to dispose of any lands at the time belonging to them, which they may not require for the purposes of their undertaking. To give power to the Company within their limits of supply to lay down, maintain. use, alter, and renew mains, pipes, ar d other conveniences for the distribution, supply, and disposal of gas and residual products, rine to open, break up, and inter- fere witk streets, roads highways, bridges, railways, canals, sewers, drains, and other passages and places. and gas and water, telegraphic, telephonic, and other pipes, wires, and apparatus. TO authorize the Company to manufacture, purchase, hire, sell, let, supply, and deal in, and to fix, alter, remove and refix gas meters, fittings, gas engines, stoves, ranges, pipes, and other appliances and apparatus for lighting, he- ting, motive power, ventilating, cooking. and other purposes for which gas may be used, and to empower the Company to supply gas for any such purposes, and to manufacture, buy, sell, and deal in coal, lime, coke, tar, ammonia-cal liquor, chemicals, and other materials used In or resulting from the manufacture of gas, and to carry on any business usually carried on by a Gas Company. To regulate the price to be charged by the Company for gas, and the rate of dividends which they may divide, and, if thought fit, to provide for the variation of the rate of divi- dends according to the price charged for gas, and to make provision for the maintenance and formation of insurance and reserve funds to meet deficiencies in divetends and accidents, strikes or other extraordinary claims and circum- stances. To make provision with respect to the purity, quality, and pressure of gas to be supplied by the Company, and the testing oi gas and meters, the supply of gas and lamps for public right- ing, and the erection, cleaning, lighting, extinguishing, and repairing of such lamps. To amend or repeal the provisions of the Act of 1847, with respect to the time of ordinary meetings, the scale of voting by ehareholders, the number and quorum of directors, the number of directors to constitute, and the quorum ef com- mittees the holding of proxies, the remuneration of directors, and such other matters relating:to the regulation and manage- ment of the Company as may be dealt with in the Bill e and to make other and further provisions in respect thereto, and to alter and fix the period of the year up to which the annual ac- counts of the Compsny shall be made up. To vary and extinguish any rights and privileges connected with any lands, streets, roads, highways, canals, sewers, chains, pipes, wires, and other apparatus and property to be acquired or interfered w,th by the Company, and any °tear rights and privileges wnich would interfere with the objects and purposes of the Bill, and to confer all such rights and pri- vileges as may be necessary or convenient for effecting such objects and purposes. To authorize the Company to demand, levy, and recover rates, rents, and charges for the supply of gas and other mat- ters and things supplied, and services rendered by them, and to alter rates, rents, and charges, and to confer, vary, or ex- tinguish exemptions from the payment of rates, rents, and charges, and to provide for the allowance of discounts. To authorize the Company to purchase, hold, and use patent rights or licenses for the use of inventions, relative to the manufacture and supply of gas, tmeters, fittings, apparatus, engines, stoves, ranges, pip's, and other apparatus and ap- pliances. Csuncillor SUTTON said he did not see what amendment Councilor Dixon had moved. He had rambled entirely from the subject, which was the appointment of certain gentlemen to form a committee. Councillor DIXON then moved as an amendment that Councillors Platt and Francomb be put on the committee In place of Aldermen Holmes and Pickmere. Thar, he said, would make a radical amendment. (Laughter.) Councillors PLATT and FRANCOMB said that their names had been suggested without their consent, the latter gentle- man remarking that Councillor Dixon 'aught to be put on the committee as he took such an interest in gas, and he rambled all over the country and brought back some valu- able information almost every month. (Laughter.)—There being no seconder to Councillor Dixon's amendment it fell through, and the committee was appointed as proposed. PRESIDING ALDERMEN.
